Modern machine-learning systems produce outputs their designers did not specify in detail and often cannot fully explain, which some take as refuting her objection; others reply that such systems still only transform their inputs and training data according to fixed procedures, exactly as she said, so that any apparent novelty is a recombination rather than true origination. The disagreement turns on deep and unresolved questions about the nature of creativity itself. What is not in doubt is that Ada Lovelace, in a few sentences written in 1843, posed one of the enduring questions of computing, and posed it clearly enough that it is still argued in the same terms she used.

sections.heading: Legacy, Rediscovery, and the Language Ada
sections.body:
For a long time after her death in 1852, Ada Lovelace was little known for her scientific work. The Analytical Engine was never built, Babbage's reputation faded, and the Notes lay largely unread outside a small circle. Ada herself was remembered mainly as the daughter of Lord Byron, a footnote in literary rather than scientific history. The thread of her ideas ran underground for the best part of a century, until the development of actual computers in the 1940s and the subsequent writing of the history of the field brought the nineteenth-century engines, and the Notes that described them, back into view.

The rediscovery gathered pace in the mid-twentieth century. In 1953 Ada's Notes were reprinted with commentary by B. V. Bowden in a book on the emerging science of computing, presenting her exposition to a new audience that could now see the machines she had written about coming into existence. As historians reconstructed Babbage's work, the significance of the Analytical Engine as a conceptual ancestor of the computer became clear, and with it the significance of Ada's account, which remained the clearest contemporary explanation of the machine's general nature. Her reputation grew alongside the field she had helped to imagine.

A conspicuous marker of that renewed standing came in 1980, when the United States Department of Defense named a newly developed programming language Ada in her honour. The language, still used in aviation, defence, and other systems where reliability is paramount, carries her name as a deliberate tribute to her role as the writer of the first algorithm for a computer. Fittingly, the military standard that defined the language was numbered 1815, the year of her birth. Beyond the language, her name has been attached to medals, buildings, and initiatives, and Ada Lovelace Day, observed each October, celebrates the achievements of women in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.

Her legacy is thus twofold, technical and symbolic, and both aspects deserve care. Technically, she is honoured as the author of the first published program and as an early prophet of general-purpose computing, a place in the history of the field that the evidence supports. Symbolically, she has become an emblem of women's capacity for scientific and mathematical achievement at a time when both were systematically discouraged, and a rallying figure for efforts to broaden participation in computing. The symbolic role sometimes tempts admirers to overstate the technical one, which is why the historical record should be represented accurately: Ada Lovelace earns her place not through legend but through a real and unusual achievement, and telling her story truthfully honours her better than exaggeration would.

sections.heading: Separating Myth from Documented Fact
sections.body:
Because Ada Lovelace has become a celebrated and symbolic figure, a body of myth has grown around her, and a responsible account must distinguish what the documents support from what has been embroidered. The primary sources are relatively limited and therefore precious: the published 1843 Sketch with her Notes, the extensive correspondence between Ada and Babbage during the Notes' preparation, her letters to her mother and to her tutors such as De Morgan, and Babbage's own later recollections in his autobiography. Against these, many popular claims can be checked, and several common assertions turn out to be exaggerations or inventions.

It is documented that Ada wrote the Notes, that they were far longer than the memoir they accompanied, that they contain the Bernoulli algorithm, and that she worked closely and critically with Babbage on the technical content, at one point correcting a mistake he had sent her. It is documented that she articulated the engine's general, symbol-manipulating nature and the point about music, and that she wrote the passage denying the machine any power to originate. These are the secure foundations of her reputation, and they are substantial. Babbage himself praised her contribution, and the surviving letters show her doing real intellectual work rather than acting as a mere scribe.

Several widespread claims, by contrast, go beyond the evidence. The description of Ada as the first computer programmer is defensible only with the qualifications discussed earlier, since Babbage had written operation sequences before her; the sweeping version of the claim is contested. Stories that she single-handedly conceived the ideas in the Notes, or that she foresaw modern computers in detail, overstate a genuine but bounded achievement. Colourful biographical tales, including exaggerated accounts of a scheme to use mathematics to win at horse racing late in her life, are poorly documented and often embellished. Even her mathematical ability, real and unusual for her circumstances, is sometimes inflated into claims of first-rank professional mathematics that the record does not sustain.

The honest conclusion is that Ada Lovelace's actual achievement is impressive enough that it requires no embellishment, and that embellishment in fact does her a disservice by inviting sceptical overcorrection. She was a gifted and seriously trained mathematician for her time and circumstances, an active collaborator rather than a passive translator, the author of the first published exposition of programming a general-purpose machine, the preparer of the first fully worked algorithm for such a machine, and the possessor of a strikingly clear understanding of what computation fundamentally is. Where the evidence is thin or the division of credit between her and Babbage is unclear, it is more faithful to say so than to resolve the uncertainty in either direction. Presented this way, her story stands on documented fact, which is the firmest ground on which any historical reputation can rest.

guides.title: Alan Turing and the Foundations of Computer Science
guides.summary: An account of Alan Turing's life and of the ideas he founded: the Turing machine, the universal machine and the stored-program computer, undecidability and the halting problem, the codebreaking work at Bletchley Park, the Turing test, and his final work on biological pattern formation.

sections.heading: Who Turing Was and Why the Ideas Still Govern Computing
sections.body: Alan Mathison Turing, born in London on 23 June 1912 and dead by his own apparent hand on 7 June 1954 at forty-one, is the closest thing computer science has to a founder. That claim needs justifying, because machines that calculate long predate him. Blaise Pascal built a mechanical adder in 1642, Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine in the 1830s, and Ada Lovelace wrote in 1843 what is usually counted the first published algorithm intended for a machine. What Turing supplied was not a device but a definition. Before 1936 nobody could say precisely what it means for a procedure to be mechanical, and therefore nobody could prove anything at all about the limits of mechanical procedures as a class. His contribution has four distinct parts, and they are separable. First, he gave a mathematical definition of computation, in the form of an idealised machine of the utmost simplicity, and used it to prove that there are perfectly well-posed mathematical questions no procedure can ever answer. Second, and within the same 1936 paper, he described a universal machine that reads the description of any other machine and imitates it, which is the abstract form of the stored-program computer and the reason a single laptop can be a word processor, a musical instrument and a flight simulator. Third, during the Second World War he led the attack on the German Enigma cipher, designing the machine and the statistical methods that made industrial-scale codebreaking possible. Fourth, after the war he designed a real computer, framed the question of machine intelligence in a form still argued over, and then turned to biology and explained how a chemically uniform embryo can spontaneously develop stripes and spots. Any one of these would secure a reputation. Together they describe a mind that repeatedly identified the deepest available question in a field and answered it from first principles. Turing's characteristic move was to take a vague human notion, being effectively calculable, being intelligent, being patterned, and replace it with something precise enough to reason about. His life ended badly and unjustly. In 1952 he was prosecuted for homosexual acts, then criminal in Britain, accepted chemical castration in place of prison, lost his security clearance, and died two years later of cyanide poisoning. The British government issued a formal apology in 2009 and a royal pardon in 2013. He has since appeared on the fifty-pound note. Understanding what he actually did, rather than the compressed legend, requires following the mathematics, and the mathematics is more approachable than its reputation suggests. It is also worth guarding against the opposite error. Popular retellings sometimes credit Turing personally with building the first computer, with breaking Enigma single-handedly, and with constructing Colossus, none of which is accurate. He worked within remarkable teams, several of his key wartime ideas built directly on Polish work done before the war, and the machine most often confused with his was designed by someone else entirely. The real record is impressive enough without embellishment, and getting the attribution right is part of respecting it.

sections.heading: Cambridge, Hilbert, and the Crisis in the Foundations of Mathematics
sections.body: Turing's early life was conventionally unhappy in the English upper-middle-class way. His father served in the Indian Civil Service, so he and his brother were left with foster families in England. At Sherborne School he was a poor fit, indifferent to classics and obsessive about science; a report complained that if he was to be solely a scientific specialist he was wasting his time at a public school. His closest attachment was to a fellow pupil, Christopher Morcom, who died of bovine tuberculosis in 1930. Biographers generally regard the loss as formative, sharpening a lifelong preoccupation with whether mind is reducible to matter. He went to King's College, Cambridge, in 1931, took a first in mathematics, and was elected a fellow in 1935 at the age of twenty-two on the strength of a dissertation proving a central limit theorem, unaware that it had already been proved by Lindeberg a dozen years earlier. He arrived at the precise moment when the foundations of mathematics were in open crisis. The background matters. In 1900 David Hilbert had set the agenda: mathematics should be placed on a completely secure footing by formalising it as a system of axioms and rules of inference, and that system should be proved consistent, meaning no contradiction can be derived, and complete, meaning every true statement can be proved. To this Hilbert added a third demand in 1928, the Entscheidungsproblem or decision problem: find a definite procedure that, given any statement in first-order logic, determines in finitely many steps whether it is provable. Hilbert expected all three to be delivered, and famously declared that in mathematics there is no ignorabimus, no we shall not know. Kurt Godel destroyed the first two in 1931. His incompleteness theorems showed that any consistent formal system strong enough to express arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency. He achieved this by a device of extraordinary ingenuity, encoding statements about the system as numbers within the system, so that a sentence could effectively assert its own unprovability. The decision problem survived, and it was different in kind. Godel's results concerned what a formal system can prove; Hilbert's third question concerned what a procedure can decide. Answering it required knowing what a procedure is, and no such definition existed. That was the gap Turing walked into when, listening to Max Newman's lectures in 1935, he heard the problem described as a search for a mechanical process. The phrase mechanical process was doing enormous unexamined work, and Turing appears to have recognised immediately that it was the phrase, rather than the problem, that needed attention first. Solving the decision problem would require first saying, with mathematical exactness, what a mechanical process is, and then proving something about every possible one at once.

sections.heading: The Turing Machine: A Definition of Mechanical Procedure
sections.body: Turing's insight was to analyse not machinery but a human being computing. A person working on paper, he observed, can attend to only finitely many symbols at once, is in one of finitely many states of mind, reads and writes one symbol at a time, and moves attention a limited distance. Stripping this to its skeleton yields a device of almost insulting simplicity, described in his 1936 paper On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem. The machine has an infinite tape divided into cells, each holding one symbol from a finite alphabet, usually including a blank. A head sits over one cell and can read it, write to it, and move one cell left or right. The machine is always in one of a finite number of internal states. Its entire behaviour is fixed by a transition table: for each combination of current state and symbol read, the table specifies the symbol to write, the direction to move, and the next state. That is the whole apparatus. There is no memory beyond the tape, no arithmetic built in, no randomness. The infinite tape is an idealisation worth being precise about. It does not mean infinite memory is available at any moment; it means the machine never runs out, so that limits proved about it are limits of the method rather than of the hardware. To see the mechanism concretely, consider a machine that adds one to a binary number written on the tape, with the head starting at the leftmost digit.
steps: Begin in state SEEK with the head on the leftmost digit of the number.
In state SEEK, if the symbol read is 0 or 1, write it back unchanged, move one cell right, and stay in state SEEK. This walks the head rightward without altering anything.
In state SEEK, if the symbol read is blank, the end of the number has been passed. Move one cell left and switch to state CARRY. The head now rests on the least significant digit.
In state CARRY, if the symbol read is 0, write 1, and switch to state DONE. The addition is complete because no carry propagates past a zero.
In state CARRY, if the symbol read is 1, write 0, move one cell left, and remain in state CARRY. This propagates the carry leftward through a run of ones.
In state CARRY, if the symbol read is blank, the carry has run off the front of the number, as when 111 becomes 1000. Write 1 and switch to state DONE.
In state DONE, halt. The tape now holds the incremented number.

To verify by hand, write 1011 on paper and trace the rules: SEEK walks right past 1, 0, 1, 1 to the blank, steps back onto the final 1, then CARRY turns that 1 to 0, the next 1 to 0, meets 0 and writes 1, giving 1100, which is eleven plus one.

sections.heading: The Universal Machine and the Stored-Program Idea
sections.body: Having defined a machine for each computable task, Turing took the step that turned an exercise in logic into the blueprint for an industry. He observed that the transition table of any machine is itself a finite body of information, and can therefore be written down as a string of symbols. If it can be written down, it can be written on a tape. And if it can be written on a tape, another machine can read it. He then constructed the universal machine: a single fixed transition table which, given on its tape both a description of some machine M and an input for M, simulates M's behaviour step by step and produces exactly the output M would have produced. The universal machine does this by keeping track of M's current state and head position in a designated region of tape, repeatedly looking up the appropriate line of M's encoded table, and carrying out whatever that line prescribes. One machine imitates all machines. The consequence is the distinction between hardware and software, and it is difficult to overstate how radical this was in 1936. Every calculating device before it was built for a purpose: Babbage's Difference Engine computed polynomial tables, a cash register added money, a bombsight solved a ballistics problem. Changing the task meant rebuilding the machine. Turing showed that a single sufficiently general device needs no rebuilding, because the description of the task is just more data. A program is not a modification of the machine but an input to it. Everything in modern computing follows from this: interpreters and compilers, operating systems that run arbitrary applications, virtual machines, emulators that let one processor architecture pretend to be another, and the fact that a phone can be a camera, a map and a library without a soldering iron. The idea reached engineering through a specific and somewhat contested route. John von Neumann encountered Turing's paper, and Turing worked near him at Princeton from 1936 to 1938, completing a doctorate under Alonzo Church. Von Neumann's 1945 First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC laid out the architecture in which instructions and data share one memory, and it circulated widely under his name alone, a fact that has caused eighty years of argument about credit. Several who knew both men, including the physicist Stanley Frankel, recorded von Neumann saying explicitly that the fundamental conception was Turing's. One implication is easy to miss. Because programs are data, programs can operate on programs. Compilers, debuggers, optimisers and self-modifying code are all applications of this, and so, less comfortably, are computer viruses and the general impossibility of perfectly analysing software by other software.

sections.heading: The Halting Problem: Proving That Some Questions Have No Method
sections.body: With computation defined, Turing could ask what no computation can do, and the answer arrived through a self-reference argument closely related to Godel's and to Cantor's older diagonal proof that the real numbers are uncountable. State the question precisely. Given a description of a machine and an input, will that machine eventually halt, or will it run forever? This is not idle: a great many practical questions reduce to it, including whether a program contains an infinite loop, whether an optimiser will terminate, and whether an equation has a solution that a search will find. Turing proved that no machine can answer it for all cases. The proof is a contradiction. Suppose some machine H exists that solves the problem: given the pair consisting of a program P and an input x, H always halts and reports either halts or loops forever, and is always right. Now build a new machine D that takes a single input, a program P. D first runs H on the pair P and P, that is, it asks what P does when fed its own description. If H answers that P halts, then D deliberately enters an infinite loop. If H answers that P runs forever, then D immediately halts. D does the opposite of whatever H predicts. D is easy to construct given H, since it is just H with a small wrapper. Now feed D its own description. If D halts on input D, then H must have reported loops forever, but H is assumed correct, so D does not halt, a contradiction. If D does not halt on input D, then H must have reported halts, and again H was wrong. Either branch is impossible, so the only false assumption is the existence of H. No such machine can exist. This is not a claim about present-day cleverness or computing power. It is a proof that the task is impossible for any procedure whatsoever, forever. From it Turing derived the answer to Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem: no, there is no general decision procedure for first-order logic. Alonzo Church had reached the same conclusion a few months earlier using his lambda calculus, which is why Turing's paper carries a note acknowledging priority, but Turing's argument was found more convincing because his machine made the notion of mechanical procedure visible rather than merely formal. Godel himself, who had been unwilling to accept earlier definitions as capturing the intuitive idea, accepted Turing's. Undecidability turned out to be common. Rice's theorem, proved in 1951, generalises the result: essentially every non-trivial question about what a program does, as opposed to how it is written, is undecidable. This is the theoretical reason no antivirus scanner can be perfect, no compiler can flag every infinite loop, and no automated tool can certify arbitrary software correct. Practical tools cope by being conservative, answering yes, no, or do not know, and by restricting themselves to languages deliberately made less powerful than a full Turing machine, which is exactly why some safety-critical and smart-contract languages forbid unbounded loops on purpose.

sections.heading: The Church-Turing Thesis and the Equivalence of Models
sections.body: A natural suspicion about the halting result is that it might be an artefact of one peculiar machine model. Perhaps a cleverer design, or some future technology, would escape the limit. The answer to this suspicion is the most striking convergence in the history of mathematics. Several people were attacking the same question in the 1930s with entirely different tools. Alonzo Church developed the lambda calculus, a formalism with no machines at all, in which everything is a function and computation is the repeated substitution of arguments into function bodies. Kurt Godel and Jacques Herbrand defined general recursive functions, built up from basic arithmetic operations by composition, primitive recursion and an unbounded search operator. Emil Post described a worker moving between boxes following instructions. Later came register machines, Markov algorithms, cellular automata, tag systems and, in practice, every programming language ever written. All of these were proved equivalent. Anything computable in one is computable in all the others, and the translations between them are explicit and mechanical. That such different starting points, some algebraic, some mechanical, some purely logical, should converge on exactly the same class of computable functions is powerful evidence that the class is natural rather than arbitrary. The claim that this class captures everything that could reasonably be called effectively calculable is the Church-Turing thesis. It is important to be honest about its status. The thesis is not a theorem and cannot be one, because it relates a precise mathematical class to an informal intuitive notion, and one side of that relation is not formalisable. It is an empirical or philosophical claim, and it could in principle be refuted by exhibiting a physically realisable procedure that computes something no Turing machine can. Nothing has come close. Quantum computers are frequently misdescribed on this point: they can solve certain problems dramatically faster, notably integer factorisation via Shor's algorithm in 1994, but they compute exactly the same class of functions and cannot solve the halting problem. Their significance is for efficiency, not computability. A related and much-misused term is Turing completeness. A system is Turing complete if it can simulate any Turing machine, and the bar is surprisingly low. Conway's Game of Life is Turing complete, as are the card game Magic the Gathering under certain rules, the Rule 110 cellular automaton, and, to the irritation of spreadsheet users, Excel formulas with lambda support. This universality is why so few systems are safely analysable and why a simple-looking configuration language can become an unpredictable programming language once it acquires loops and conditionals. A final clarification prevents a common overreach. The thesis concerns what can be computed, not what minds do, and Turing was careful about the difference even while suspecting the two might coincide. Arguments that human thought exceeds mechanical computation, most prominently those of the philosopher John Lucas and the physicist Roger Penrose appealing to Godel's theorem, remain a live minority position, widely criticised but not conclusively settled.

sections.heading: Enigma: How the Machine Worked and Why It Seemed Unbreakable
sections.body: Turing joined the Government Code and Cypher School at Bletchley Park on 4 September 1939, the day after Britain declared war. Understanding what he achieved there requires first understanding the machine he faced. Enigma was an electromechanical cipher device resembling a typewriter. Pressing a key sent current through a plugboard, then through three rotating wheels chosen from a set, then through a reflector, back through the three rotors by a different path, back through the plugboard, and finally to a lampboard where a letter lit up. Each rotor was a disc with twenty-six contacts on each face wired to scramble the alphabet, and the right-hand rotor advanced one position with every keystroke, with the middle and left rotors stepping occasionally like an odometer. The substitution therefore changed for every single letter, defeating the frequency analysis that breaks simple ciphers. The scale of the key space was formidable. Choosing three rotors from five gives sixty orderings; each has twenty-six starting positions, giving 17,576 combinations; ring settings add more; and the plugboard, typically connecting ten pairs of letters, contributes roughly 150 trillion possibilities on its own. The total is often quoted at around 159 million million million. The German authorities considered it unbreakable, and by brute force it was. Two design features were fatal. First, the reflector made the machine self-reciprocal, so that if A enciphered to G then G enciphered to A under the same setting, which was operationally convenient because the same machine both encrypted and decrypted. Second, and decisively, no letter could ever encipher to itself, since current returning through the reflector had to emerge on a different path. That single constraint gives an attacker enormous leverage, because a guessed piece of plaintext can be slid along the ciphertext and instantly rejected at any position where a letter matches itself. Operator practice supplied further weaknesses: repeated stereotyped message openings, weather reports sent at the same time daily, the word Wetter appearing predictably, keys chosen as girlfriends' names or as adjacent keyboard letters, and the retransmission of identical messages on different networks. Crucially, the first breaks were not British. Polish mathematicians at the Biuro Szyfrow, principally Marian Rejewski with Jerzy Rozycki and Henryk Zygalski, reconstructed the internal wiring from 1932 using permutation group theory and built an electromechanical device called the bomba kryptologiczna. In July 1939, weeks before the invasion, they handed everything to British and French intelligence at Pyry near Warsaw. Bletchley began with a working knowledge of the machine that it had not obtained itself, a debt often omitted from popular accounts. Rejewski's original insight deserves stating in its own right: he recovered the internal rotor wiring from traffic alone, using the algebra of permutations, a result the British had considered impossible and which one senior figure later described as achieving what was thought beyond human ingenuity.

sections.heading: The Bombe: Mechanising the Search for Contradictions
sections.body: The Polish bomba exploited a specific German procedural habit, the double encipherment of the message key, and became useless when that procedure changed in May 1940. Turing's insight, developed with Gordon Welchman, was to design a machine that depended on no procedural quirk at all, only on the physical structure of Enigma and on a guessed fragment of plaintext. That fragment is called a crib. Because German messages were formulaic, a codebreaker could often guess with confidence that a particular stretch of ciphertext corresponded to a known phrase, such as KEINE BESONDEREN EREIGNISSE, no special occurrences, or ANX, the German for to preceded by a spacing convention. Aligning the crib with the ciphertext was made easy by the no-letter-encodes-to-itself rule: any alignment producing a coincidence is impossible and is discarded immediately, usually leaving only a few candidate positions. The heart of the method is the logical structure Turing exploited. Write the crib above the ciphertext and draw the implied letter pairings. Frequently these form a closed loop; for example, position one links A to G, position four links G to M, and position seven links M back to A. Such a loop is enormously informative, because it must remain consistent for the true rotor setting whatever the plugboard does. The Bombe was in effect a machine for reasoning by contradiction at high speed. It contained thirty-six sets of rotor assemblies wired to simulate Enigmas at various relative offsets, connected according to the crib's loop structure. An operator would hypothesise a plugboard connection, say that A is steckered to X, and the machine would propagate the electrical consequence around the loop. If the hypothesis led to a contradiction, such as A being simultaneously connected to two different letters, the current spread through the whole network and the setting was rejected, and the drum assembly advanced. Welchman's addition, the diagonal board, exploited the reciprocity of the plugboard to propagate contradictions far more aggressively and increased the machine's power by roughly an order of magnitude. The first Bombe, named Victory, ran in March 1940; the improved version with the diagonal board followed in August. By the end of the war around 210 were operating in Britain, run largely by members of the Women's Royal Naval Service, with more built in the United States. A run took roughly twelve to twenty minutes to test all 17,576 positions for a rotor order, and surviving candidate settings, called stops, were then tested by hand for German plaintext. It is worth being clear about what the Bombe was and was not. It was not a computer. It had no memory, no program and no stored instructions, and it could not be repurposed for any other task; it was a special-purpose logical engine that eliminated impossible hypotheses very quickly. The genuinely programmable machine at Bletchley was Colossus, built for a different cipher, and Turing did not design it.

sections.heading: Naval Enigma, Banburismus and Wartime Bayesian Statistics
sections.body: Naval Enigma was substantially harder than the army and air force variants and mattered most, because the Battle of the Atlantic was a supply war that Britain could lose outright. The Kriegsmarine used eight rotors rather than five, adopted more disciplined operating procedures that starved codebreakers of stereotyped cribs, and in February 1942 introduced a fourth rotor for the U-boat network, called Triton by the Germans and Shark at Bletchley, which multiplied the search space by twenty-six and produced a near-total blackout lasting most of that year. Turing led Hut 8, which handled naval traffic, and his most original contribution there was statistical rather than mechanical. Bombe runs were expensive and scarce, so the priority was reducing the number of rotor orders that needed testing. His method, called Banburismus after the town of Banbury where the perforated sheets were printed, compared two intercepted messages by sliding long punched strips against each other and counting positions where the same letter appeared in both. In genuinely unrelated text such coincidences occur at about one in 26. Because both messages were enciphered by the same machine, matching letters occur more often when the messages are aligned at the correct relative offset, at roughly one in 17, since German plaintext has its own letter frequencies. The excess is small but statistically detectable across long messages. To handle the accumulation of weak evidence rigorously, Turing devised a measure he called the ban, defined as a factor of ten in the odds in favour of a hypothesis, with the deciban as one tenth of a ban and roughly the smallest change in plausibility a human can perceive. Each observed coincidence contributed a certain number of decibans, and the evidence was summed until a threshold was crossed. This is, in modern terms, sequential Bayesian hypothesis testing with log-likelihood ratios, developed independently and years before such methods were established in the open statistical literature. Turing's colleague I. J. Good, later a distinguished statistician, refined the technique and published on it after the war, and the closely related Good-Turing frequency estimator, which estimates the probability of species or words not yet observed, remains standard in computational linguistics and ecology. The Shark blackout was ultimately broken not by pure cryptanalysis but by capture. The seizure of cipher material from U-559 in October 1942, during which two Royal Navy sailors, Tony Fasson and Colin Grazier, drowned recovering documents from the sinking submarine, provided the short weather cipher that gave the cribs needed to re-enter the traffic in December. Cryptanalysis and physical capture were complementary throughout the war, and the codebreakers depended on both. Estimates that the work shortened the war by two to four years and saved many millions of lives are widely repeated but are informed judgements rather than measurements, and historians differ on them.

sections.heading: From Theory to Hardware: the ACE and the Manchester Machines
sections.body: After the war Turing joined the National Physical Laboratory at Teddington, where in late 1945 he produced a detailed design for the Automatic Computing Engine, the ACE. The document is remarkable because it is not a study of principles but a full engineering specification, with circuit-level detail, a memory built from mercury delay lines in which pulses of sound circulate and are refreshed, an instruction format, and estimates of speed and cost. In several respects it was ahead of von Neumann's EDVAC report: it envisaged a faster machine, used a hardware stack for subroutine calls, and treated software as central rather than incidental. Turing anticipated that programming would become the harder half of the discipline and wrote about subroutine libraries and about the machine being able to modify its own instructions. Progress was frustratingly slow, hampered by institutional caution and by the fact that much of Turing's relevant experience was classified and could not be cited. A reduced version, the Pilot ACE, finally ran in May 1950 and proved to be one of the fastest machines in the world at the time. By then Turing had left, moving in 1948 to Manchester University to work with his former lecturer Max Newman. Manchester produced the genuine milestone. The Small-Scale Experimental Machine, universally known as the Baby, ran its first stored program on 21 June 1948, executing a search for the highest proper factor of a number over fifty-two minutes. It is generally recognised as the first electronic stored-program computer to operate, meaning the first physical realisation of the universal machine, with instructions and data held in the same read-write memory. Its store was a Williams-Kilburn tube, a cathode ray tube on whose phosphor bits were held as charge spots, giving 32 words of 32 bits. Turing did not build the Baby, which was the work of Freddie Williams, Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill, but he became deputy director of the computing laboratory and wrote the programmer's handbook for its successor, the Manchester Mark 1. His programming work there was characteristically forward-looking and slightly eccentric. He implemented random number generation, worked on floating-point routines, and used the machine to search for zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Christopher Strachey wrote a draughts program and a love-letter generator on the same machine, and it was made to play simple tunes through its hooter, arguably the first computer music. Turing also wrote what is often counted the first chess program, in 1948, though no machine existed that could run it; he executed it by hand, taking about half an hour per move, in a game against a colleague. The program, called Turochamp, lost, which is unsurprising given that it searched only two moves deep, but it contained the essential ideas of position evaluation and lookahead that all later chess engines use.

sections.heading: The Turing Test and the Question of Machine Intelligence
sections.body: In October 1950 the philosophy journal Mind published Computing Machinery and Intelligence, which opens with the sentence that he proposes to consider the question, can machines think. Turing immediately dismisses the question as too meaningless to deserve discussion, on the grounds that answering it would require agreed definitions of machine and think that do not exist and are unlikely to be produced by argument. He replaces it with something testable. The substitute is the imitation game. A human interrogator communicates by text with two hidden participants, one human and one machine, and attempts to determine which is which. If the interrogator cannot do reliably better than chance, Turing argues, we have no principled reason to withhold the description thinking from the machine. The design deliberately strips away appearance and voice so that only the quality of the responses matters. Turing predicted that by the year 2000 a machine with about 128 megabytes of storage would fool an average interrogator at least thirty per cent of the time in a five-minute conversation, a prediction he presented as a guess. Much of the paper's strength lies in its systematic treatment of objections, which he lists and answers in turn. To the theological objection that thinking requires a soul he replies that this arbitrarily limits divine power. To the mathematical objection from Godel's theorem, that there are truths a machine cannot prove, he replies that humans are also fallible and that no one has shown human reasoning to be free of analogous limits. To Lady Lovelace's objection that a machine can only do what it is told, he replies that machines routinely surprise their programmers and that learning systems need not have their conclusions anticipated. To the argument from consciousness, that a machine cannot know it is thinking, he observes that the same solipsistic doubt applies to other people, whom we credit with minds on behavioural evidence alone. The paper also proposes machine learning explicitly, suggesting that rather than programming an adult mind it would be easier to build a child machine and educate it, using rewards and punishments to shape its behaviour, a description recognisable as reinforcement learning. Criticism has been substantial and deserves airing. John Searle's Chinese Room argument of 1980 contends that manipulating symbols by rule produces no genuine understanding. Others object that the test measures the ability to imitate human conversation, including human ignorance and error, rather than intelligence as such, and that it rewards deception. Modern large language models have made the test far less discriminating than Turing imagined, which arguably confirms his critics rather than his prediction. Systems can now sustain fluent conversation for long periods while lacking capacities Turing would surely have expected to accompany it, which suggests that conversational imitation and general intelligence are more separable than the test assumes. The paper's lasting value lies less in the test itself than in its insistence that vague questions be replaced by operational ones.

sections.heading: Morphogenesis: Explaining How Patterns Form in Living Things
sections.body: Turing's last major work, published in 1952 as The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis, is the least known and among the most original. It asks a question that had troubled biology for centuries: how does an embryo that begins as an almost uniform ball of cells develop structure, and specifically how do stripes, spots, whorls and regular spacings arise when nothing in the initial state marks out where they should be. The intuitive expectation is that pattern must come from a pre-existing template. Turing showed that it need not. Consider two chemicals, which he called morphogens, that diffuse through a tissue and react with one another. Let the first be an activator that promotes both its own production and that of the second, and let the second be an inhibitor that suppresses the first. Crucially, let the inhibitor diffuse faster than the activator. The result is local self-amplification combined with longer-range suppression: wherever a chance fluctuation raises the activator slightly, it builds itself up locally while pushing the inhibitor outward to prevent neighbouring peaks. The uniform state becomes unstable, and the system settles spontaneously into a regular pattern of peaks and troughs whose spacing is set by the ratio of the diffusion rates and the reaction constants. Turing worked this out as a system of coupled partial differential equations and analysed the stability of the uniform solution, showing which combinations of parameters permit patterns to grow. Depending on those parameters and on the geometry of the tissue, the same mechanism yields spots, stripes, or travelling waves. He performed some of the numerical work on the Manchester machine, making this among the earliest uses of a computer for a biological simulation. He also noted the connection to phyllotaxis, the spiral arrangement of leaves and seeds in Fibonacci-related numbers, which occupied him at the end of his life. For decades the theory was admired but unproven, since the morphogens were hypothetical. Experimental vindication came much later. Reaction-diffusion dynamics have since been shown to govern the ridges on the roof of the mouse palate, the spacing of hair follicles and feather buds, the pigment stripes of the zebrafish, the digits of the vertebrate limb, and patterns on marine angelfish that shift as the animal grows in precisely the way the equations predict. The system is now standard in developmental biology and is universally called a Turing pattern. That a mathematician with no laboratory should have deduced the mechanism from first principles, decades before the molecules were identified, is a fitting last demonstration of his method. Honesty requires a qualification: not every biological pattern is a Turing pattern, and developmental biologists continue to debate how much of embryonic patterning is reaction-diffusion and how much comes from positional information supplied by gradients and by direct genetic instruction. The mechanism is real and demonstrated; its scope is still being mapped.

sections.heading: Prosecution, Death, and What the Record Actually Shows
sections.body: In January 1952 Turing's Manchester house was burgled. He reported it to the police, and in the course of the investigation disclosed a sexual relationship with a nineteen-year-old man, Arnold Murray, who was connected to the burglar. Homosexual acts between men were criminal in Britain under the Labouchere Amendment of 1885, the same provision under which Oscar Wilde had been convicted. Turing was charged with gross indecency, and appears to have regarded the law as absurd rather than to have felt shame; he made no attempt to deny the relationship. He was convicted in March 1952 and given a choice between imprisonment and probation conditional on hormone treatment. He chose the latter. The treatment was a synthetic oestrogen, at the time called stilboestrol and now known as diethylstilbestrol, administered for a year to suppress libido. The physical effects included impotence and breast growth. The professional consequences were arguably worse: his security clearance was revoked, ending his consultancy with the codebreaking establishment at a moment of Cold War anxiety about the loyalty of homosexual men, and he was barred from travel to the United States. The state that had depended on him in wartime now treated him as a risk. On 8 June 1954 his housekeeper found him dead in bed. A partly eaten apple lay nearby. The post-mortem found cyanide poisoning, and the inquest recorded suicide, concluding that he had taken the poison while of unsound mind, the standard formula of the period. The circumstances are less certain than the popular account suggests, and it is worth being accurate. The apple was never tested for cyanide. Turing kept a small laboratory in his spare room where he electroplated spoons using potassium cyanide, and he was habitually careless with chemicals, so accidental inhalation or ingestion is possible. His mother maintained this explanation for the rest of her life. Against that, he was known to have discussed suicide methods, and the biographer Andrew Hodges, whose 1983 life remains the standard account, considers suicide the likeliest reading, possibly staged to allow his mother the comfort of doubt. Others, notably Jack Copeland, have argued the accident hypothesis deserves more weight, noting that Turing's mood in the preceding weeks was reported as good and that he had left notes about future work. The honest position is that suicide is probable but not established beyond doubt. Formal redress came late. Gordon Brown issued a government apology in 2009 after a public petition, Queen Elizabeth II granted a posthumous royal pardon in 2013, and the 2017 Policing and Crime Act, informally the Alan Turing law, extended pardons to tens of thousands of other men convicted under the repealed statutes.

sections.heading: The Legacy: Complexity, Cryptography and the Shape of the Discipline
sections.body: The intellectual line from Turing's 1936 paper runs directly into most of theoretical computer science, and the most important development refines his question. Turing asked what can be computed at all. The next generation asked what can be computed efficiently, which turns out to be a far more practical and equally deep question. Complexity theory measures how the resources a computation requires grow with the size of its input. A problem is in class P if some algorithm solves it in time bounded by a polynomial in the input size, such as n squared or n cubed; such problems are considered tractable. A problem is in NP if a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time, even if finding one seems to require searching an exponential space. Factoring a large number, finding a route visiting many cities under a distance limit, and scheduling under constraints are all in NP. Whether P equals NP, that is, whether every problem whose answers are easy to check is also easy to solve, is the central open question of the field and carries a million-dollar Clay Institute prize. Most researchers expect the answer is no, but no proof exists in either direction after more than fifty years. The stakes are practical: if P equalled NP, most deployed cryptography would collapse, since its security rests on certain problems being hard to solve but easy to verify. Stephen Cook and Leonid Levin independently showed around 1971 that certain NP problems are NP-complete, meaning any NP problem can be efficiently transformed into them, so a fast algorithm for one would yield fast algorithms for all. Thousands of problems across scheduling, logistics, biology and design have since been proved NP-complete, which is why practitioners meeting one stop looking for an exact fast method and turn to approximation and heuristics. The vocabulary of the field is Turing's throughout. Computability, decidability, universality and reduction all descend from the 1936 paper. The Turing Award, established in 1966 and generally regarded as computing's highest honour, carries his name. Beyond the technical, the discipline inherited his framing: that the interesting questions concern what procedures can and cannot do in principle, and that the way to answer them is to define terms precisely enough to prove something. It also inherited an intellectual temperament worth noting. Turing repeatedly treated boundaries between fields as unimportant, moving from logic to engineering to cryptanalysis to biology and bringing the same method to each: take the loose word, find the precise structure underneath it, then prove what that structure can and cannot do. His cryptographic legacy is likewise indirect but substantial. The wartime work established that codebreaking is a machine-assisted statistical discipline rather than a puzzle-solver's art, a shift that produced the modern signals intelligence agencies and, by reaction, the academic cryptography of the 1970s. Modern cipher design assumes an adversary with vast computing resources, known algorithms and captured plaintext, which is precisely the situation Bletchley exploited. The lesson that Enigma's operators, not its mathematics, gave the cipher away remains the first thing taught about operational security.

sections.heading: Limits of the Framework and Common Misunderstandings
sections.body: A guide of this kind should end with what the ideas do not deliver, because Turing's results are unusually prone to overstatement in both directions. The most frequent error is treating undecidability as a practical obstacle in ordinary work. The halting problem is unsolvable in general, but that says nothing about particular cases. Most real programs can be shown to terminate by straightforward reasoning, and static analysers, type systems and termination checkers handle enormous numbers of cases successfully. What is impossible is a single method guaranteed to work on every input; what is entirely possible is a method that works on almost everything encountered in practice and honestly reports uncertainty on the rest. Treating the theorem as a licence for defeatism about program verification misreads it. The opposite error is treating the Turing machine as a good model of a real computer. It is not, and was never meant to be. It has no random access, so retrieving a distant tape cell takes time proportional to the distance, whereas real memory is addressed in roughly constant time. It has no concurrency, no interrupts, no input or output during execution, no notion of interaction with an environment that changes while the computation proceeds. For questions about what is computable these differences are provably irrelevant, since the models are equivalent. For questions about performance, distributed systems, real-time control or user interaction they matter enormously, and other formalisms such as the pi-calculus, process algebras and interactive machine models were developed precisely because the classical model is silent on them. A third misunderstanding concerns physical realisability. The infinite tape means no real machine is literally a Turing machine; every actual computer is a finite state machine with a very large number of states. This is a technicality for practical purposes but occasionally matters in theory. Conversely, proposals for hypercomputation, machines that would exceed Turing's limits by exploiting infinite precision, infinitely many steps in finite time, or exotic spacetime geometries, remain speculative and have no experimental support. Finally, the Turing test should not be taken as a definition of intelligence, and Turing did not present it as one. He offered it as a sufficient condition for declining to withhold the word thinking, in a paper whose main purpose was to clear away bad objections. Modern systems that pass casual versions of it while failing at reasoning tasks a child manages show that the test measures something narrower than it was long assumed to. Recognising these boundaries is not a diminishment of the work. It is the ordinary fate of foundational results that later workers discover exactly where they apply. For a reader who wants to retain one thing, it should be the shape of the argument rather than any individual conclusion. Turing took an idea everyone used and nobody had defined, built the simplest possible object that captured it exactly, and then proved permanent limits on everything that object could ever do. That method, replacing an intuition with a precise model and then reasoning about the model's boundaries, is available far beyond computing, and it is the most transferable thing he left behind.

guides.title: The ENIAC and the First Electronic Computers
guides.summary: How the first electronic computers were designed, built and used between the 1930s and 1950 — the vacuum-tube technology that made them possible, ENIAC's internal architecture and plugboard programming, the rival machines in Britain, Germany and Iowa, and how the stored-program idea ended the era it began.

sections.heading: Why the First Electronic Computers Still Matter
sections.body: Every general-purpose computer in existence descends from a short, chaotic burst of engineering that ran roughly from 1937 to 1950. In those thirteen years the machine that calculates went from a room of clerks with desk calculators to an assembly of electronic switches that could perform thousands of arithmetic operations per second without a human hand in the loop. The change was not incremental. It was a jump of three to four orders of magnitude in speed, and it happened because of a single design decision: to stop moving metal and start moving electrons. Understanding that transition is not antiquarian curiosity. Almost every concept a modern programmer uses without thinking — the distinction between memory and processor, the notion that a program is data, the idea that a machine can branch on the result of its own computation — was invented, contested or first physically realised in this period, usually by people who were arguing bitterly with each other about who had thought of it first. The most famous of these machines is the ENIAC, the Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, switched on at the Moore School of Electrical Engineering at the University of Pennsylvania in 1945 and publicly unveiled on 15 February 1946. It occupied about 1,800 square feet, weighed roughly 30 tons, contained around 17,468 vacuum tubes, and drew approximately 150 kilowatts. It was not the first electronic calculating device, it was not the first programmable machine, and it was not the first computer in the modern architectural sense. What it was, uniquely, was the first machine that was simultaneously electronic, programmable, general-purpose and actually put into sustained productive service on real problems. That combination is why it anchors the story. It is also the machine that trained the first generation of people who knew, from direct experience, what a computer was for — and nearly every important American machine of the following decade was built by someone who had worked on it or attended lectures about it. The period is genuinely tangled, and the popular account of it is often wrong in specific, correctable ways. Several machines were built in secret and stayed classified for decades, which distorted the historical record for a generation. A court case in the 1970s invalidated the ENIAC patent and rewrote the official priority. Contributions by women who did the actual programming were misattributed as clerical work for fifty years. Any honest treatment has to hold several independent lines of development in view at once — American, British and German — and be careful about what "first" means in each sentence, because the answer changes depending on whether you mean first electronic, first programmable, first digital, first Turing-complete, or first to store its own program in memory. Those five criteria pick out five different machines, built in three countries, two of them in secret. Anyone who tells the story as a single line of descent from one inventor to the next is simplifying something that was genuinely simultaneous, competitive and frequently unaware of itself.

sections.heading: Computing Before Electronics: Clerks, Gears and Relays
sections.body: Before about 1940 the word "computer" named a person, usually a woman, who performed arithmetic to order. Observatories, insurance offices, artillery ranges and census bureaus employed rooms of them. They worked from printed forms, used mechanical desk calculators such as the Marchant, Friden and Monroe, and were organised in production lines: one person computed a column of multiplications, passed the sheet along, and the next did the additions. The Mathematical Tables Project in New York, funded under the Works Progress Administration, employed over a hundred human computers, many with only basic arithmetic training, organised so that the difficult judgement was embedded in the forms rather than in the workers. This is worth stating plainly because the first machines were designed to replace exactly this workflow, and their architecture reflects it. The mechanical tradition ran deep. Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine from 1822 and the far more ambitious Analytical Engine from 1837, the latter incorporating a separate "store" and "mill", punched-card input, and conditional branching — recognisably a general-purpose computer in concept. He never completed either, defeated by cost, precision engineering limits and his own tendency to redesign. Ada Lovelace's 1843 notes on the Analytical Engine, published as a translator's commentary, contain what is usually cited as the first published algorithm intended for machine execution, along with the observation that such a machine could manipulate symbols generally rather than merely numbers. Whether Lovelace or Babbage originated specific ideas in those notes remains genuinely disputed among historians; the notes themselves are unambiguous. By the 1930s the practical state of the art was electromechanical: the relay. A relay is an electrically operated switch in which a coil pulls a metal armature to close or open contacts. It is a physical moving part, so it is slow — a good relay switches in something like 5 to 15 milliseconds, giving perhaps 50 to 200 operations per second — but it is reliable, it is a genuine binary device, and telephone companies already manufactured them by the million, which meant components were cheap and well characterised. George Stibitz at Bell Labs built a relay adder on his kitchen table in 1937 and went on to build a series of relay computers, one of which he famously operated remotely over a telegraph line from Dartmouth in September 1940 — arguably the first remote computer session. Howard Aiken's Harvard Mark I, built with IBM and running in 1944, was a 51-foot electromechanical monster that could multiply two 23-digit numbers in about six seconds. It worked, it was useful, and it was about a thousand times too slow for what the war needed next. The relay had reached a hard ceiling that no amount of refinement could lift, because the limit was mechanical: an armature has mass, and mass takes time to move. Anyone who wanted a large speedup had to abandon moving parts altogether, which is exactly what the next generation did.

sections.heading: The Ballistics Problem That Paid for ENIAC
sections.body: ENIAC was not built to advance science. It was built to compute firing tables for artillery, and the specific bureaucratic pressure that funded it is worth understanding because it shaped the machine's design in ways that persisted. When a gun fires a shell, where the shell lands depends on the elevation and azimuth of the barrel, the propellant charge, the shell's mass and shape, and the state of the air it flies through — density, temperature, and crucially wind at every altitude the shell passes. A firing table is a printed booklet that lets a gun crew look up the correct elevation for a target at a given range under given conditions. Each table covers one combination of gun and shell, and each contains roughly 2,000 to 4,000 individual trajectories. Every trajectory is the numerical solution of a system of ordinary differential equations describing a body under gravity and a drag force that varies nonlinearly with velocity, particularly around the speed of sound where the drag coefficient rises steeply. The US Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, solved these numerically by stepwise integration. A human computer with a desk calculator took roughly 20 hours per trajectory. The Moore School's differential analyser — a mechanical analogue machine using rotating discs and wheels to perform integration, of a type devised by Vannevar Bush at MIT — got that down to about 10 to 20 minutes per trajectory, but analogue machines accumulate error, need constant recalibration, and had to be physically reconfigured for each problem. When the United States entered the war in 1941 the Army was commissioning new guns and new shells faster than tables could be produced. A single new table represented something like a month of continuous work for a large staff, and guns were reaching the field with no table at all, which meant they could not be aimed accurately. In April 1943 John Mauchly, a physicist at the Moore School, and J. Presper Eckert, a young and exceptionally capable electronics engineer there, proposed to the Army an all-electronic calculator to solve the problem. Mauchly had written a memorandum in August 1942 outlining the idea; Lieutenant Herman Goldstine, the Army's liaison at the Moore School, pushed it through. Project PX was approved on 5 June 1943 with an initial budget of $61,700, which eventually grew to just under $500,000 — perhaps $8 million in 2020s terms. The contract's stated goal was firing tables. The machine was not finished until late 1945, after the war in Europe had ended, so it never computed a wartime firing table in anger. Its first real production run was something else entirely.

sections.heading: The Vacuum Tube: What Made a Machine Electronic
sections.body: The entire era rests on one component, and the machines cannot be understood without understanding it. A vacuum tube — called a valve in British usage — is a sealed glass envelope with the air pumped out, containing metal electrodes. A heated filament warms a cathode until it emits electrons by thermionic emission, a process described by the Richardson equation, in which emitted current rises steeply with temperature. Those electrons are attracted across the vacuum to a positively charged anode, or plate. Because electrons flow only from the hot cathode to the cold anode and not the reverse, the simplest two-electrode tube, the diode, conducts in one direction only. The critical refinement was Lee de Forest's 1906 triode, which inserts a fine wire mesh — the grid — between cathode and anode. A small voltage on the grid controls a much larger current flowing from cathode to anode, because the grid's electric field either helps or hinders electrons passing through it. That is amplification, and it is also, if you drive the grid hard enough, switching: a sufficiently negative grid voltage cuts the plate current off entirely, and a sufficiently positive one saturates it. A tube driven between cut-off and saturation is a binary switch with no moving parts, and its switching time is set by how fast charges redistribute in the tube, on the order of a microsecond or better — roughly ten thousand times faster than a relay. That speed is the whole argument for electronics. But tubes brought three severe penalties. First, power: each tube's filament must be continuously heated, typically drawing a few watts. Multiply by 17,468 and ENIAC's heaters alone account for most of its 150-kilowatt draw, which is why the machine needed forced-air cooling and why the persistent story about Philadelphia's lights dimming, though almost certainly apocryphal, felt plausible. Second, heat: all that power becomes waste heat inside a closed room, and heat shortens component life, creating a vicious circle. Third, and most seriously, reliability. Tubes fail. Filaments burn out like light bulbs, cathodes lose emission as they age, and vacuum seals leak. The reliability objection was the standard reason experts gave for saying an electronic computer was impossible. The arithmetic seemed damning: if a single tube had a mean time between failures of, say, 2,500 hours, then 17,000 tubes would produce a failure roughly every nine minutes, and a machine that breaks every nine minutes cannot finish a calculation. Eckert's answer was engineering discipline rather than a new idea. He ran tubes far below their rated voltages and currents — typically at 50 to 75 percent of ratings — which dramatically extends life; he selected tubes by burn-in testing and rejected marginal ones; he mounted them in sockets for fast replacement; and he left the machine powered on continuously, since thermal cycling during warm-up and cool-down is what kills filaments. The result was a failure rate of roughly two or three tubes per day, and eventually stretches of over 100 hours of error-free operation.

sections.heading: Inside ENIAC: Accumulators, Decimal Arithmetic and Speed
sections.body: ENIAC was physically organised as about forty panels, each roughly 2 feet wide, 8 feet high and 3 feet deep, arranged in a U-shape around three walls of a room. Its logical organisation was modular and, to modern eyes, strange: it was not one processor but a collection of specialised arithmetic units that were wired together to cooperate on a problem. The core units were twenty accumulators. An accumulator is a device that both stores a number and adds to it, and each ENIAC accumulator held a signed ten-decimal-digit number, giving a range of plus or minus 9,999,999,999. Crucially, ENIAC counted in decimal, not binary. Each digit was represented by a ring counter of ten flip-flops, of which exactly one was on at a time — a one-hot decimal encoding. Adding was done by transmitting a number as a train of pulses on a set of wires, one wire per decimal digit position, with the number of pulses on each wire equal to that digit; the receiving ring counter simply advanced that many positions, carrying automatically into the next digit when it rolled past nine. Ten pulses per digit at a 100 kHz basic pulse rate gave an addition time of 200 microseconds, or 5,000 additions per second. The decimal choice was deliberate: it made input, output and human checking straightforward, at the cost of using ten flip-flops per digit where four bits would have sufficed. Beyond the accumulators there was a high-speed multiplier that used hard-wired multiplication tables and could multiply two ten-digit numbers in about 2.8 milliseconds — around 357 multiplications per second; a combined divider and square-rooter, considerably slower at roughly 30 milliseconds per division; three portable function tables, which were large arrays of rotary switches set by hand to hold 104 twelve-digit constants each, used for tabulated data such as the drag coefficient as a function of Mach number; a constant transmitter fed by punched cards; and a master programmer that provided nested loop counting up to six levels deep with stepper switches. Input and output were IBM punched-card equipment: a card reader at the front, a card punch at the back, with a tabulator used offline to print. This mattered practically, because card handling was mechanical and therefore slow. A machine that could do 5,000 additions a second could easily outrun its own ability to get numbers in and results out, so problems were structured to load a batch of data, compute for a long time, and emit relatively few results. For scale: ENIAC performed a multiplication about 2,400 times faster than the Harvard Mark I and several thousand times faster than a human with a desk calculator. A trajectory that took 20 hours by hand and 15 minutes on the differential analyser took ENIAC about 30 seconds — faster than the shell itself flew.

sections.heading: Programming by Plugboard, and the Six Women Who Did It
sections.body: ENIAC as originally built had no program memory in any sense. It was programmed by physically rewiring it. Setting up a problem meant deciding which accumulators would hold which quantities, in what order operations would fire, and then expressing that plan as several thousand switch settings and a spaghetti of patch cables between panel sockets. Two kinds of wire ran between units. Digit trays carried the numeric pulse trains that moved values from one unit to another. Program lines carried single control pulses: when a unit finished its operation it emitted an output pulse, and that pulse, routed by cable to another unit's program input, triggered the next operation. Sequencing was therefore not a list of instructions read from anywhere; it was a directed graph physically instantiated in copper. Because several chains could be triggered at once, ENIAC could and did execute operations in parallel — a capability later machines gave up for decades in exchange for simplicity. The consequence was that changing problems took a long time. A full setup could take a team days of planning followed by one to two days of physical wiring, and then further days of debugging, during which the only diagnostic tools were the neon indicator lamps on the accumulator faces, a single-step mode, and an intimate mental model of what should be happening. Historians estimate setup dominated ENIAC's early schedule far more than computation did. The people who did this work were six women recruited from the Army's pool of human computers: Kathleen McNulty, Frances Bilas, Betty Jean Jennings, Ruth Lichterman, Elizabeth Snyder and Marlyn Wescoff — later known by married names including Kay Antonelli, Jean Bartik, Betty Holberton and Marlyn Meltzer. They were given wiring diagrams and block schematics of a machine they were initially not cleared to enter, learned it from the documents, and worked out how to map mathematical problems onto its topology. In doing so they invented, empirically, much of the practice of programming: subroutine-like reuse of wired configurations, systematic desk-checking of a program before running it, and single-stepping a machine to localise a fault. Holberton went on to write the first sort-merge generator and to influence COBOL; Bartik led the team that later converted ENIAC to stored-program operation. For roughly fifty years the standard histories described them as operators or, worse, as models posed beside the machine for publicity photographs. The correction, driven largely by research from the 1980s onward, is now firmly established: they were the programmers, and the intellectual content of their work was substantial. It is a useful caution about how easily a technical record can be distorted by assumptions about who does which kind of work.

sections.heading: Atanasoff, Berry and the Machine That Came First
sections.body: Between 1937 and 1942 at Iowa State College, physicist John Vincent Atanasoff and his graduate student Clifford Berry built a machine now called the Atanasoff–Berry Computer. It was electronic, it was digital, it used binary rather than decimal, and it predated ENIAC. It is a genuine and under-taught landmark, and it also illustrates precisely why "first computer" is a question that needs qualifiers. Atanasoff's problem was solving systems of simultaneous linear equations, which arise constantly in physics and engineering, and which by hand are brutally laborious for more than a handful of unknowns. His machine was designed to solve up to 29 equations in 29 unknowns by Gaussian elimination. It used about 280 vacuum tubes for arithmetic, performing addition and subtraction in binary — a much more natural fit for two-state electronics than ENIAC's decimal rings. Its most striking innovation was memory: a pair of rotating drums, each carrying 1,600 small capacitors arranged in 32 tracks of 50, holding 30 numbers of 50 binary digits each. A capacitor holds charge that leaks away, so Atanasoff had the drum brushes read each capacitor once per revolution and immediately write the value back at full strength. That is dynamic memory with refresh, the same principle underlying every DRAM chip made since. He called it "jogging" the memory. What the machine could not do was run a program. It executed one fixed algorithm; there was no sequencing mechanism a user could alter, no branching, no loops beyond those built into the hardware. It was a special-purpose electronic calculator, not a general-purpose computer. It was also never fully debugged: its weak point was the intermediate-results system, which punched holes in paper cards by burning them with sparks and read them back, and which had an error rate of roughly one bit in 100,000 — tolerable for small problems, fatal for large ones. The machine was dismantled around 1948 when the basement was needed, without documentation of its final state. The reason this machine is famous is legal. John Mauchly visited Atanasoff in Ames, Iowa, in June 1941, stayed several days, and saw the machine and read a manuscript describing it. Decades later, in the antitrust-adjacent case Honeywell v. Sperry Rand, Judge Earl Larson ruled on 19 October 1973 that the ENIAC patent was invalid and that "Eckert and Mauchly did not themselves first invent the automatic electronic digital computer, but instead derived that subject matter from one Dr. John Vincent Atanasoff." The ruling put the invention into the public domain. How much Mauchly actually took is genuinely contested and probably unresolvable. Mauchly maintained he learned little he did not already have in mind; Atanasoff maintained otherwise. The judgment settled a patent question, not a historical one, and historians differ on how much weight to give it. What is not contested is that the ABC worked, was electronic and binary, and came first in time.

sections.heading: Colossus: The Machine That Was Secret for Thirty Years
sections.body: While ENIAC was being designed in Philadelphia, a larger electronic machine was already running in Buckinghamshire, and almost nobody knew. Colossus, built at the Post Office Research Station at Dollis Hill under engineer Tommy Flowers, began operating at Bletchley Park in December 1943 and was fully operational by February 1944 — well over a year before ENIAC. Its target was not the Enigma machine, which is the common confusion, but the Lorenz SZ40/42, a far more sophisticated German cipher attachment used for high-level teleprinter traffic between army headquarters, which Bletchley called Tunny. Lorenz encrypted teleprinter characters in the five-bit Baudot code by adding a pseudorandom key stream generated by twelve pinwheels. British cryptanalysts, notably Bill Tutte, had reconstructed the machine's logical structure without ever seeing one — an extraordinary feat of pure inference from intercepted traffic. Breaking a message then required finding the wheel start positions, which meant statistically comparing the ciphertext against candidate key streams across enormous numbers of possible settings. Colossus did this by reading a loop of paper tape carrying the ciphertext at 5,000 characters per second — photoelectrically, past a light and photocells, with the tape running fast enough that the machine was as much a mechanical achievement as an electronic one — while generating the candidate key stream internally with electronic counterparts of the Lorenz wheels, and counting coincidences in high-speed decade counters. Mark 1 had about 1,600 tubes; Mark 2, first running on 1 June 1944, had about 2,400 and processed five tape positions in parallel for a fivefold speedup. Ten Colossi were operating by the end of the war. Flowers had to overcome the same scepticism about tube reliability, and reached the same answer independently: keep the machine permanently powered on, and do not thermally cycle the valves. He also had to fund early work partly out of his own pocket, since Bletchley's management initially did not believe it would work. Colossus was programmable in a limited sense — its logical function was set by switches and plugs, and it could evaluate different Boolean combinations of the tape and key streams — but it was not general-purpose and could not perform arbitrary arithmetic. It was a special-purpose electronic counting machine of great sophistication. Its historical significance was suppressed. On Churchill's orders most Colossi were broken into pieces; two survived at GCHQ into the 1960s. The existence of the machines remained classified until the mid-1970s, and full technical details until the 1990s. British engineers who built the world's first large-scale programmable electronic digital machines spent thirty years unable to say so, and the standard American-centred history of computing hardened in the meantime. Flowers returned to the Post Office after the war, was refused a loan to build a similar machine commercially because he could not explain what he had already done, and received a modest grant that did not cover his wartime outlay. A working reconstruction, led by Tony Sale, was completed at Bletchley Park in 2007 and can be seen there.

sections.heading: Konrad Zuse and the German Line
sections.body: The third independent line ran in Berlin, largely in isolation, and produced what is arguably the first working programmable general-purpose digital computer of any technology — though not an electronic one. Konrad Zuse was a civil engineering graduate who found the structural calculations of his profession intolerably tedious and set out to mechanise them. Working in his parents' apartment, he completed the Z1 in 1938: a purely mechanical machine using sliding metal plates for logic, operating in binary, with 22-bit floating-point arithmetic and a 16-word memory, programmed from punched 35 mm film stock. Its architecture was strikingly modern — separate memory and arithmetic unit, floating point with exponent and mantissa, binary throughout — but mechanically it was unreliable, since the plates jammed. The Z2 replaced the arithmetic unit with telephone relays. The Z3, completed in May 1941, replaced everything with relays: about 2,600 of them, 600 in the arithmetic unit and 1,400 in memory, holding 64 words of 22 bits. It ran at about 5 to 10 Hz, performing an addition in roughly 0.8 seconds and a multiplication in about 3 seconds. That is slow even by relay standards, but the Z3 was fully programmable from punched film and executed a stored sequence of instructions automatically.
