It is generally accepted as the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer. The Z3 had no conditional branch instruction, which for a long time was taken to disqualify it from being Turing-complete. In 1998 Raúl Rojas showed that a Z3 program could in principle be made Turing-complete by exploiting its handling of undefined operations and by running a program loop that evaluates all branches and selects among results — a construction that is valid but wildly impractical, requiring enormous program tapes. It is a good example of a claim that is technically true and practically irrelevant, and it should be quoted with that caveat. The Z3 was destroyed in an Allied bombing raid on Berlin in 1943; a replica was built in the 1960s. The larger Z4, which survived the war after being moved to a village in the Bavarian Alps, was installed at ETH Zurich in 1950 and became continental Europe's first operational commercial computer, running there until 1955. Zuse also designed Plankalkül between 1942 and 1945, a remarkably complete high-level programming language with arrays, records, assertions and structured control flow. It was not published in full until 1972 and never implemented at the time, so it influenced nothing, but as a piece of design it was decades ahead of what was independently reinvented later. Zuse's isolation is the point: his work had almost no effect on the mainstream because nobody outside Germany knew of it until it no longer mattered.

sections.heading: The Stored-Program Idea and the First Draft
sections.body: The single most consequential idea of the period was not a component but an abstraction: that the program should live in the same read-write memory as the data, in the same numeric form, so that the machine can fetch instructions at electronic speed and, if desired, compute on them. The realisation came from ENIAC's central frustration. The machine could add in 200 microseconds but took two days to reconfigure. That imbalance is absurd, and Eckert, Mauchly and their colleagues saw it clearly while ENIAC was still being built. Eckert had also been working on mercury delay-line memory, developed from radar work: a tube of mercury with a quartz crystal at each end, in which a pulse train is converted to an acoustic wave, travels the length of the tube in about a millisecond, is detected, reshaped and re-injected at the far end. It stores data as a circulating pattern rather than in discrete cells, and it made bulk read-write memory affordable for the first time — perhaps 500 to 1,000 bits per tank, against a tube flip-flop's one bit for two tubes. John von Neumann, then one of the most prominent mathematicians alive and consulting on the Manhattan Project, met Goldstine on a railway platform at Aberdeen in mid-1944, learned of ENIAC, and joined the project as a consultant. Out of the group's discussions about the successor machine came a document von Neumann wrote in spring 1945, the "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC". It described a machine with five parts — a central arithmetic unit, a central control unit, memory, input and output — with instructions and data sharing one addressable memory, instructions executed sequentially from that memory unless a jump changed the sequence, and binary arithmetic throughout. This is the architecture nearly every computer since has used, and it is why the term "von Neumann architecture" is standard. The document also caused lasting damage. Goldstine circulated the 101-page draft in June 1945 with only von Neumann's name on the title page, though it distilled the collective work of the Moore School group. Because it was distributed publicly, it also constituted prior publication, which destroyed Eckert and Mauchly's ability to patent the ideas. They were furious; the dispute broke the group; Eckert and Mauchly left in March 1946 to found their own company. Von Neumann does not appear to have intended the credit grab, and his own contribution — particularly the clean logical abstraction, and the framing in terms of idealised neurons drawing on McCulloch and Pitts — was real and substantial. But the historical shorthand that credits him with the stored-program concept alone is not defensible. There is also a genuine intellectual antecedent. Alan Turing's 1936 paper on computable numbers described a universal machine that reads a description of another machine from its tape and simulates it — program as data, in the purest form. Von Neumann knew the paper well. How directly that shaped the EDVAC design is debated, but the conceptual link is not accidental.

sections.heading: Baby, EDSAC and the First Machines to Store Their Own Programs
sections.body: The first machine actually to execute a program stored in read-write electronic memory was small, British and built to test a memory device rather than to compute anything useful. At the University of Manchester, Freddie Williams and Tom Kilburn had developed a way to store bits on the phosphor screen of an ordinary cathode-ray tube. Writing a charged spot at a location and reading it back by detecting the induced pickup signal gives a random-access memory with no moving parts — the Williams–Kilburn tube, typically holding 1,024 to 2,048 bits per tube, refreshed continuously because the charge decays in about 0.2 seconds. To prove it, they built the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, universally called the Baby: 32 words of 32 bits, seven instructions, about 550 tubes. On 21 June 1948 it ran a program written by Kilburn to find the highest proper factor of a number, taking 52 minutes and executing roughly 3.5 million operations. That is the first execution of a stored program in history. The Baby grew into the Manchester Mark 1, which added index registers — the first machine to have them — and a magnetic drum backing store. Ferranti built a commercial version, the Ferranti Mark 1, delivered in February 1951, which has a decent claim to being the first commercially available general-purpose electronic computer. At Cambridge, Maurice Wilkes had attended the Moore School lectures in summer 1946 and returned determined to build the EDVAC design rather than merely discuss it. EDSAC — Electronic Delay Storage Automatic Calculator — ran its first program on 6 May 1949, computing a table of squares. It used mercury delay lines, about 3,000 tubes, and executed roughly 650 instructions per second. EDSAC matters less for being early than for being useful: it went into service for Cambridge scientists, and around it Wilkes, David Wheeler and Stanley Gill built the first real software infrastructure — a subroutine library on punched paper tape, the "initial orders" bootstrap loader, and in 1951 the first book on programming. Wheeler's method for calling and returning from a subroutine is still called the Wheeler jump. The American line delivered slightly later but on a larger scale. BINAC ran in 1949; the EDVAC itself, delayed by the Moore School breakup, not until 1951. UNIVAC I, from Eckert and Mauchly's company, was delivered to the US Census Bureau in March 1951 — the first American commercial computer — and became famous on 4 November 1952 when CBS used one to predict the presidential election from early returns. It forecast a Republican landslide, the network refused to broadcast a result it disbelieved, and the machine turned out to be right. Forty-six were built.

sections.heading: Reliability, Power and What Running These Machines Was Like
sections.body: Operating a first-generation electronic computer was closer to running a small power plant than to using an appliance, and the practical texture of it explains many design decisions that otherwise look arbitrary. Power and heat dominated. ENIAC's roughly 150 kilowatts had to be removed from the room, which meant substantial forced-air ducting; ambient temperatures around the machine ran high, and summer heat degraded reliability measurably. Sites needed dedicated electrical service, and switching the machine on was a graduated procedure rather than a switch, because inrush current on thousands of cold filaments is severe and thermal shock is what kills tubes. The maintenance regime was continuous. ENIAC's tube complement failed at roughly two to three tubes per day once the machine was mature. Finding which one had failed among 17,468 was the real problem, and the technique developed for it was to run diagnostic routines that exercised units in isolation, plus a "high-voltage / low-voltage margin test" in which supply voltages were deliberately swung out of specification: a tube that is weakening will fail at the margins before it fails at nominal, so stressing the machine surfaces the dying components on a schedule rather than in the middle of a computation. This idea — deliberately degrade the operating conditions to precipitate latent faults during a maintenance window — is still standard practice in hardware engineering. Errors that were not hard failures were worse. A tube with drifting characteristics produces intermittent wrong answers, and there is no obvious signal that anything is wrong. The standard defence was to run every important computation twice and compare, or to build in mathematical checks — computing a quantity by two different routes, or verifying that a conserved quantity stayed conserved. Getting a wrong answer silently is the failure mode that everything in first-generation practice was organised against, and it is why numerical work of the period is full of redundant checks that look wasteful today. Physical operation was laborious. Punched cards jammed and had to be cleared; paper tape tore; mercury delay lines had to be held at a stable temperature, because the speed of sound in mercury varies with temperature and the timing of the whole memory depends on it, so tanks were held in ovens at around 40 degrees Celsius. Williams tubes were sensitive to electrical noise — a well-attested Manchester story has a nearby lift or a passing vehicle inducing errors — and patterns of bits that were physically adjacent on the screen could interfere with each other, producing the memorable failure mode of a program that works until you store a particular value at a particular address. Machine time was scarce and precious. Users booked slots, often overnight, and the culture of careful desk-checking before running — reading your own program line by line, simulating it on paper — arose directly from the cost of wasting a session.

sections.heading: What ENIAC Actually Computed
sections.body: ENIAC's real workload is more interesting than the firing tables it was funded for, and it shows how quickly a general-purpose machine escapes its stated purpose. Its first major problem, run in December 1945 before the public unveiling, was a calculation for the hydrogen bomb programme at Los Alamos. Stanley Frankel and Nicholas Metropolis arrived with a problem in thermonuclear ignition, brought by Edward Teller's group, and ran roughly a million punched cards through the machine over about six weeks. The physicists were not told what the calculation was for; the ENIAC team certainly were not. The results were negative for the design being tested, which was useful information. That a machine commissioned for artillery tables first ran a weapons-physics simulation is a fair summary of the period's priorities. The machine then did compute firing and bombing tables, though the war was over. But its most scientifically consequential work was in two other areas. The first was Monte Carlo simulation. Stanislaw Ulam conceived the method in 1946 while convalescing and playing solitaire, wondering what fraction of layouts could be won and realising it was easier to deal many hands and count than to compute the combinatorics. Von Neumann saw immediately that neutron diffusion could be attacked the same way — follow many simulated individual neutrons through random scattering and absorption events, and take statistics — and ENIAC ran the first such calculations in 1948. Monte Carlo methods are now fundamental across physics, finance and statistics, and they exist because a machine fast enough to make brute-force sampling practical had appeared. The second was numerical weather prediction. In April 1950 a team including Jule Charney, Ragnar Fjörtoft and von Neumann ran the first computerised weather forecast on ENIAC, integrating a simplified barotropic vorticity equation over North America on a coarse grid. Producing a 24-hour forecast took about 24 hours of machine time, so the forecast arrived exactly as the weather did — useless operationally, decisive as proof of concept. Every weather forecast since descends from that run. ENIAC also did work in random-number generation, cosmic-ray studies, wind-tunnel design and the first computer-assisted calculation of pi and e to 2,000 digits in 1949. In 1948 the machine was converted to a rudimentary stored-program mode. Rather than rewiring, a set of instructions was encoded in the function tables — read-only, set by hand-turned switches — and a fixed wiring pattern made the machine fetch and interpret them, an idea proposed by von Neumann and Adele Goldstine and implemented by a team including Richard Clippinger and Jean Bartik. This cut throughput to roughly a sixth, because instructions now had to be decoded rather than being physically present, but it made setup a matter of hours instead of days, and on balance the machine got far more useful work done. ENIAC ran until 11:45 pm on 2 October 1955.

sections.heading: How the Machines Compare: Reading the Word 'First' Carefully
sections.body: Claims about which machine was first are usually arguments about definitions rather than facts, and the disagreements dissolve once the criteria are stated explicitly. Six independent properties do most of the work. Digital versus analogue is the first. An analogue machine, such as the Moore School differential analyser or a slide rule, represents a quantity by a continuously variable physical magnitude — a shaft angle, a voltage. A digital machine represents it by discrete symbols. Analogue machines were often faster in their era but are limited in precision by the physical accuracy of their parts, typically three or four significant figures, and they do not compose: errors accumulate without any way to correct them. Electronic versus electromechanical is the second, and it is a claim about switching elements. Zuse's Z3 and Aiken's Harvard Mark I are electromechanical: relays and gears. ENIAC, Colossus and the ABC are electronic: vacuum tubes, no moving parts in the logic. The practical difference is three to four orders of magnitude in speed. Programmable versus fixed-function is the third. The ABC ran one algorithm. Colossus could be reconfigured but only within a family of cryptanalytic counting operations. ENIAC and the Z3 could be set up for arbitrary computations. General-purpose versus special-purpose overlaps with programmability but is not identical: it asks whether the machine's instruction repertoire is rich enough to express any computation, given enough time and storage — roughly, Turing-completeness. ENIAC qualifies; Colossus does not. Stored-program is the fifth, and it is the sharpest line in the whole period. Does the machine hold its instructions in the same alterable memory as its data? ENIAC as built did not; the Manchester Baby in June 1948 was the first that did. Operational versus demonstrated is the sixth and most often glossed over. The ABC was never fully debugged. Babbage's Analytical Engine was never built. A design, however brilliant, is not a machine, and a machine that has never completed a real problem is not evidence that the design works. This criterion is the one most often quietly dropped by advocates of a favoured claimant, because it is the one that separates an idea from an achievement. Applying these: first electronic digital calculating device is the ABC, 1942. First programmable electronic digital machine is Colossus, 1943 to 1944, though special-purpose. First working programmable general-purpose digital computer of any technology is the Z3, 1941, electromechanical. First electronic general-purpose programmable computer put into sustained productive use is ENIAC, 1945. First stored-program computer is the Manchester Baby, 1948. First commercially delivered general-purpose computer is the Ferranti Mark 1, February 1951, with UNIVAC I the following month in the United States. None of these statements contradicts any other. Almost every popular dispute about the "first computer" comes from dropping one of the qualifiers.

sections.heading: How the Era Ended: Transistors, Cores and the Second Generation
sections.body: The first generation ended not because anyone lost interest in tubes but because two component inventions made them obsolete within about a decade, and it is worth being precise about which problems each solved. The transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs on 23 December 1947 by John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, working under William Shockley, who developed the more manufacturable junction transistor shortly after. A transistor does what a triode does — a small signal at one terminal controls a larger current between two others — but in solid silicon or germanium rather than in a vacuum. It needs no heater, so it draws perhaps a thousandth of the standing power; it produces correspondingly little heat; it is physically tiny; and it does not have a filament to burn out, so its lifetime is measured in decades rather than thousands of hours. The three penalties of the tube era all vanish at once. Early transistors were expensive and inconsistent, so the changeover took time: the Manchester Transistor Computer of 1953 and MIT's TX-0 of 1956 were experimental, and mainstream commercial second-generation machines such as the IBM 7090 arrived around 1959. Magnetic-core memory solved the other half of the problem. Delay lines were sequential — you waited for your data to come round, giving average access times around half a millisecond — and Williams tubes were fast but fragile and small. Core memory, developed principally by Jay Forrester at MIT for the Whirlwind project around 1949 to 1953, threads tiny ferrite rings on a wire grid. Each ring is magnetised clockwise or anticlockwise for one and zero, retains its state with no power at all, and can be addressed randomly by driving currents on the intersecting wires that select it. Access times were a few microseconds, it was genuinely non-volatile, and it was reliable enough that core dominated computer memory from the mid-1950s until semiconductor RAM displaced it around 1970 — which is why a memory image of a crashed program is still called a core dump. The scale of the change is easiest to see in numbers. ENIAC: 17,468 tubes, 150 kilowatts, 1,800 square feet, 5,000 additions per second, 20 words of fast storage. An IBM 7090 a decade and a half later: transistorised, roughly 100,000 additions per second, 32,768 words of core memory, and it fitted in an ordinary machine room. A single modern processor die contains more transistors than every vacuum tube ever manufactured, switches roughly a billion times faster than an ENIAC accumulator, and consumes a few tens of watts. What did not change is the architecture. Fetch an instruction from memory, decode it, execute it, repeat, with branches altering the sequence. That structure was fixed by 1949 and is still what a processor does underneath every layer of modern elaboration.

sections.heading: Myths, Contested Claims and How to Read the Record
sections.body: The history of early computing is unusually infested with confident errors, for identifiable reasons: much of it was classified, much of it was litigated, several key participants wrote self-serving accounts, and the field's own practitioners have rarely been trained historians. Knowing the common failure modes makes the literature far easier to use. The most persistent myth is the origin of the word "bug". The story that a moth found in a relay of the Harvard Mark II on 9 September 1947 gave computing the term is charming and the moth is genuinely preserved, taped into a logbook now at the Smithsonian. But the log entry reads "First actual case of bug being found", and the joke only works because the word was already in long-standing engineering use — Thomas Edison used it in this sense in an 1878 letter. The moth is the first literal bug, not the origin of the metaphor. Grace Hopper popularised the anecdote; she was not present when the moth was found. The claim that ENIAC dimmed the lights of Philadelphia when switched on is unsupported. The Moore School was fed from a dedicated supply, and 150 kilowatts, while large for a machine, is trivial against a city's load. The description of ENIAC as "the first computer" is defensible only with several qualifiers, and most sources that use it do not supply them. Similarly, calling von Neumann the inventor of the stored-program computer overstates a real but shared contribution, and the "von Neumann architecture" label has become a historical injustice frozen into standard terminology. A subtler distortion is the effect of secrecy on the record. Because Colossus was classified until the mid-1970s, thirty years of histories were written as though large-scale electronic computing began in America. Those histories were then cited by later ones. The correction is now well established, but older sources — including some still-standard textbooks — encode the gap. Similarly, Zuse's work was unknown outside Germany when it mattered, and the ABC was practically forgotten until litigation resurrected it, which is a poor mechanism for establishing scientific priority in either direction. The practical reading advice follows from all this. Treat any unqualified "first" as an incomplete sentence and ask which of the six criteria is meant. Prefer sources that give dates for specific verifiable events — a first program run, a delivery, a patent filing — over sources that make categorical claims. Be suspicious of narratives with a single hero, since every machine here was built by teams of dozens, and the named individuals are usually the ones who wrote memoirs or gave interviews. Check whether an account was written before or after 1975, because the Colossus declassification is a hard boundary in the reliability of the record. And treat the 1973 patent judgment as what it was: a legal finding about derivation under patent law, decided on a particular evidentiary record, not a historian's verdict about who thought of what.

guides.title: The Transistor and the Birth of Modern Electronics
guides.summary: The full story of the transistor: the semiconductor physics that makes it work, its invention at Bell Labs in 1947, the bipolar and MOSFET families, integrated circuits, CMOS logic, Moore's law and modern fabrication, and how transistors fail.

sections.heading: The Most Manufactured Object in History
sections.body:
More transistors have been made than any other artefact humans have ever produced. The cumulative total passed
one sextillion, that is a one followed by twenty-one zeros, around 2018, and the annual production rate now
exceeds a hundred billion transistors per second averaged across the year. There are more transistors in a
single modern smartphone processor, on the order of twenty billion, than there were grains of rice harvested
worldwide in any given hour. The individual device costs on the order of a billionth of a currency unit, a price
decline of roughly ten orders of magnitude since 1954. Nothing else in the history of manufacturing comes close
on any of these measures.

A transistor is a device that lets a small electrical signal control a much larger one, and that can be switched
fully on or fully off by a voltage. Those two functions, amplification and switching, are the whole of
electronics. Amplification is what makes a radio, a hearing aid, a sensor readout, or a mobile phone
transmitter possible, because real-world signals arrive far too weak to use directly. Switching is what makes
digital logic possible, because a switch controlled by another switch's output is all you need to build a
logic gate, and logic gates are all you need to build a computer.

What makes the transistor revolutionary is not that it performs these functions, since the vacuum tube performed
both from 1907 onwards. It is that it performs them in a piece of solid crystal with no vacuum, no heated
filament, no glass envelope and no moving parts, and that this solid-state construction turned out to be
indefinitely miniaturisable. A vacuum tube has a minimum practical size set by the need to physically house a
heated cathode and maintain a vacuum. A transistor's size is set by how finely you can pattern a crystal
surface, and the answer to that has improved by a factor of many thousands.

The consequences run well beyond electronics. Digital computing, telecommunications, the internet, medical
imaging, satellite navigation, industrial automation and machine learning are all downstream of the fact that
switching became almost free. Economists have struggled to measure the resulting productivity gains precisely,
but there is no serious dispute that the transistor and its integrated descendants constitute one of the two or
three most consequential technological developments since the steam engine.

The story of how it came to exist is also unusually well documented and unusually instructive, because it
involved a deliberate, funded, theory-guided research programme that succeeded roughly on schedule, which is
rare enough in the history of invention to be worth understanding in detail. It also involved a bitter personal
falling-out that reshaped the geography of the industry, and a series of manufacturing innovations that mattered
as much as the physics.

sections.heading: Before the Transistor: The Vacuum Tube and Its Ceiling
sections.body:
To understand what the transistor solved you have to understand what came before. In 1904 John Ambrose Fleming
patented the thermionic diode, a glass bulb containing a heated filament and a metal plate. Heating a metal
boils electrons off its surface, a process called thermionic emission, and those electrons will flow to a
positively charged plate but not from a cold plate back to the filament. The device therefore conducts in one
direction only, which is what a radio detector needs.

In 1906 Lee de Forest inserted a wire mesh, the grid, between filament and plate, creating the triode. A small
voltage on the grid controls a much larger current from filament to plate, because the grid's electric field
either helps or hinders electrons crossing the gap. That is amplification, and it made long-distance telephony,
radio broadcasting, radar, sound film and eventually electronic computing possible. The first transcontinental
telephone call in the United States, in January 1915, depended on tube repeaters placed along the line.

The problems were serious and got worse with scale. A tube's filament must be heated to roughly 1000 to 1200
kelvin, and that heater typically consumes one to several watts continuously, whether or not the tube is doing
anything useful. Tubes are physically large, a few centimetres at best. They are fragile glass. They require
high supply voltages, commonly 100 to 300 volts. Most damagingly, they wear out: the cathode coating gradually
depletes, the filament eventually breaks, and typical service life is a few thousand hours.

The ENIAC computer, completed at the University of Pennsylvania in 1945, is the standard illustration. It
contained about 17,468 vacuum tubes, occupied roughly 167 square metres, weighed about 27 tonnes, and consumed
around 150 kilowatts. With that many tubes, and a mean time between failures per tube measured in thousands of
hours, a tube failed on average every day or two, and finding which one had failed among seventeen thousand was
itself a substantial task. The operators eventually learned never to switch the machine off, because thermal
cycling on power-up killed far more tubes than continuous running.

Scaling the telephone network faced the same wall. Bell Telephone Laboratories, the research arm of the American
Telephone and Telegraph Company, ran a network with millions of electromechanical relay switches and hundreds of
thousands of vacuum tube amplifiers, all of which required maintenance. Mervin Kelly, who became Bell Labs
director of research in 1936, concluded that the future of the telephone system required a solid-state
replacement for both, and after the interruption of the Second World War he authorised a dedicated solid-state
physics group in 1945 to find one. That decision, and the theoretical understanding of semiconductors that had
matured during the 1930s, are what made the invention a planned outcome rather than an accident.

sections.heading: Semiconductors: Bands, Gaps and Why Silicon Won
sections.body:
The physics that makes a transistor possible is the band structure of crystalline solids, worked out in the late
1920s and 1930s by Felix Bloch, Alan Wilson, Rudolf Peierls and others applying quantum mechanics to periodic
lattices. In an isolated atom electrons occupy discrete energy levels. Bring atoms together into a crystal and
those levels broaden into bands of allowed energies separated by forbidden gaps.

Whether a material conducts depends on how those bands are filled. In a metal, the highest occupied band is only
partly full, so electrons can move into nearby empty states with negligible energy cost and current flows
freely. In an insulator the highest occupied band, the valence band, is completely full, and the next band up,
the conduction band, is empty and separated by a large energy gap, typically above 4 electronvolts. No electron
can gain a small amount of energy, because there is nowhere to put it, so no current flows.

A semiconductor is an insulator with a small gap. Silicon's bandgap is 1.12 electronvolts at room temperature,
germanium's is 0.66, gallium arsenide's 1.42. At room temperature the average thermal energy, kT, is about
0.026 electronvolts, so only an exponentially small fraction of electrons have enough energy to jump the gap.
For silicon this gives an intrinsic carrier concentration of roughly 10 to the 10th per cubic centimetre, out of
about 5 times 10 to the 22nd atoms per cubic centimetre. Pure silicon is therefore a poor conductor, but not a
hopeless one, and crucially its conductivity can be manipulated.

When an electron leaves the valence band it leaves behind a vacancy that neighbouring electrons can hop into.
Tracking that vacancy is far easier than tracking the billions of electrons around it, and it behaves exactly
like a particle with positive charge. This is a hole, and holes are as real, for engineering purposes, as
electrons. Semiconductors conduct by both.

Silicon's dominance was not obvious in 1948; the first transistors were germanium, which has higher carrier
mobility and was easier to purify at the time. Silicon won for four reasons. Its larger bandgap means far less
thermal leakage, so silicon devices work reliably to 150 degrees Celsius while germanium becomes unusable above
about 75. Silicon is the second most abundant element in the Earth's crust, at roughly 28 percent by mass, so
raw material is effectively free. Silicon can be purified to extraordinary levels, better than one impurity atom
in ten billion, by the Czochralski and float-zone processes. And decisively, silicon forms a native oxide,
silicon dioxide, which is an excellent electrical insulator, adheres perfectly to the crystal, and can be grown
simply by heating the wafer in oxygen or steam. Germanium's oxide is water-soluble and useless. That single
chemical accident determined the material basis of the entire electronics industry.

sections.heading: Doping and the p-n Junction: The Foundational Device
sections.body:
Pure semiconductor is not useful on its own. The controlling trick is doping: deliberately introducing tiny
quantities of a different element to supply mobile charge carriers. Silicon sits in group 14 of the periodic
table, with four valence electrons, and in the crystal each atom shares one with each of four neighbours in a
tetrahedral arrangement, using all four.

Replace one silicon atom in ten million with phosphorus, from group 15, which has five valence electrons. Four
bond to neighbours and the fifth is left over, bound only weakly, needing about 0.045 electronvolts to break
free, which thermal energy supplies easily at room temperature. Each phosphorus atom therefore donates one
mobile electron. This is n-type material, n for negative carriers. Now instead use boron from group 13, with
three valence electrons. One bond is left incomplete, and a neighbouring electron can hop in to fill it, moving
the vacancy along. Each boron atom accepts an electron and creates a mobile hole. This is p-type.

Typical doping levels run from 10 to the 14th to 10 to the 20th atoms per cubic centimetre, which even at the
high end is about one dopant per five hundred silicon atoms and at the low end one in a hundred million. That
sensitivity is why semiconductor manufacturing demands cleanliness measured in parts per trillion, and why a
fingerprint on a wafer ruins it.

The decisive structure is what happens when p-type and n-type material meet in a single crystal. Electrons from
the n side diffuse across into the p side and fall into holes; holes diffuse the other way. Both leave behind
the fixed, ionised dopant atoms, negative on the p side and positive on the n side. A region near the junction is
thus stripped of mobile carriers, called the depletion region, and carries a built-in electric field. That field
opposes further diffusion, and equilibrium is reached with a built-in potential of about 0.7 volts for silicon.

The result is a one-way valve. Apply positive voltage to the p side and the applied field opposes the built-in
field, the depletion region narrows, and once the applied voltage approaches 0.6 to 0.7 volts current flows
freely and rises exponentially, described by the Shockley diode equation, in which current equals a saturation
current times the quantity exponential of qV over nkT, minus one. Apply positive voltage to the n side instead
and the depletion region widens, almost no current flows, and the device blocks until reverse breakdown occurs.

Russell Ohl at Bell Labs stumbled onto this in 1940 while studying a silicon sample with an accidental impurity
boundary, observing that it produced a voltage under illumination, the first silicon solar cell effect, and
that it rectified strongly. Understanding that structure, and Shockley's subsequent theoretical treatment of
it, is what turned semiconductor work from empirical craft into engineering.

sections.heading: December 1947: Bardeen, Brattain and the Point-Contact Transistor
sections.body:
Mervin Kelly's solid-state group at Bell Labs was led by William Shockley, a theoretical physicist of
formidable ability and difficult temperament. It included John Bardeen, a quiet theorist who would later become
the only person to win two Nobel Prizes in Physics, and Walter Brattain, an outstanding experimentalist with a
gift for building apparatus that worked.

Shockley's initial idea, pursued from 1945, was the field effect: place a metal plate near a thin semiconductor
film, apply a voltage, and the resulting electric field should attract or repel carriers and change the film's
conductivity, producing amplification. It is a sound idea and is essentially how a modern transistor works. It
comprehensively failed to work in 1945. The measured effect was smaller than predicted by a factor of more than
a thousand.

Bardeen diagnosed why in March 1946, in one of the more important pieces of theoretical work of the century. He
proposed that electrons become trapped in surface states, localised energy levels at the semiconductor's
surface caused by the abrupt termination of the crystal lattice. These trapped charges screen the applied field,
shielding the interior from it entirely. The insight redirected the whole programme towards understanding and
defeating surface states.

Through late 1947 Bardeen and Brattain experimented with ways to neutralise the surface, including immersing
samples in electrolytes. On 16 December 1947, working with a germanium slab, Brattain used a wedge of
polystyrene wrapped in gold foil, slit with a razor blade to create two contacts about 50 micrometres apart,
pressed against the surface. Applying a small signal to one contact produced an amplified version at the other.
The measured power gain was substantial, and voltage gain roughly a hundredfold. On 23 December they
demonstrated it to Bell Labs management, amplifying speech. That date is conventionally the transistor's
birthday.

The device worked by a mechanism nobody had predicted: minority carrier injection. One contact, the emitter,
injected holes into the n-type germanium; those holes diffused the short distance to the second contact, the
collector, which was reverse-biased and collected them. It was not a field-effect device at all.

Shockley, who had been away and had not been present for the breakthrough, reacted with a mixture of
professional excitement and personal fury at having been excluded from a discovery in his own programme. Over
the Christmas and New Year period he worked intensively, and in January 1948 conceived the junction transistor,
a far more manufacturable structure. Bell Labs announced the invention publicly on 30 June 1948. The name
transistor, a contraction of transconductance and varistor, was coined by the engineer John R. Pierce in an
internal ballot. The three men shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sections.heading: The Bipolar Junction Transistor and How Amplification Works
sections.body:
The point-contact transistor was fragile, noisy, hard to reproduce and manufactured by a process closer to
craft than engineering. Shockley's junction transistor, described in his 1949 Bell System Technical Journal
paper and demonstrated in working form by 1951, replaced it and defined the field for two decades.

The structure is three doped regions in one crystal: an n-p-n or p-n-p sandwich, with the middle layer, the
base, made very thin, in early devices tens of micrometres and in modern ones well under a micrometre. The outer
layers are the emitter, doped very heavily, and the collector, doped more lightly and made physically larger.

Consider an n-p-n device in normal operation. The emitter-base junction is forward-biased by roughly 0.7 volts,
so it conducts, and because the emitter is far more heavily doped than the base, the current across that
junction consists overwhelmingly of electrons flowing from emitter into base rather than holes flowing the other
way. Those electrons are now minority carriers in p-type material, where they should quickly recombine with
holes. But the base is deliberately made thinner than the distance an electron typically diffuses before
recombining. Consequently the great majority, commonly 99 percent or more, cross the base without recombining
and arrive at the base-collector junction, which is reverse-biased. A reverse-biased junction blocks majority
carriers but sweeps minority carriers straight across, so those electrons are collected.

The amplification follows arithmetically. Suppose 99.5 percent of emitter electrons reach the collector and 0.5
percent recombine in the base and must be replaced by base current. Then collector current is about 199 times
base current. That ratio is the current gain, called beta or hFE, typically between 50 and 500 in real devices.
A tiny base current controls a large collector current, which is amplification. Because the collector can be
connected through a large load resistance, a small input power controls a much larger output power.

Two ways of describing the same device coexist and it is worth knowing both. The current-control view treats
base current as the input and is convenient for design. The physically more accurate view, expressed in the
Ebers-Moll model of 1954, treats base-emitter voltage as the input, with collector current rising exponentially
with it: roughly a tenfold increase in current for every 60 millivolts of extra base-emitter voltage at room
temperature. This exponential relationship makes bipolar transistors superb analogue amplifiers, with high gain
and excellent matching, which is why they still dominate precision analogue, radio frequency and power
applications despite having lost the digital world entirely.

Two operating regions matter in practice. In the active region, with the collector-base junction reverse-biased,
the device amplifies faithfully. Drive the base hard enough and the collector voltage falls until the
collector-base junction also forward-biases, at which point the device saturates: collector-emitter voltage
drops to about 0.2 volts and further base current produces no more collector current. Saturation is what you
want in a switch, because it minimises dissipation, and what you must avoid in an amplifier, because it clips
the signal.

sections.heading: Silicon, the Planar Process and the Move to Manufacturing
sections.body:
The physics was settled by 1951; the industry was created by manufacturing. Three developments in the 1950s
mattered as much as the original invention.

The first was silicon. Germanium devices leaked badly above about 75 degrees Celsius, which ruled out military
and automotive use, the two most lucrative early markets. Gordon Teal, who had developed single-crystal
germanium growth at Bell Labs, moved to Texas Instruments and produced a working silicon transistor in early
1954. He announced it at a conference in Dayton, Ohio in May 1954, at a session where previous speakers had
described silicon as years away, and demonstrated it by dropping a germanium-based record player amplifier into
hot oil, whereupon it died, then repeating the test with his silicon device, which kept playing. Texas
Instruments had the market to itself for roughly three years.

The second was diffusion doping, developed at Bell Labs by Calvin Fuller and others. Instead of growing doped
layers during crystal pulling, a wafer is heated to roughly 1000 to 1200 degrees Celsius in an atmosphere
containing the dopant, which diffuses into the surface to a depth controlled by time and temperature. This gave
precise, reproducible, very thin base layers, which directly improved gain and frequency response.

The third, and arguably the most important single manufacturing invention in the field's history, was the planar
process, devised by Jean Hoerni at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1958 and 1959. Hoerni's insight was to exploit
silicon's oxide. Grow a layer of silicon dioxide over the whole wafer surface; use photolithography to etch
windows in it exactly where dopant should enter; diffuse through those windows; regrow oxide to seal the
result. The junctions end up buried under a protective glass layer rather than exposed at the edge of a mesa,
which solved the chronic reliability and leakage problems caused by surface contamination. It also left a flat
surface on which metal interconnections could simply be evaporated and patterned.

Everything about modern chip manufacture descends from that combination. The wafer stays flat, all processing
happens from one side, and every step is a photographic pattern transfer applied to the entire wafer at once
rather than to individual devices. That last point is the economic engine: the cost of processing a wafer is
roughly independent of how many devices are on it, so shrinking devices directly divides cost per device.

The consumer breakthrough came quickly. The Regency TR-1, sold from late 1954 at 49.95 dollars, was the first
commercial transistor radio, using four Texas Instruments germanium transistors. Sony, then a small Japanese
company called Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo, licensed Bell's patents and released the TR-55 in 1955, then built its
global business on pocket radios. The transistor's first mass market was not computing but portable
entertainment, which funded the volume manufacturing that computing would later require.

sections.heading: The Field-Effect Transistor and the MOSFET
sections.body:
Shockley's original field-effect idea, defeated by surface states in 1945, was not wrong, only premature. In
fact the concept substantially predated him: Julius Edgar Lilienfeld filed patents in Canada in 1925 and the
United States in 1926 and 1928 describing a device in which a field controls conductivity in a thin
semiconductor film, and Oskar Heil filed a British patent on a similar idea in 1934. Neither built a working
device, and their patents later complicated the industry's intellectual property landscape considerably.

The obstacle was always the semiconductor surface. Bardeen's surface states trapped charge and screened the
applied field. The solution came from the same oxide that made the planar process work. In 1959 Mohamed Atalla
and Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs found that a carefully grown thermal silicon dioxide layer passivates the silicon
surface remarkably well, reducing the density of interface trap states by orders of magnitude. In 1959 and 1960
they built the first working metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, the MOSFET, and the device that
now constitutes something above 99.9 percent of all transistors ever manufactured came into existence.

The structure is simple enough to describe in a sentence. On a p-type silicon substrate, form two heavily
n-doped regions, the source and the drain, separated by a gap called the channel. Over the channel grow a very
thin insulating oxide, historically 100 nanometres, in the 2000s about 1.2 nanometres, which is only four or
five atomic layers. On top of the oxide place a conducting gate, originally aluminium metal, later heavily doped
polycrystalline silicon, and since around 2007 metal again.

Operation is electrostatic. With zero gate voltage, source and drain are separated by p-type material, so the
structure is two back-to-back diodes and no current flows. Raise the gate voltage and its field repels holes
from the region under the oxide and attracts electrons. Above a threshold voltage, typically 0.3 to 0.7 volts in
modern devices, enough electrons accumulate to invert the surface from p-type to n-type, forming a continuous
conducting channel from source to drain. The transistor is on. Remove the gate voltage and the channel vanishes.

Two features made the MOSFET dominant. First, the gate is insulated, so it draws essentially no steady current,
only the transient charge needed to change its voltage. A bipolar transistor's base current flows continuously
and costs power. Second, the device is far simpler to make than a bipolar transistor and scales down more
gracefully, because it is fundamentally a capacitor controlling a resistor rather than a carefully engineered
stack of junctions. Its early disadvantage was speed, since surface carrier mobility is lower than in the bulk,
which is why bipolar logic dominated until the mid-1970s and MOS devices took over only when scaling had made
them fast enough.

sections.heading: The Integrated Circuit: Kilby, Noyce and the Tyranny of Numbers
sections.body:
By the late 1950s the industry had a problem its own success created, which the military called the tyranny of
numbers. A complex electronic system might need tens of thousands of individually packaged transistors,
resistors and capacitors, each requiring soldered connections. Reliability of the whole is the product of the
reliability of every joint, so systems failed at their interconnections long before their components wore out,
and assembly cost dominated.

Jack Kilby, newly hired at Texas Instruments, was left working through the company's July 1958 shutdown because
he had not accrued holiday. He reasoned that since all components could be made from semiconductor material,
resistors from undoped bulk resistance and capacitors from reverse-biased junctions, an entire circuit could be
fabricated in one piece of material. On 12 September 1958 he demonstrated a phase-shift oscillator built on a
single germanium bar to TI management. It worked. His connections, however, were fine gold wires bonded by
hand, which reintroduced exactly the assembly problem he had solved in principle.

Robert Noyce at Fairchild, working from Hoerni's planar process in January 1959, supplied the missing half.
Because the planar process leaves the wafer covered in an insulating oxide with a flat top surface, aluminium
can be evaporated over the whole surface and photolithographically patterned into interconnections, wiring the
devices together in the same batch process that made them. No hand wiring at all. Noyce also solved isolation,
using reverse-biased p-n junctions to electrically separate adjacent devices on one substrate.

The patent dispute between Texas Instruments and Fairchild ran for a decade, ending in cross-licensing.
Historically the fair summary is that Kilby had the concept first and Noyce had the manufacturable
implementation, and both are properly called co-inventors. Kilby received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000;
Noyce had died in 1990 and Nobel Prizes are not awarded posthumously.

The business context is worth noting because it shaped the industry's geography. Shockley left Bell Labs and
founded Shockley Semiconductor in Mountain View, California in 1956, attracting outstanding young researchers.
His management was so erratic that in 1957 eight of them, including Noyce and Gordon Moore, resigned together
and founded Fairchild Semiconductor with backing from Sherman Fairchild. Shockley called them the traitorous
eight. From Fairchild came dozens of spin-off companies, including Intel, founded by Noyce and Moore in 1968,
and Advanced Micro Devices. Silicon Valley exists because of a personality conflict at a company that failed.

The integrated circuit's early market was not commercial but governmental, and that mattered enormously. The
first devices cost far more than the equivalent discrete components, so nobody building consumer goods wanted
them. The Apollo Guidance Computer, designed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Instrumentation
Laboratory, used about 2,800 integrated circuits, each a single three-input NOR gate, and at its peak the Apollo
programme consumed a substantial share of world production. The Minuteman II guidance system was the
other anchor customer. Guaranteed orders at high prices funded the yield improvements that then
drove prices down by a factor of roughly fifty over the 1960s, at which point commercial markets opened.
Procurement created the industry rather than merely buying from it.

sections.heading: From Transistor to Logic Gate to Computer
sections.body:
A transistor by itself computes nothing. The path from device to computer runs through a specific and rather
beautiful hierarchy of abstraction, and understanding it demystifies the whole of digital electronics.

Start with a switch. A MOSFET with its gate at supply voltage conducts between source and drain; with its gate
at ground it does not. Assign the labels one to a high voltage and zero to a low one, and that switch becomes a
logical element. Connect an n-channel MOSFET between an output node and ground, and a resistor between the
output node and the supply. When the input is high the transistor conducts and pulls the output to ground, that
is to zero. When the input is low the transistor is off and the resistor pulls the output high, to one. The
output is the logical negation of the input: this is an inverter, or NOT gate.

Put two such transistors in series and the output only goes low when both inputs are high, giving NOT AND, or
NAND. Put them in parallel and the output goes low when either input is high, giving NOT OR, or NOR. NAND and
NOR are each functionally complete, meaning any Boolean function whatsoever can be built from copies of either
one alone, a result following from the algebra George Boole published in 1854 and Claude Shannon connected to
switching circuits in his 1937 master's thesis.

From gates you build arithmetic. A half adder, made from an exclusive-OR gate and an AND gate, adds two bits and
produces a sum and a carry. A full adder, roughly nine gates, adds two bits plus an incoming carry. Chain
sixty-four full adders and you have a 64-bit adder. Add multiplexers to select between operations and you have
an arithmetic logic unit.

From gates you also build memory. Cross-couple two inverters so each drives the other's input and the pair has
two stable states, holding one bit indefinitely as long as power is applied. Add access transistors and it
becomes a static RAM cell, six transistors per bit. Dynamic RAM is simpler still: one transistor and one
capacitor per bit, storing charge that leaks away and must be refreshed thousands of times per second, invented
by Robert Dennard at IBM in 1966 and the reason main memory is cheap.

Combine an arithmetic unit, registers, memory and a control unit that fetches instructions and sequences
operations, and you have a processor. Intel's 4004, released in November 1971 and designed principally by
Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff and Masatoshi Shima, put all of that on one chip: 2,300 transistors, a 10 micrometre
process, 740 kilohertz clock, 4-bit words. A modern high-end processor has roughly ten million times as many
transistors. The architectural principles are unchanged; only the count and the speed differ.

sections.heading: CMOS and Why Almost Every Chip Uses It
sections.body:
The logic described with a pull-up resistor works, and it was how early NMOS logic was built, but it has a fatal
flaw at scale. Whenever the transistor is on, current flows continuously from supply to ground through the
resistor and the device. Every gate holding a low output burns power constantly. Multiply by a hundred million
gates and the chip melts.

The solution is complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor logic, CMOS, invented by Frank Wanlass with Chih-Tang
Sah at Fairchild and published in 1963. It uses two kinds of MOSFET. An n-channel device conducts when its gate
is high; a p-channel device, built with the doping reversed, conducts when its gate is low. Build every gate as
a complementary pair of networks: a pull-up network of p-channel devices connecting the output to the supply,
and a pull-down network of n-channel devices connecting it to ground, arranged so that exactly one network
conducts for any input combination.

A CMOS inverter is one p-channel and one n-channel transistor with gates tied together. Input high turns the
n-device on and the p-device off, pulling the output low. Input low does the reverse. In either stable state,
one device in the path is off, so no direct current path exists from supply to ground at all. Static power
consumption is, in principle, zero.

Power is instead consumed only during transitions, when charging and discharging the capacitance of wires and
transistor gates. That dynamic power is given by a formula every chip designer knows: power equals alpha times C
times V squared times f, where C is the switched capacitance, V the supply voltage, f the clock frequency and
alpha the fraction of nodes switching each cycle. The quadratic dependence on voltage is why supply voltages
fell from 5 volts in the 1980s to around 0.7 volts today, and why reducing voltage is the most powerful lever
available for saving energy.

CMOS also gives excellent noise immunity, since outputs are driven hard to the supply rails rather than to
intermediate levels, and it is symmetric, so the same design methodology works everywhere. Its cost is roughly
twice the transistor count and a more complex fabrication sequence requiring both n-wells and p-wells on one
wafer, plus a vulnerability called latch-up in which parasitic bipolar structures inherent in the layout can
trigger a self-sustaining short circuit, controlled by careful well design and guard rings.

The honest qualification is that static power is no longer zero. Below roughly 90 nanometre feature sizes,
leakage through the thin gate oxide by quantum tunnelling, and subthreshold leakage through nominally off
transistors, became significant, and in some designs leakage now accounts for a third or more of total power.
CMOS's founding advantage has eroded, though it remains overwhelmingly the best available option.

sections.heading: Moore's Law, Dennard Scaling and the Economics of Shrinking
sections.body:
In April 1965 Gordon Moore, then research director at Fairchild, wrote a short article for Electronics magazine
observing that the number of components on an integrated circuit had doubled roughly every year since 1959, and
predicting the trend would continue for at least a decade. In 1975 he revised the doubling period to about two
years. This became known as Moore's law, though it is not a law of nature but an observation about an industry
that then organised itself around fulfilling it, making it partly self-fulfilling through coordinated roadmaps.

The physics that made shrinking beneficial rather than merely space-saving was set out by Robert Dennard and
colleagues at IBM in a 1974 paper. Dennard scaling says that if you shrink all dimensions of a MOSFET by a
factor k, and also reduce the supply voltage by k and increase doping by k, then several things happen at once
and in a mutually reinforcing way. Area falls by k squared, so you fit k squared more devices in the same space.
Delay falls by k, so the circuit runs k times faster. Power per device falls by k squared. Therefore power per
unit area stays constant while the number and speed of devices rise.

That last point is the crucial one. For roughly thirty years each new generation gave more transistors, faster
switching, and no increase in power density, all simultaneously and essentially for free. That is the real
engine behind the extraordinary improvement in computing between 1975 and 2005.

Dennard scaling ended in the mid-2000s, and the reason is worth understanding precisely. Voltage could not keep
falling because the threshold voltage could not keep falling, and the threshold voltage could not keep falling
because subthreshold leakage rises exponentially as it does. The fundamental limit is that a MOSFET's current
below threshold falls by no more than one factor of ten for every kT over q times the natural logarithm of ten,
which at room temperature is about 60 millivolts, an absolute floor set by the thermal distribution of electron
energies. Lower the threshold by 300 millivolts and off-state leakage rises a thousandfold.

With voltage stuck near 1 volt, power density began rising with each generation. The industry's response, from
about 2005, was to stop increasing clock frequency, which had risen from 1 megahertz to nearly 4 gigahertz and
then stopped almost dead, and instead to add parallel cores. This is why processors have four or eight or
sixty-four cores rather than a single much faster one, and why software had to become concurrent. A further
consequence is dark silicon: on a modern chip, a substantial fraction of the transistors must be powered down at
any moment to stay within the thermal budget, which pushes designs towards many specialised accelerators used
intermittently rather than one general-purpose engine used constantly.

sections.heading: Inside the Fab: How a Chip Is Actually Made
sections.body:
Semiconductor fabrication is arguably the most precise manufacturing process humans perform routinely. A modern
facility costs between ten and twenty billion currency units, runs air filtered to fewer than one particle
larger than 100 nanometres per cubic metre, roughly ten thousand times cleaner than a hospital operating
theatre, and executes between eight hundred and fifteen hundred process steps over two to
three months to turn a blank wafer into finished chips.

The core technique is photolithography, and it has not changed in principle since Hoerni: coat the wafer in a
light-sensitive polymer, project a pattern onto it, develop away the exposed or unexposed regions, then use the
remaining polymer as a stencil for etching or ion implantation. What has changed relentlessly is the wavelength
of light. Early systems used 436 nanometre mercury lamps, then 365, then 248 nanometre krypton fluoride lasers,
then 193 nanometre argon fluoride, extended by immersing the final lens in purified water. Since around 2019
leading-edge layers use extreme ultraviolet at 13.5 nanometres, generated by firing a laser at droplets of
molten tin, and focused entirely by mirrors because no material transmits at that wavelength.
steps: Grow a single crystal ingot. Melt electronic-grade polysilicon, purified to better than one impurity atom in ten billion, and slowly withdraw a rotating seed crystal from the melt by the Czochralski method to pull a cylindrical boule up to 300 millimetres in diameter and two metres long.

Slice the boule into wafers about 775 micrometres thick with a wire saw, then lap, etch and chemically-mechanically polish one face to a mirror finish flat to within a few nanometres across the whole 300 millimetre span.
Grow or deposit the first insulating and device layers, typically a thermal silicon dioxide grown by heating the wafer in oxygen or steam at 900 to 1100 degrees Celsius.
Apply photoresist by spin coating, dispensing liquid polymer onto the spinning wafer to leave a film of controlled thickness, then soft-bake it.

Expose the pattern. A scanner projects a reticle image, typically reduced four times, onto one field of the wafer, steps to the next field and repeats, aligning each layer to the previous one to within a few nanometres.
Develop the resist and etch, usually by reactive ion etching in a plasma, which removes material anisotropically so that vertical sidewalls are preserved rather than undercut.

Implant dopants by accelerating ionised phosphorus, boron or arsenic to energies of a few kiloelectronvolts to several megaelectronvolts, then anneal, often by rapid thermal or laser annealing lasting milliseconds, to repair lattice damage and activate the dopants without letting them diffuse far.

Deposit metal and dielectric layers for interconnection, typically copper by electroplating into etched trenches in a damascene process, and planarise after each layer by chemical-mechanical polishing. A modern chip has ten to twenty such wiring levels.
Repeat the pattern-etch-deposit cycle for every mask layer, commonly sixty to over a hundred masks in total.

Test each die on the wafer with a probe card, mark the failures, then dice the wafer, package the good dice and test again. The fraction of good dice is the yield, the number that determines profitability.

sections.heading: FinFET, Gate-All-Around and the End of the Flat Transistor
sections.body:
As channel lengths fell below about 100 nanometres, a family of problems collectively called short-channel
effects began to dominate. The essential difficulty is that the gate is supposed to have exclusive control over
the channel's potential, but as source and drain move closer together their own fields begin to influence the
channel too. The drain's field lowers the potential barrier the gate is trying to maintain, an effect called
drain-induced barrier lowering, so the transistor leaks when it should be off, the threshold voltage falls with
channel length, and the subthreshold slope degrades away from its 60 millivolt per decade ideal.

Conventional fixes ran out. Making the gate oxide thinner improves gate control but by 2005 it was down to
around 1.2 nanometres, five atomic layers, and tunnelling leakage through it was rising exponentially. The
answer, adopted by Intel at the 45 nanometre node in 2007, was to replace silicon dioxide with hafnium-based
high-permittivity dielectrics, which are physically thicker, so tunnelling is suppressed, but electrically
equivalent to a much thinner oxide because of their higher dielectric constant, together with metal gates to
avoid depletion effects in polysilicon.

That bought a generation. The structural answer came next: stop making the transistor flat. In a FinFET the
channel is a thin vertical fin of silicon standing proud of the wafer, and the gate wraps over its top and both
sides, so the gate surrounds the channel on three faces instead of one. Electrostatic control improves
dramatically, because almost every point in a fin only 5 to 10 nanometres wide is close to a gate surface. The
concept was demonstrated by Chenming Hu's group at Berkeley in the late 1990s, and Intel brought it to volume
production as Tri-Gate at 22 nanometres in 2011, with the rest of the industry following at 16 and 14
nanometres.

The successor, now entering production, is gate-all-around, in which the channel is a stack of horizontal
nanosheets or nanowires with the gate material completely surrounding each one on all four sides. Samsung
shipped a 3 nanometre gate-all-around process in 2022 and Intel's RibbonFET follows the same principle. Control
is better still, and sheet width can be tuned to trade drive current against area.

One point causes endless confusion and should be stated plainly. Process node names such as 5 nanometre or 3
nanometre no longer correspond to any physical dimension on the chip. They are marketing designations. In a
so-called 3 nanometre process the smallest actual features, gate lengths and metal pitches, are more like 12 to
25 nanometres. Comparing nodes across manufacturers by name is meaningless; the meaningful comparison is
transistor density in millions per square millimetre, together with power and performance at a given operating
point.

sections.heading: How Transistors Fail: Reliability Physics and Diagnosis
sections.body:
Transistors are extraordinarily reliable but not immortal, and knowing the failure mechanisms is what separates
a designer who produces equipment lasting twenty years from one whose product returns under warranty.

Electrostatic discharge is the commonest killer of discrete devices in handling. A gate oxide 2 nanometres
thick breaks down at a field around 10 million volts per centimetre, which corresponds to only a few volts
across it. A person walking on carpet can accumulate several thousand volts, and a discharge that a human cannot
even feel, below about 3,000 volts, will destroy an unprotected MOSFET gate instantly. Chips include on-die
protection diodes rated for a couple of kilovolts under the human body model, but bare devices and exposed
connectors demand wrist straps, conductive mats and grounded soldering irons.

Thermal failure is the commonest killer in service. Almost every degradation mechanism in silicon follows an
Arrhenius temperature dependence, with rate proportional to the exponential of minus an activation energy over
kT. A useful rule of thumb, accurate enough for planning, is that lifetime roughly halves for every 10 degrees
Celsius rise in junction temperature. A device running at 125 degrees rather than 85 degrees may last a
sixteenth as long. Thermal runaway is a specific hazard in bipolar devices, because a hotter junction conducts
more current at fixed base-emitter voltage, which produces more heat, which raises the temperature further; MOS
devices are largely self-protecting here because carrier mobility falls with temperature, so the on-resistance
rises and current is throttled.

Several slow wear-out mechanisms dominate integrated circuit lifetime. Electromigration is the gradual transport
of metal atoms by momentum transfer from flowing electrons, thinning interconnect until it opens; it sets a
current density limit of roughly one to two megaamps per square centimetre for copper. Time-dependent dielectric
breakdown is the accumulation of defects in the gate oxide until a conducting path forms. Bias temperature
instability, especially negative bias temperature instability in p-channel devices, shifts threshold voltage
over time under stress, slowing circuits until timing fails. Hot carrier injection occurs when high-field
carriers gain enough energy to be injected into the oxide, where they become trapped.

Soft errors are a distinct category worth knowing about because they are not failures of the device at all. A
cosmic-ray secondary neutron or an alpha particle from trace radioactive contamination in packaging can deposit
enough charge in a memory cell to flip a stored bit while damaging nothing. At sea level the rate is on the
order of a few thousand failures in time per megabit, where one FIT is one failure per billion device-hours,
rising sharply with altitude. This is why servers and avionics use error-correcting memory and why aircraft
electronics are designed with redundancy. The device is undamaged; the data is simply wrong, and the only
defence is detection and correction at the system level.

sections.heading: Limits, Successors, and What to Do When Something Fails
sections.body:
The transistor is approaching genuine physical limits, and it is worth being precise about which ones are real.
Gate lengths are already around 12 to 20 nanometres, meaning a channel perhaps forty silicon atoms long. Below
about 5 nanometres, quantum tunnelling of electrons directly from source to drain becomes significant regardless
of gate control, since the barrier is simply too thin. The 60 millivolt per decade subthreshold limit is set by
thermodynamics and cannot be beaten by any conventional field-effect device at room temperature. Silicon's
lattice constant is 0.543 nanometres, so a 3 nanometre feature is about five unit cells wide, and statistical
variation in the placement of individual dopant atoms already causes measurable device-to-device mismatch.

The responses now being pursued fall into three groups, and their prospects differ. Continuing dimensional
scaling with new geometries, including gate-all-around nanosheets, complementary FET designs that stack n and p
devices vertically, and backside power delivery, is well-established engineering with a visible roadmap through
roughly the early 2030s. Continuing density scaling by building upwards, using three-dimensional stacking,
chiplets on silicon interposers, and hybrid bonding of wafers face to face, is already shipping and probably has
more headroom than lateral scaling. Genuinely new device physics, including tunnel FETs and negative-capacitance
transistors that aim to beat the 60 millivolt limit, two-dimensional channel materials such as molybdenum
disulphide monolayers, carbon nanotube transistors, spintronic and photonic logic, remains at research stage
with no clear winner and a long history of overpromising.

Quantum computing deserves a specific caution, because it is frequently misrepresented as a successor. It is not
a faster general-purpose computer. It offers dramatic speed-up for a narrow class of problems, notably factoring
and quantum simulation, and no advantage whatsoever for most ordinary computation. Classical transistors will
run the world for the foreseeable future.

For practical work, a short diagnostic discipline handles most transistor-related failures. When a circuit does
not work, measure voltages rather than guessing. For a bipolar device in linear operation, a base-emitter
voltage near 0.6 to 0.7 volts indicates it is conducting; near zero means it is off; above 0.8 volts usually
means the junction is shorted. A collector sitting at supply voltage means the device is off or open; a
collector at almost zero means it is saturated or shorted. Test a suspect device out of circuit with a
multimeter's diode range: a good bipolar transistor reads like two diodes back to back from the base, and
conducts in neither direction between collector and emitter.

When a device has failed, always ask why before replacing it, because semiconductors rarely die of old age in
the field. Look for the upstream cause: inadequate heatsinking, a missing gate resistor, an inductive load
without a flyback diode, a supply transient, or a shorted output. Replacing the transistor without removing the
cause simply destroys the replacement.

guides.safetyNote: Working on electronics carries two distinct hazards. Mains-powered equipment can hold lethal charge in capacitors long after it is unplugged, particularly in switch-mode supplies and anything containing a cathode-ray tube, where several hundred to tens of thousands of volts may persist for minutes or longer; discharge capacitors deliberately through a resistor and verify with a meter before touching anything. Separately, static discharge you cannot feel will silently destroy semiconductor devices, so use a grounded wrist strap and antistatic packaging when handling bare components.

guides.title: The Integrated Circuit and Moore's Law
guides.summary: How the silicon chip works and how it came to double in complexity every two years for half a century. Covers the transistor and CMOS logic, photolithography and the full fabrication flow, what Moore and Dennard actually claimed, why the free lunch ended, and the physical and economic limits now reshaping the industry.

sections.heading: The Central Artefact of the Modern World
sections.body:
An integrated circuit is a complete electronic circuit — transistors, the wires connecting them, and often resistors and capacitors — fabricated as a single inseparable piece of semiconductor crystal, usually silicon. That description sounds modest. Its consequences are not. Essentially every computation performed on Earth, every telephone call routed, every image displayed, every engine timed and every heart monitored happens inside one. Roughly a trillion chips are manufactured each year. A modern high-end processor contains on the order of 100 billion transistors on a piece of silicon smaller than a postage stamp, each switch a few tens of atoms across in its narrowest dimension, and the entire assembly is sold for a price that, per transistor, is smaller than any manufactured object in history by many orders of magnitude.

That last fact is the important one, and it is what people are pointing at when they say Moore's Law. The cost of a transistor fell from roughly thirty dollars in 1960 to a small fraction of a millionth of a cent today, a decline of about a factor of a billion. No other technology has ever done anything remotely like this. Cars did not become a billion times cheaper. Neither did steel, or light, or air travel. The economic and social transformations of the last sixty years — personal computing, the internet, mobile telephony, machine learning — are downstream consequences of a single manufacturing cost curve that kept falling for fifty years.

Understanding chips means understanding two separate things that are easily conflated. The first is the physics: how a piece of doped silicon becomes a switch, how switches become logic, how logic becomes a computer. That part is elegant, comprehensible, and largely settled since the 1960s. The second is the manufacturing: how to print a hundred billion of those switches, all of them working, in a process with more than a thousand steps, at a yield high enough to be profitable. That part is arguably the most difficult thing the human species knows how to do, involves machines costing 400 million dollars each, and is where almost all of the difficulty and nearly all of the money now reside.

The scaling story sits on top of both. Moore's Law was never a law of nature; it was an observation about an industry, which then became a self-fulfilling roadmap that the industry organised itself to meet. It has been declared dead roughly once every five years since 1990, and something specific has genuinely died on several of those occasions — the frequency scaling that ended around 2005, the single-threaded performance growth that slowed after it, the straightforward cost-per-transistor decline that flattened around the 14-nanometre generation. What continues, in a changed form, is the accumulation of function on silicon, now pursued through three-dimensional structure, specialised architectures and advanced packaging rather than through simple shrinking.

sections.heading: Before the Chip: Tubes, Transistors and the Tyranny of Numbers
sections.body:
Early electronic computing ran on vacuum tubes. A tube is a small glass envelope containing a heated cathode that boils off electrons, an anode that collects them, and a grid between the two whose voltage controls the flow. It works as an amplifier and, driven hard, as a switch. ENIAC, completed in 1945, contained about 17,468 of them, consumed roughly 150 kilowatts, filled a room, and failed frequently: with tube lifetimes measured in thousands of hours, a machine with 17,000 of them suffers a failure every few hours by simple arithmetic. Tubes were also physically large, slow to switch by later standards, and required a warm-up.

The replacement arrived at Bell Telephone Laboratories in December 1947, when John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, working under William Shockley, demonstrated the point-contact transistor: two closely spaced gold contacts pressed onto a slab of germanium, in which a small current at one contact controlled a much larger current between the others. Shockley, irritated at being sidelined, worked out the theory of the more manufacturable junction transistor over the following weeks and published it in 1949. The three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Transistors were smaller, cooler, more reliable and faster than tubes, and by the mid-1950s they were displacing them. But they did not solve the deeper problem, which the engineer Jack Morton of Bell Labs named in 1957: the tyranny of numbers. Every discrete transistor, resistor, capacitor and diode in a circuit had to be individually manufactured, individually tested, individually placed, and individually soldered — typically by hand — with each of its two or three leads forming a separate joint. A circuit with 100,000 components required perhaps 300,000 solder joints, and each joint was an opportunity for failure. Reliability fell geometrically as complexity rose. Military and aerospace customers, who needed both complexity and reliability, felt this most acutely; the guidance computer for a missile could not be allowed to fail.

Several escape routes were attempted. The British engineer Geoffrey Dummer proposed in 1952, at a symposium in Washington, that electronics might be built as a solid block with no connecting wires, layers of insulating, conducting and amplifying material cut to perform their functions directly; he tried to build one and failed. The United States Army funded Micro-Module, an effort to standardise components into uniform wafers that could be stacked. The Air Force backed molecular electronics. All of these treated the problem as one of packaging rather than of fabrication.

The decisive insight was different and, in retrospect, simple. If all the components could be made out of the same material by the same process at the same time, then the number of components would stop mattering, because none of them would be separately handled. Complexity would become free. That idea occurred to two people, independently, within months of each other.

sections.heading: Kilby, Noyce and the Planar Process
sections.body:
Jack Kilby joined Texas Instruments in May 1958 and, as a new employee, had no vacation entitlement during the company's July shutdown. Working alone in a nearly empty building, he reasoned that since resistors and capacitors could be made from semiconductor material, an entire circuit could be built from a single piece of it.
