On 12 September 1958 he demonstrated a phase-shift oscillator built on a sliver of germanium about 11 millimetres long, with the components connected by fine gold wires bonded by hand. It worked. It was also ugly, fragile and not manufacturable at scale, precisely because of those hand-bonded flying wires.

Robert Noyce, co-founder of Fairchild Semiconductor, arrived at the same idea a few months later from a different direction, and his version solved the problem Kilby's had not. Fairchild had recently developed, largely through the work of the Swiss physicist Jean Hoerni, the planar process. Hoerni's insight was that a layer of silicon dioxide grown thermally on the silicon surface — silicon's native oxide, which is an excellent insulator and forms readily when the wafer is heated in oxygen or steam — could both protect the delicate junctions underneath from contamination and serve as a mask through which impurities could be selectively introduced. Every device was made flat, with all junctions terminating under the protective oxide.

Noyce realised in January 1959 that if the whole surface was already covered with an insulator, then metal could simply be deposited on top of it and patterned into interconnections, with holes etched through the oxide wherever a connection to the silicon below was needed. The wires became part of the same photolithographic process as the devices. Nothing had to be handled individually. That is the integrated circuit as it has been built ever since.

The patent history was contentious. Kilby filed in February 1959, Noyce in July 1959; Noyce's patent, being narrower and better drafted around the planar interconnect, issued first in 1961, while Kilby's issued in 1964. A decade of litigation ended in cross-licensing and an industry consensus that both were inventors. Kilby received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000; Noyce had died in 1990 and Nobel Prizes are not awarded posthumously.

Early adoption was driven by government. The Minuteman II missile guidance system and the Apollo Guidance Computer were the first large customers, and for a period in the mid-1960s the Apollo programme consumed a substantial fraction of all integrated circuits produced. Price fell from around 50 dollars per circuit in 1962 to about 2 dollars by 1968 as volumes rose. Commercial electronics followed, first in calculators — Kilby himself co-invented the handheld electronic calculator in 1967 largely to create a mass market — then in watches, then in everything.

sections.heading: Silicon, Doping and the Junction
sections.body:
Silicon is the fourteenth element, the second most abundant in the Earth's crust after oxygen, and it became the basis of the industry for reasons that are worth being specific about, because germanium got there first and was in several ways better.

A pure silicon crystal has each atom covalently bonded to four neighbours in a diamond lattice, with every valence electron committed to a bond. At absolute zero it is an insulator. At room temperature, thermal energy frees a small number of electrons across the band gap of 1.12 electron volts, leaving behind vacancies called holes that behave as mobile positive charges. Intrinsic silicon is therefore a poor conductor — its resistivity is around 2,300 ohm-metres, some fourteen orders of magnitude higher than copper.

Doping changes this completely. Introduce phosphorus, arsenic or antimony, all of which have five valence electrons, and the fifth electron has no bond to occupy; it is loosely bound and easily freed, so the material acquires mobile negative carriers and is called n-type. Introduce boron, gallium or indium, with three valence electrons, and a bond is left incomplete, creating a hole; the material is p-type. Doping concentrations are extraordinarily small — typically between one part in ten million and one part in ten thousand — yet they change conductivity by many orders of magnitude and set the electrical behaviour of every device.

Where n-type meets p-type, a junction forms, and here the essential asymmetry appears. Electrons diffuse from the n side into the p side and holes diffuse the other way; each leaves behind a fixed charged dopant ion, so a region depleted of mobile carriers builds up, carrying a built-in electric field that opposes further diffusion. Apply a voltage that reinforces this field, and almost no current flows; reverse it, and the barrier collapses and current flows freely. A junction is a diode, and diodes are the raw material of transistors.

Silicon's advantage over germanium was not its electron mobility, which is lower, nor its band gap alone. It was the oxide. Silicon dioxide grows on silicon as a dense, stable, adherent, electrically superb insulator with a breakdown field around 10 million volts per centimetre, and it masks the diffusion of common dopants. Germanium's oxide is water-soluble and useless. Silicon's larger band gap also permits operation up to about 150 degrees Celsius against germanium's roughly 75, and silicon can be purified and grown into single crystals of extraordinary perfection by the Czochralski method, in which a seed crystal is dipped into molten silicon and slowly withdrawn while rotating, pulling out a cylindrical boule now up to 300 millimetres in diameter with fewer than one defect per square centimetre and impurity levels below one part in a billion.

sections.heading: The MOSFET: The Switch Everything Is Built From
sections.body:
Almost every transistor manufactured today is a metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, universally abbreviated MOSFET. Its structure is simple enough to describe in a paragraph and subtle enough to have taken thirty years to make work reliably.

Take a p-type silicon substrate. Create two heavily doped n-type regions a short distance apart; call them the source and the drain. Between them lies p-type material, and because source-to-substrate and drain-to-substrate are both diodes pointing in opposing directions, no current can flow from source to drain no matter which way you push. Now grow a very thin layer of silicon dioxide over the gap and place a conducting electrode on top of it. That electrode is the gate, and it is separated from the silicon by an insulator, so no current flows into it at all.

Apply a positive voltage to the gate. The resulting electric field repels holes from the surface of the p-type silicon beneath and attracts the sparse free electrons. Above a certain threshold voltage, typically 0.2 to 0.5 volts in modern devices, so many electrons accumulate at the surface that the material there stops behaving as p-type and inverts to n-type. A thin conducting channel now bridges source and drain, and current flows. Remove the gate voltage and the channel vanishes. The device is a voltage-controlled switch that draws essentially no current at its control terminal — the gate is one plate of a capacitor, so it takes charge to switch but no steady current to hold.

That last property is why MOSFETs won. A bipolar transistor, the older type, requires continuous base current to stay on, so a circuit made of them burns power constantly. A MOSFET burns power only while switching.

The idea long predates its realisation. Julius Lilienfeld patented a field-effect device in 1925 and Oskar Heil in 1934, neither of them buildable with the materials of the time. Shockley tried in the 1940s and failed, because charge trapped at the semiconductor surface screened the field before it could reach the bulk; that failure is what drove him toward the bipolar device instead. The obstacle was finally removed when Mohamed Atalla at Bell Labs showed around 1959 that a carefully grown thermal oxide passivated the silicon surface, dramatically reducing those trapped states. Atalla and Dawon Kahng demonstrated the working silicon MOSFET in 1960.

Two flavours exist. The n-channel device described above conducts when its gate goes high. Swap all the dopings and you get a p-channel device, built in an n-type well, whose channel is made of holes and which conducts when its gate goes low. Having both types available, with exactly opposite behaviour, is what makes the dominant logic family possible, and it is why they are almost always fabricated together on the same die.

sections.heading: From Switch to Logic: How CMOS Works
sections.body:
Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor logic, CMOS, is the arrangement used in virtually all digital chips made since the mid-1980s. Its principle is that every logic gate is built from two complementary networks: a pull-up network of p-channel transistors connecting the output to the supply voltage, and a pull-down network of n-channel transistors connecting the output to ground, wired so that for any input combination exactly one network conducts.

The simplest case is the inverter, two transistors. Connect a p-channel device between the supply and the output and an n-channel device between the output and ground, and tie both gates to the same input. When the input is low, the p-channel device conducts and the n-channel one is off, so the output is pulled up to the supply: a high. When the input is high, the reverse happens and the output is pulled down to ground. The output is always the logical opposite of the input, and — crucially — in either steady state there is no path from supply to ground, so no current flows and no power is consumed.

A NAND gate takes four transistors: two n-channel devices in series to ground, two p-channel devices in parallel to the supply. The output goes low only when both inputs are high, because only then do both series devices conduct. A NOR gate is the dual, with the series and parallel arrangements swapped. Since NAND alone is functionally complete — every Boolean function can be built from NAND gates — a manufacturing process that can make good NAND gates can make any digital circuit whatsoever.

Above that level the hierarchy is one of composition rather than new physics. Gates combine into adders, multiplexers and flip-flops; flip-flops hold state and, clocked in unison, turn combinational logic into a synchronous machine; those machines become register files, arithmetic units, caches and control logic; and the assembly is a processor. Static random-access memory is six transistors per bit, a pair of cross-coupled inverters holding each other's state plus two access devices. Dynamic memory is one transistor and one capacitor, far denser but requiring refresh every few tens of milliseconds because the capacitor leaks. Flash memory adds a floating gate, an isolated conductor buried in the oxide onto which charge can be forced and where it will sit for years, shifting the transistor's threshold voltage and storing a bit without power.

The power story deserves emphasis because it drives everything later. Ideal CMOS burns energy only in transitions, at roughly one half times the capacitance times the supply voltage squared per switching event. Total dynamic power is that quantity times the switching frequency times the number of switching gates. The quadratic dependence on voltage is the single most important number in chip design.

sections.heading: Photolithography: Printing With Light
sections.body:
Everything on a chip is defined by photolithography, the process of projecting a pattern onto a light-sensitive coating and developing it, and this single step sets the industry's pace, its cost and its limits.

A wafer is coated with photoresist, a polymer whose solubility changes on exposure to light, spun on to a thickness of a few hundred nanometres. Light is projected through a photomask — a quartz plate carrying the pattern in opaque chrome — and through a reduction lens that shrinks the image, typically by a factor of four. Exposed resist is developed away, leaving a stencil. Material is then etched away, or dopants implanted, or metal deposited, only where the resist has opened. The resist is stripped and the cycle repeats. A modern process runs this loop 80 to 100 times, each with its own mask, building the device layer by layer.

Resolution is governed by the Rayleigh criterion, which states that the smallest resolvable feature equals a process constant k1 multiplied by the wavelength and divided by the numerical aperture of the lens. Three levers follow. Shorten the wavelength: the industry moved from mercury lamps at 436 and 365 nanometres to deep-ultraviolet excimer lasers at 248 and then 193 nanometres, and after twenty years stuck at 193 finally to extreme ultraviolet at 13.5 nanometres. Raise the numerical aperture: immersion lithography, introduced around 2007, floods the gap between lens and wafer with ultrapure water of refractive index 1.44, raising the effective aperture from about 0.93 to 1.35. Reduce k1: through phase-shifting masks, off-axis illumination, optical proximity correction that deliberately distorts the mask so diffraction produces the intended shape, and multiple patterning, in which a single layer is built from two, three or four separate exposures whose combined pattern is finer than any one could achieve.

Extreme ultraviolet lithography is worth describing because it is the most extraordinary machine in commercial existence. Because everything absorbs 13.5-nanometre light, including air and glass, the entire optical path is in vacuum and every optic is a mirror coated with forty to fifty alternating molybdenum-silicon layers, each pair a fraction of a wavelength thick, reflecting perhaps 70 per cent. The light source is generated by firing a carbon dioxide laser at droplets of molten tin fifty thousand times per second, twice per droplet, the first pulse flattening it and the second vaporising it into a plasma at around 220,000 degrees. Each machine costs 150 to 400 million dollars, weighs 180 tonnes, and is built by a single company, ASML of the Netherlands, which itself depends on Zeiss for the mirrors. The mirror figure accuracy is such that scaled to the size of Germany the largest deviation would be under a millimetre.

sections.heading: The Full Fabrication Flow
sections.body:
Turning sand into a working processor takes roughly three months of continuous processing across a thousand or more individual steps. The outline below is the standard flow for a logic chip, simplified but in the correct order.

Cleanliness dominates everything. A modern fab maintains ISO Class 1 conditions in the critical areas, meaning fewer than about ten particles larger than 100 nanometres per cubic metre of air — hundreds of thousands of times cleaner than an operating theatre. A single dust particle landing on a wafer destroys every die it touches. Air is recirculated through the entire cleanroom volume roughly ten times a minute, wafers travel between tools in sealed nitrogen-purged pods, and the human operators, who are the largest particle source in the building, are increasingly absent from the process areas altogether.
steps: Grow the crystal: purify metallurgical silicon to semiconductor grade, better than 99.9999999 per cent, then pull a single-crystal boule by the Czochralski method and saw it into wafers 300 millimetres across and about 775 micrometres thick.
Polish and clean: lap, etch and chemically-mechanically polish one face to a flatness measured in nanometres, then clean it in a sequence of acid and solvent baths.
Form isolation: etch shallow trenches between the areas where devices will sit and fill them with oxide, so neighbouring transistors cannot leak into one another.
Create wells: implant deep n-type and p-type regions, the substrate volumes in which p-channel and n-channel devices respectively will be built.
Grow or deposit the gate dielectric: for older nodes a thermal silicon dioxide layer as thin as 1.2 nanometres, about five atoms; for modern nodes a high-permittivity hafnium-based oxide instead.
Deposit and pattern the gate: originally doped polysilicon, since about 2007 a metal gate, patterned lithographically. This is the most critical dimension on the chip.

Implant source and drain: fire dopant ions at energies of a few kiloelectronvolts to hundreds, using the gate itself as a mask so the doped regions align to it automatically — the self-aligned gate, one of the key inventions of the field.
Anneal: heat the wafer rapidly, sometimes by laser to over 1,000 degrees for milliseconds, to repair implantation damage and move dopants onto lattice sites without letting them diffuse far.

Build the interconnect: deposit insulating layers, etch trenches and vias in them, line them with a barrier metal, electroplate copper into the openings and polish back the excess. Repeat ten to fifteen times to create the stacked wiring levels, whose total length on a large chip exceeds fifty kilometres.
Test at wafer level: probe every die electrically, mapping good from bad. Yields for a large, mature die may reach 90 per cent; for a new process on a big die they may start below 50.

Thin, dice, package and test again: grind the wafer down, saw or laser-cut it into individual dies, attach each to a package that provides mechanical protection and electrical connection, and run final tests, including burn-in at elevated temperature and voltage to precipitate early-life failures.

sections.heading: What Gordon Moore Actually Said
sections.body:
In April 1965, Gordon Moore, then director of research and development at Fairchild Semiconductor, wrote a short article for the thirty-fifth anniversary issue of Electronics magazine titled "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits". He had four data points and a projection. The most economical number of components per chip — the number at which cost per component was lowest — had roughly doubled every year since 1962, and he extrapolated that this would continue for another decade, reaching about 65,000 components on a single chip by 1975. The extrapolation proved close to right.

Three things about the original claim are consistently misremembered. First, it was fundamentally an economic statement, not a physical one. Moore's curve was of the minimum-cost complexity: at any moment there is a chip size beyond which yield losses outweigh integration savings, and it was that optimum that doubled. Second, the doubling period was annual, not eighteen months. Moore revised it in a 1975 talk at the International Electron Devices Meeting to a doubling every two years, having decomposed the historical gains into contributions from die size growth, feature shrinkage, and what he called device and circuit cleverness, and noted that the third contribution was largely exhausted. The frequently quoted eighteen months came from David House, an Intel colleague, who combined the two-year transistor doubling with concurrent frequency gains to estimate that performance doubled every eighteen months. Third, Moore never called it a law. Carver Mead, the Caltech professor, gave it that name around 1975.

What made the observation extraordinary was not that it described the past but that it organised the future. Once the industry believed in it, it became a coordination device. Equipment makers, materials suppliers, chip designers and fabs are separate companies with multi-year lead times, and all of them need to know what everyone else will deliver and when. From 1993 the International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors, a formal document produced by a consortium of industry bodies, published the expected specifications node by node, and the ecosystem invested against it. Moore's Law became less a prediction than a schedule that thousands of engineers were paid to meet, which is why it held so precisely for so long and why its slowing has been as much an institutional event as a physical one.

The numbers give the scale. Intel's 4004 in 1971 held 2,300 transistors at a 10-micrometre feature size. The 8086 in 1978 held 29,000. The Pentium in 1993 held 3.1 million. By 2010 a server processor held over a billion. In the 2020s the largest logic dies hold 50 to 100 billion, and stacked memory devices exceed that. Fifty-plus years of doubling amounts to a factor of tens of millions.

sections.heading: Dennard Scaling: The Physics That Made Shrinking Free
sections.body:
Moore's Law described how many transistors could be economically integrated. A separate and equally important result explained why smaller transistors were also better ones, and it is the reason the industry got faster and cooler chips as a byproduct of getting denser ones.

In 1974, Robert Dennard and colleagues at IBM published a paper on the design of miniaturised MOSFETs setting out a scaling rule. Take every dimension of a transistor — channel length, channel width, oxide thickness — and divide it by a factor, call it k, typically about 1.4 per generation so that area falls by half. Simultaneously divide the supply voltage by k and multiply the doping concentration by k. Under these rules the electric fields inside the device stay constant, which means the physics does not change: the device behaves like the old one, only smaller.

The consequences are remarkable. Area falls as k squared, so twice as many devices fit. Capacitance falls as k, and with the voltage also falling as k, the switching energy — one half capacitance times voltage squared — falls as k cubed. Delay falls as k, so the circuit can run about 1.4 times faster each generation. Power per transistor falls as k squared. Since the number of transistors per unit area rises as k squared, the power per unit area, the power density, stays constant. That is the crucial line: you could double the transistor count, raise the clock frequency by 40 per cent, and the chip would consume the same power and run at the same temperature. Performance improved for free, generation after generation.

This is what people experienced through the 1980s and 1990s. Clock speeds rose from 5 megahertz in 1981 to 1 gigahertz by 2000 and about 3.8 gigahertz by 2004 — nearly a factor of a thousand — with no fundamental change in how programs were written. Existing software simply ran faster on new hardware. A generation of programmers grew up assuming this was a law of nature, and the industry organised its economics around a replacement cycle driven by it.

A worked example fixes the magnitudes. Take a device with a 1-micrometre channel at 5 volts and scale it by k equal to 1.4. The channel becomes 0.71 micrometres, the supply 3.6 volts, the area 51 per cent of the original, the delay 71 per cent, and the switching energy 36 per cent. Two devices now fit where one sat, switching 1.4 times more often, for the same total power. That arithmetic, repeated every couple of years for three decades, is the whole of the golden age.

Two independent scaling laws were therefore operating at once, and confusing them causes most of the muddle in later discussions. Moore's Law is about density and cost, and in a weakened form it continues. Dennard scaling is about voltage, power and speed, and it stopped. When commentators say Moore's Law is dead and point at stagnant clock speeds, they are describing the end of Dennard scaling. When others reply that transistor counts still rise, they are describing Moore's Law. Both are correct about different things.

sections.heading: The Power Wall and the Turn to Parallelism
sections.body:
Dennard scaling broke around 2005, and the reason is leakage.

The rule required supply voltage to fall in step with dimensions. Supply voltage cannot fall unless threshold voltage falls with it, or the transistor will not turn on properly. But a MOSFET does not switch off cleanly at its threshold; below it, current falls exponentially, at a rate set by a quantity called the subthreshold slope, which is limited by thermodynamics to about 60 millivolts per decade of current at room temperature. That limit comes from the Boltzmann distribution of carrier energies and cannot be evaded by better engineering. Lowering the threshold by 60 millivolts therefore multiplies the off-state leakage current by ten. Meanwhile, gate oxides had thinned to a few atomic layers, at which point electrons tunnel quantum-mechanically straight through the insulator, adding gate leakage that also rises exponentially as thickness falls.

By the 130- and 90-nanometre generations, static leakage power had grown from a rounding error to a substantial fraction of total chip power, in some designs approaching half. Voltage scaling stalled around 1 volt and has since crept down only slowly, to roughly 0.7. With voltage no longer falling, switching energy stopped falling as k cubed and fell only as k, while density kept rising as k squared. Power density therefore began to increase. Intel's cancellation of the 4-gigahertz Pentium 4 in October 2004 is the conventional marker for the moment the industry conceded.

What followed is called the power wall, and its practical form is a thermal budget. A chip in a desktop can dissipate perhaps 100 to 250 watts before cooling becomes impractical; a phone processor perhaps 3 to 5 watts sustained. Since transistors keep getting denser but power per transistor no longer falls proportionally, not all of them can be switched at full speed simultaneously. The portion that must be left idle or slowed is called dark silicon, and by the mid-2010s it was estimated to exceed half the die at the most advanced nodes.

The architectural response was to stop raising frequency and start adding cores. If one core at 4 gigahertz is thermally impossible, four cores at 2.5 gigahertz may be feasible and deliver more total throughput. This shifted the burden onto software in a way that had never happened before: parallel speedup is bounded by Amdahl's Law, which states that if a fraction of a program is inherently serial, then no number of processors can speed it up by more than the reciprocal of that fraction. A program 90 per cent parallelisable cannot exceed a tenfold speedup regardless of core count. Two decades later, exploiting parallel hardware remains among the hardest problems in software engineering.

sections.heading: Going Vertical: FinFET, Gate-All-Around and the Node-Name Fiction
sections.body:
As channels shrank below about 30 nanometres, the flat transistor began to fail in a family of ways collectively called short-channel effects. With source and drain close together, the drain's own electric field starts reaching into the channel and pulling it partly open regardless of the gate — an effect named drain-induced barrier lowering. The gate loses control, leakage rises, and the threshold voltage becomes dependent on channel length, so ordinary manufacturing variation produces devices with wildly different behaviour.

The fix was to give the gate more grip by wrapping it around the channel. In a fin field-effect transistor, the channel is etched as a thin vertical ridge of silicon, a fin, and the gate is deposited over it so that it contacts the top and both sides. Three surfaces of control instead of one restores electrostatic authority and cuts leakage sharply. The concept was developed at Berkeley in the late 1990s by Chenming Hu, Tsu-Jae King Liu and Jeffrey Bokor; Intel put it into volume production in 2011 at its 22-nanometre node under the name tri-gate, and the rest of the industry followed by about 2014. Drive current is also improved because a device can have several fins in parallel, so transistor width becomes quantised in fin increments rather than continuously adjustable.

The next step, entering production from about 2022 onward, replaces the fin with horizontal sheets of silicon stacked above one another with the gate material filling the gaps entirely — gate-all-around, marketed as nanosheet or, in Intel's terminology, RibbonFET. The gate now surrounds the channel on all four sides, giving still better control, and sheet width can be tuned continuously, restoring a design freedom that FinFETs removed. Beyond that lie complementary FET structures stacking an n-channel device directly above a p-channel one, and backside power delivery, which moves the power distribution network to the underside of the wafer so the crowded front-side wiring can be devoted entirely to signals.

A caution about names is necessary. Node designations such as 5-nanometre or 3-nanometre no longer correspond to any physical dimension on the chip. Until roughly the 45-nanometre generation the number tracked the gate length; since then it has been a marketing label. In a nominal 5-nanometre process, gate lengths are perhaps 16 to 20 nanometres and the tightest metal pitch is around 28 to 30 nanometres. Worse, the names are not comparable between manufacturers: densities at one company's 7-nanometre node have been comparable to another's 10. The industry's own attempts to substitute meaningful metrics — transistor density in millions per square millimetre, or a composite of contacted gate pitch and metal pitch — have not displaced the marketing numbers in public usage.

sections.heading: The Economics: Rock's Law, Masks and Yield
sections.body:
The counterpart to Moore's Law is far less famous and considerably more brutal. Rock's Law, named for the venture capitalist Arthur Rock, observes that the capital cost of a semiconductor fabrication plant doubles roughly every four years. In 1970 a fab cost a few million dollars. In 1990, several hundred million. A leading-edge facility today costs 20 billion dollars or more, and the largest announced projects approach 40 billion. The two laws are on a collision course by construction: if the cost of the factory doubles every four years and the value of its output doubles every two, the arithmetic works only while volumes keep expanding.

The consequence has been relentless consolidation. In 2002 there were around 25 companies manufacturing at the leading edge. Today there are three that can produce the most advanced logic — TSMC in Taiwan, Samsung in South Korea, and Intel in the United States — and only one of those has consistently led. Everyone else either designs chips and has them made by a foundry, the fabless model pioneered in the 1980s and now dominant, or manufactures at trailing nodes where the economics remain benign and where, importantly, the majority of the world's chips by unit count are still made.

Mask costs shape design decisions directly. A full mask set for a leading-edge process costs several million to tens of millions of dollars, and multiple patterning multiplies the count. Combined with design and verification, the non-recurring engineering cost of a new advanced chip runs from 100 million to over 500 million dollars before a single unit ships. Only products expected to sell in enormous volume, or at enormous margin, can justify that, which is why leading-edge silicon is concentrated in phone processors, data-centre accelerators and a handful of other categories.

Yield is the other lever, and it obeys a simple statistical model. If defects are randomly distributed at density D over a die of area A, the fraction of dies with no defects is approximately e to the power of minus D times A — Poisson statistics, since the number of defects landing on a given die is a Poisson variable and yield is the probability of drawing zero. Real yield models add corrections for clustering, but the exponential dependence on area is the essential point: doubling die size does not halve yield, it squares the good fraction. A defect density of 0.1 per square centimetre gives 90 per cent yield on a 1-square-centimetre die and 37 per cent on an 8-square-centimetre one. This is why very large dies are extraordinarily expensive, why redundancy is built into memories and multi-core processors so that a die with one bad block can be sold as a lower-tier part, and why chiplets became attractive.

sections.heading: Designing a Chip: EDA, IP and Tape-Out
sections.body:
No human being has ever laid out a hundred billion transistors by hand, and no team could. Modern chip design is an exercise in automated synthesis from an abstract description, supported by a software industry — electronic design automation — that is small in revenue but utterly load-bearing, dominated by three firms: Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens EDA.

Design begins with a specification and an architecture, then descends through levels of abstraction. Behaviour is written in a hardware description language, usually SystemVerilog or VHDL, at the register-transfer level: a description of what data moves between registers on each clock edge, and what logic operates on it in between. This is code, but it describes structure rather than sequence, and reasoning about it requires a different mental model from software.

Logic synthesis then compiles that description into a netlist of specific gates drawn from a standard cell library — a set of pre-characterised layouts for inverters, NANDs, flip-flops and so on, supplied by the foundry and available in variants trading speed against area and leakage. Place-and-route tools then decide where each cell physically sits and how the wires connecting them are routed through the metal layers, solving an optimisation problem with billions of variables under constraints on timing, power, signal integrity and manufacturability. Static timing analysis verifies that every path from one register to the next completes within a clock period across the full range of process variation, supply voltage and temperature, usually at several corners representing worst and best cases simultaneously.

Verification consumes more effort than design — commonly cited as 60 to 70 per cent of the total. Simulation exercises the design against directed and randomly generated stimulus; formal verification proves properties mathematically rather than by testing; emulation runs the design on large arrays of field-programmable gate arrays fast enough to boot an operating system before silicon exists. The reason for the disproportion is economic: a functional bug discovered after manufacture requires a new mask set and a three-month respin, at a cost of millions and a schedule slip that may be fatal. The Pentium FDIV bug of 1994, an error in a lookup table affecting a small class of floating-point divisions, cost Intel 475 million dollars and remains the standard cautionary example.

Very little of a modern chip is designed from scratch. Processor cores, memory controllers, interface blocks for USB or PCI Express, and analogue components are licensed as intellectual property blocks, either as synthesisable code or as fixed layouts. Arm's business consists almost entirely of licensing such cores. The final database, once verified and checked against foundry design rules, is sent for manufacture in a step still called tape-out, after the magnetic tapes on which such data was once physically shipped.

sections.heading: Chiplets, Packaging and More Than Moore
sections.body:
When shrinking became expensive, the industry found gains in a direction it had long neglected: the package. For decades packaging was regarded as plumbing — a way to get signals off the die without breaking anything. It is now a primary axis of innovation, and the phrase advanced packaging describes a set of techniques that deliver, in aggregate, benefits comparable to a process generation.

The central idea is disaggregation. Instead of building one enormous die, build several smaller ones — chiplets — each optimised for its function and manufactured on whichever process suits it, then connect them within a single package at a density approaching on-die wiring. The economic argument is the yield exponential: four dies of 100 square millimetres each will collectively yield far better than one die of 400, and defective chiplets are discarded individually rather than condemning the whole assembly. The technical argument is heterogeneity: logic benefits from the newest node, but analogue circuits, input-output drivers and static memory scale poorly and are cheaper and often better on an older, mature process.

Several assembly technologies make this work. In 2.5-dimensional integration, chiplets sit side by side on a silicon interposer, a passive slab carrying dense wiring beneath them; this is how high-bandwidth memory stacks are placed beside a processor, connected by thousands of parallel wires. In true 3D integration, dies are stacked vertically and connected by through-silicon vias, vertical copper columns punched through the thinned silicon itself. Hybrid bonding takes this furthest, joining two wafers or dies directly copper-to-copper and oxide-to-oxide with no solder at all, achieving connection pitches under a micrometre and interconnect densities orders of magnitude beyond what bumps allow.

AMD's adoption of chiplets across its processor line from 2017, and its 3D-stacked cache products, demonstrated the commercial case decisively; Intel, Apple and others followed with their own packaging platforms. An industry standard for chiplet interconnection, Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express, was published in 2022 to permit mixing chiplets from different vendors, though a genuine open marketplace has been slow to appear.

The costs are real and worth stating. Splitting a design across chiplets adds latency and energy at every boundary crossed, since driving a signal between dies costs more than driving it across one; die-to-die links must be designed and verified as products in their own right; and testing a bare chiplet well enough to guarantee it before assembly, the known-good-die problem, is hard, because one bad chiplet ruins an expensive package. Thermal management is worse in a stack, since the die in the middle has no direct path to a heatsink.

Running alongside is a distinct trend usually labelled More than Moore. Rather than making transistors smaller, it integrates functions that are not digital logic at all — radio-frequency circuits, power management, microelectromechanical sensors such as accelerometers and microphones, image sensors, biological and chemical sensors, photonics. These do not follow Moore's Law and do not need to; their value lies in being integrated with logic rather than in being scaled. A modern phone contains dozens of such devices, and by unit volume they represent a large share of what the semiconductor industry actually makes.

sections.heading: Limits, Failure Modes and What Comes Next
sections.body:
Several hard boundaries are now visible, and it is worth distinguishing the ones that are genuinely fundamental from the ones that are merely expensive.

Atomic granularity is fundamental. A silicon lattice spacing is about 0.54 nanometres, so a channel 10 nanometres long contains fewer than twenty atoms end to end. Dopant atoms in such a volume number in the tens, and the difference between eighteen and twenty-two dopants is a measurably different transistor. This random dopant fluctuation, together with line-edge roughness of the printed patterns, makes variability an irreducible design problem rather than a manufacturing defect to be eliminated. Quantum tunnelling is likewise fundamental: below roughly 5 nanometres of channel length, electrons pass from source to drain regardless of the gate, and below about 1 nanometre of oxide thickness they pass through the gate dielectric. The 60-millivolt-per-decade subthreshold limit is thermodynamic and applies to any conventional field-effect device.

Heat is the practical binding constraint. Power density on an active region of a modern chip can locally exceed that of a nuclear reactor core per unit volume, and removing it through a few square centimetres of surface sets the ceiling on everything. Data centres now devote a substantial fraction of their capital and energy budgets to cooling, and liquid cooling has moved from exotic to routine.

Beyond these sit the reliability failure modes that determine how long a chip lasts. Electromigration is the gradual displacement of metal atoms by the momentum of flowing electrons, which thins wires until they open; it is why current density in interconnects is a design rule. Time-dependent dielectric breakdown is the slow accumulation of defects in the gate oxide until a conductive path forms. Negative-bias temperature instability shifts threshold voltages over years of operation. Hot carrier injection embeds energetic electrons in the oxide. Chips are designed with these ageing mechanisms budgeted in, typically for a ten-year life at specified temperature and voltage — which is also why overclocking and running hot genuinely shorten lifespan rather than merely voiding a warranty.

What continues is less a single trajectory than several. Structural innovation — gate-all-around, complementary stacking, backside power — has perhaps three or four generations of headroom. Packaging and chiplets have more. Architectural specialisation is currently delivering the largest gains: a tensor accelerator or video codec built for one task can outperform general-purpose logic by one to three orders of magnitude in energy per operation, which is why processors now bristle with fixed-function blocks. Further out lie genuinely different substrates — carbon nanotube and two-dimensional-material channels, superconducting logic, spintronics, photonic interconnect, and quantum computing, which solves a different problem class rather than replacing classical logic. None is close to displacing silicon CMOS, whose sixty-year accumulation of manufacturing knowledge is an asset no challenger can easily match.

guides.title: The Microprocessor Revolution
guides.summary: How the computer's central processor collapsed onto a single silicon chip, and what followed: the physics of transistors, the machines and companies that defined each generation, Moore's law and its end, and the architectural ideas that keep processors getting faster.

sections.heading: What a Microprocessor Is, and Why It Mattered
sections.body:
A microprocessor is a complete central processing unit — the part of a computer that fetches instructions, decodes them, performs arithmetic and logic, and moves data — fabricated on a single piece of silicon. That definition sounds like an engineering detail. It was in fact the hinge on which the second half of the twentieth century turned, because it changed computing from something a large organisation rented into something an individual could own.

To see why, consider what a processor was before 1971. The IBM System/360 Model 50, a mainstream commercial machine of 1965, implemented its processor across several large printed circuit boards populated with thousands of discrete components, housed in cabinets occupying a room, drawing tens of kilowatts, and costing on the order of a million dollars in the money of the day. A minicomputer such as the Digital Equipment Corporation PDP-8 shrank that to a refrigerator-sized box for around eighteen thousand dollars, which was revolutionary in its own right, but the processor was still dozens of chips wired together on backplanes. The cost of a computer was dominated by the cost of assembling and testing that interconnection.

Integration removed it. When the entire processor is patterned onto one die by a photographic process, the marginal cost of the hundredth thousand copies is essentially the cost of the silicon and the packaging, a few dollars. The design cost is enormous and fixed; the reproduction cost is trivial. That economic shape — high fixed cost, near-zero marginal cost — is the same shape as publishing, and it produced the same result: an explosion of volume and a collapse of price. A processor that cost the equivalent of a house in 1965 cost the equivalent of a restaurant meal by 1985 and is now given away inside a greetings card.

The consequences ran far beyond desktop computers. Because a microprocessor is small, cheap and low-powered, it can be embedded in things that are not computers at all. A modern car contains between fifty and a hundred and fifty of them, running the engine, the brakes, the airbags, the windows. A washing machine, a thermostat, a hearing aid, a light bulb, a passport, a credit card: all contain processors. By count, well over ninety-nine percent of all processors manufactured are embedded in objects whose users never think of them as computers. Roughly thirty billion or more are shipped each year, the overwhelming majority of them small microcontrollers costing well under a dollar.

The revolution therefore has two faces. The visible one is the personal computer, the mobile phone, the internet. The invisible one is the quiet saturation of the physical world with computation, which is arguably the larger change. Understanding how it happened requires understanding both the physics that made shrinking possible and the architectural ideas that turned raw transistor counts into useful speed.

sections.heading: Before the Chip: Valves, Transistors and the Minicomputer
sections.body:
The first electronic computers switched with vacuum tubes. ENIAC, completed in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania, used about 17,500 of them, filled a room of roughly 170 square metres, weighed 27 tonnes and drew around 150 kilowatts. Tubes worked by boiling electrons off a heated cathode and steering them with a grid, which meant every one of them was a small electric heater with a finite filament life. With 17,500 tubes and a mean tube life of a few thousand hours, something failed every day or two, and a substantial part of operating the machine was finding the dead one.

The transistor, demonstrated at Bell Telephone Laboratories in December 1947 by John Bardeen and Walter Brattain and explained theoretically by William Shockley, replaced the hot cathode with the controlled flow of charge carriers through a solid crystal. A transistor needs no heater, occupies a fraction of the space, switches faster, and can last decades. The physical principle is that a semiconductor such as silicon can be doped with impurities to have either an excess of mobile electrons or an excess of vacancies called holes, and that a junction between the two types passes current in one direction only. Arranging three such regions lets a small current or voltage at one terminal control a much larger current between the other two, which is the definition of an amplifier and, driven to its extremes, of a switch.

Transistorised computers arrived commercially in the late 1950s and changed the economics substantially, but they still had a fundamental problem that the industry of the time called the tyranny of numbers. Each transistor, resistor and capacitor was a separate physical object with wire leads that had to be individually placed and individually soldered. A machine with a hundred thousand components needed several hundred thousand hand-made joints, each of which could fail. Reliability and cost were dominated not by the components but by the connections between them.

Meanwhile the shape of computing was changing. The Digital Equipment Corporation PDP-8, launched in 1965 at $18,000, was small enough to sit in a laboratory and cheap enough for a department rather than an institution to buy. Over fifty thousand were eventually sold. It established that there was enormous latent demand below the mainframe price point, and it trained a generation of engineers and scientists to expect direct, interactive access to a machine rather than submitting punched cards to an operator.

The stage was therefore set by 1968 with three ingredients in place: a reliable solid-state switching device, a demonstrated market for smaller and cheaper machines, and a clearly identified bottleneck in the cost of interconnection. What was needed was a way to make the connections at the same time, and by the same process, as the devices themselves.

sections.heading: The Integrated Circuit and the Planar Process
sections.body:
The idea of building multiple components in one piece of semiconductor occurred independently to two people within a year of each other. Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrated a working oscillator on a single germanium bar in September 1958, with the components connected by fine gold wires bonded by hand. Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor arrived at the more consequential version in early 1959: build the components in silicon and connect them with metal traces deposited photographically on an insulating oxide layer covering the surface. Kilby's device came first; Noyce's method is what the industry actually uses, and the two men are jointly credited.

The enabling technique was the planar process, developed at Fairchild by Jean Hoerni in 1958. Silicon has a property that no other common semiconductor shares: heating it in oxygen grows a layer of silicon dioxide, ordinary glass, that adheres perfectly, is chemically stable, and is an excellent electrical insulator. That oxide can be used as a mask. The sequence is to grow oxide over the whole wafer, coat it with a light-sensitive polymer called photoresist, project an image of the desired pattern onto it through a mask, develop away the exposed resist, etch holes through the oxide where the resist has gone, and then introduce dopant atoms which enter the silicon only through those holes. Repeating this with different masks builds up transistors, resistors and, finally, aluminium wiring, all in registered layers.

The critical property of this process is that it is photographic rather than mechanical. Making a hundred transistors takes exactly the same time and effort as making one, because they are all patterned in the same exposure. The tyranny of numbers dissolves: interconnection becomes free. It is also why shrinking is so powerful. If the optics can resolve a finer feature, more devices fit on the same wafer, each costs less, and each also switches faster because the charge that must be moved is smaller. Cost and performance improve together, which is unusual in engineering and is the deep reason the industry has been able to run for six decades on a single strategy.

Early integrated circuits used bipolar transistors, which are fast but consume current continuously. The alternative, the metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor or MOSFET, works by using a voltage on an insulated gate electrode to attract carriers into a thin channel beneath it, switching the channel between conducting and non-conducting. A MOSFET's gate is insulated, so it draws essentially no steady current. MOS devices were initially slower and plagued by contamination that made their threshold voltages drift, and it took until the late 1960s to get them reliable. But they were far denser and used far less power, and complementary MOS, or CMOS, in which n-type and p-type transistors are paired so that one is always off, consumes power only while switching. CMOS eventually displaced everything else and remains the basis of essentially all digital chips.

sections.heading: 1971: The Intel 4004 and the Single-Chip Processor
sections.body:
The first commercial microprocessor came out of a contract job that nobody expected to be historic. In 1969 a Japanese calculator company, Busicom, approached Intel — then a three-year-old firm making memory chips — with a design for a printing calculator that required a dozen custom logic chips. Intel's Marcian Edward Hoff, known as Ted, argued that building twelve special-purpose chips was the wrong approach: it would be simpler and more flexible to build one general-purpose processor and store the calculator's behaviour as a program in a separate read-only memory. Federico Faggin, who joined Intel in 1970 from Fairchild bringing silicon-gate MOS technology with him, turned that architecture into a working circuit, assisted by Busicom's Masatoshi Shima. The result, released in November 1971, was the Intel 4004.

By modern standards it was almost comically limited. It contained about 2,300 transistors on a die of roughly 12 square millimetres, fabricated with a 10-micrometre process, ran at 740 kilohertz, and processed data four bits at a time — enough for a single decimal digit, which is exactly what a calculator needs. It could address 4,096 bytes of program memory and executed most instructions in eight or sixteen clock cycles, delivering something like 90,000 instructions per second. Intel's own advertisement described it, with fair accuracy, as a microprogrammable computer on a chip.

Two things about the 4004 mattered far more than its specifications. The first was the principle Hoff had insisted on: separating what the hardware can do from what it is currently doing. A fixed-function chip does one job forever. A processor plus a program memory does whatever the program says, so the same silicon serves a calculator, a traffic light controller, a scale, or a pinball machine. That converts a hardware design problem into a software problem, which can be solved faster, by fewer people, and changed after manufacture.

The second was a commercial decision. Busicom had paid for exclusive rights. When the calculator market turned brutally price-competitive, Intel's Robert Noyce negotiated to return $60,000 of the development fee in exchange for the right to sell the chip to anyone outside the calculator business. It is difficult to name a better bargain in industrial history.

Priority claims deserve a note, because the story is genuinely contested at the edges. Texas Instruments' TMS 1000, a single-chip microcontroller with memory on board, was developed in parallel and shipped in 1974. The Central Air Data Computer built by Garrett AiResearch for the F-14 Tomcat used a multi-chip MOS processor set designed by Ray Holt around 1970, classified until 1998. Four-Phase Systems' AL1 of 1969 had a comparable claim. What is not contested is that the 4004 was the first such device offered for general sale to any customer, which is what made it the start of an industry rather than a curiosity.

sections.heading: Inside a Processor: Fetch, Decode, Execute
sections.body:
Strip away six decades of refinement and every processor still does the same thing in a loop. Understanding that loop makes the rest of the field legible.

A processor holds a special register called the program counter, which contains the memory address of the next instruction. In the fetch step it presents that address on the memory bus and reads back a pattern of bits. In the decode step it interprets that pattern: a field of bits identifies the operation, other fields identify which registers or memory locations supply the operands and where the result goes. In the execute step it performs the operation, typically by routing the operands into an arithmetic logic unit — a block of combinational circuitry that can add, subtract, compare, and perform bitwise AND, OR, NOT and shifts — and routing the output back to a register. Then the program counter advances and the loop repeats, millions or billions of times per second.

Everything else is elaboration. Registers are a small set of extremely fast storage locations inside the processor, typically eight to thirty-two of them, used because reading external memory is slow. Condition flags record facts about the last result — was it zero, was it negative, did it overflow — so that a subsequent branch instruction can load a different value into the program counter and thereby make the machine choose between two paths. Subroutine call instructions push the current program counter onto a stack in memory and jump, so that a return instruction can pop it back and resume. Interrupts allow external hardware to force the processor to save its state and jump to a handler, which is how a keyboard or a network card gets attention without the program constantly checking.

Two design philosophies govern how the decode step works. In a hardwired design the instruction bits drive combinational logic directly, which is fast but rigid. In a microcoded design, an approach formalised by Maurice Wilkes in 1951, each machine instruction is itself a tiny program in an internal read-only memory, executed as a sequence of micro-operations that open and close gates along internal data paths. Microcode made complex instruction sets practical and made bug fixes possible after manufacture, and it is why the IBM System/360 family could offer one instruction set across wildly different hardware implementations.

The clock ties it together. A clock signal, a square wave distributed across the whole chip, defines the moments at which every storage element samples its input. The clock period must be long enough for the slowest signal path between two registers — the critical path — to settle. This is why clock frequency and logic depth trade against each other, and why a great deal of processor design consists of finding ways to shorten the longest path.

sections.heading: The Eight-Bit Era and the Birth of Personal Computing
sections.body:
Between 1972 and 1976 the microprocessor grew up. Intel's 8008, released in April 1972, extended the concept to eight bits and 16,000 bytes of memory, but it was awkward, slow, and required a dozen supporting chips before it could do anything useful. The 8080 of April 1974 was the machine that made the industry: about 6,000 transistors, a 2-megahertz clock, 64 kilobytes of addressable memory, a proper stack held in main memory rather than in a handful of internal registers, and usable interrupt handling. It cost $360 at launch, a figure chosen as a joke at the expense of IBM's System/360.

Competition arrived immediately and from people who had built the incumbent. Motorola's 6800, also 1974, offered a cleaner architecture. When Motorola declined to pursue a cheaper version, Chuck Peddle and a group of colleagues left, joined MOS Technology, and produced the 6502 in 1975 at $25 against the 8080's $360 — a price so far below the market that attendees at the trade show where it debuted assumed it was a fraud. It was not. The 6502 was simply small, with about 3,500 transistors, few registers, and a clever addressing scheme that used the first 256 bytes of memory as extended fast storage. Meanwhile Faggin left Intel to found Zilog and produced the Z80 in 1976, binary-compatible with the 8080 but with more registers, built-in memory refresh logic and a single power supply, which made it dramatically easier to design around.

These four chips carried personal computing into existence. The MITS Altair 8800, an 8080-based kit announced on the January 1975 cover of Popular Electronics for $439, sold thousands within months to an audience nobody had known existed, and it was for the Altair that Paul Allen and Bill Gates wrote the BASIC interpreter that founded Microsoft. In 1977 three machines shipped as finished consumer products: the Apple II with a 6502, the Commodore PET with a 6502, and the Tandy TRS-80 with a Z80. The 6502 went on to power the Atari 2600, the BBC Micro, the Commodore 64 and the Nintendo Entertainment System, making it very probably the most widely experienced processor of its generation.

The other decisive development was software portability. Gary Kildall, working at Digital Research, wrote CP/M in 1974, an operating system for 8080 and Z80 machines that isolated hardware differences behind a small layer called the BIOS. Because CP/M presented the same interface on every machine, a program written once ran on hundreds of different computers from dozens of manufacturers. That was the first demonstration of the pattern that has governed the industry ever since: the value accumulates in the software ecosystem, and hardware that cannot run the existing software is worth very little regardless of its technical merits.

sections.heading: Sixteen and Thirty-Two Bits: The Architectures That Stuck
sections.body:
The eight-bit machines were limited above all by address space. Sixteen address lines reach 65,536 bytes, and by the late 1970s that was becoming a serious constraint. The next generation widened both the data path and the address space, and in doing so established two architectural lineages that dominated the following forty years.

Intel's 8086, released in 1978, was a hurried design intended to hold the line while a more ambitious project matured. It processed sixteen bits at a time and reached one megabyte of memory, but did so through segmentation: a twenty-bit address was formed by taking a sixteen-bit segment register, shifting it left four bits, and adding a sixteen-bit offset. This preserved a degree of source compatibility with 8080 code, which was the commercial point, but it meant that data structures larger than 64 kilobytes were awkward for the next fifteen years. A cost-reduced variant, the 8088, was identical internally but had an eight-bit external bus, making it cheaper to build a system around.

Motorola's 68000, also 1979, was the opposite in spirit: a clean design with sixteen general-purpose 32-bit registers, a flat 24-bit address space reaching sixteen megabytes with no segmentation, and an orthogonal instruction set in which most operations worked with most addressing modes. Engineers overwhelmingly preferred it, and it powered the original Apple Macintosh, the Atari ST, the Commodore Amiga, Sun and Apollo workstations, and countless laser printers.

The decisive event was not technical. In 1980 IBM decided to enter the personal computer market and, to move quickly, built the machine from off-the-shelf parts with an open bus specification and documented interfaces. It chose the 8088, partly for cost and partly because Intel could supply in volume with a second source. It licensed an operating system from a small firm called Microsoft, which had bought a CP/M-like system from Seattle Computer Products, and — critically — licensed it non-exclusively. The IBM PC shipped in August 1981. Within two years Compaq had legally reverse-engineered the BIOS, clone manufacturers proliferated, and the combination of the x86 instruction set and Microsoft's operating system became the industry standard by sheer volume.

From that point Intel's architecture was locked in by compatibility rather than merit. The 80286 added protected mode and a 16-megabyte address space in 1982; the 80386 of 1985 was the real transformation, providing a full 32-bit architecture with paged virtual memory and a compatibility mode that ran existing 16-bit code unmodified. That backward-compatibility discipline, maintained through the 486, the Pentium, and AMD's 64-bit extension of 2003, is why a program compiled in 1985 will still execute on a processor sold today. It is also why x86 carries architectural decisions made under deadline pressure in 1978 into machines built in the 2020s.

sections.heading: Moore's Law and Dennard Scaling
sections.body:
In April 1965 Gordon Moore, then director of research at Fairchild, was asked to write a short piece for the thirty-fifth anniversary issue of Electronics magazine. He plotted the number of components on the most cost-effective integrated circuit for each year since 1959 — the counts were 1, 8, 16, 32 and 64 — noticed that the points fell on a straight line on a logarithmic scale, and extrapolated that the count would keep doubling annually for at least a decade. In 1975 he revised the rate to a doubling roughly every two years. That observation, named Moore's law by Carver Mead, held with remarkable fidelity for half a century.

It is essential to be clear about what it is. Moore's law is not a law of physics. It is an observation about an economic and engineering trajectory, and to a large extent it became a self-fulfilling prophecy: the industry adopted it as a planning target, coordinated roadmaps around it, and invested to hit it. The quantity it describes is transistors per chip at minimum cost per transistor — a statement about economics, not speed.

The companion principle that turned density into performance was described by Robert Dennard and colleagues at IBM in 1974 and is called Dennard scaling. If every linear dimension of a MOSFET is reduced by a factor k, and the supply voltage is reduced by the same factor, then several things follow from the physics. The area falls by k squared, so k squared times as many transistors fit. The capacitance of each device falls by k, and since the delay of a gate is proportional to capacitance times voltage divided by current, the device switches roughly k times faster. Most importantly, dynamic power, which is proportional to capacitance times voltage squared times frequency, falls in such a way that power per unit area stays constant. That last point is the magic: chips could get denser and faster without getting hotter.

For roughly thirty years the two together delivered compounding gains of a kind unmatched in any other industry. Between 1971 and 2000, transistor counts rose from 2,300 to 42 million, clock frequencies from 0.74 megahertz to over 1,000 megahertz, and cost per transistor fell by something like six orders of magnitude. A 2020s processor contains tens of billions of transistors, and a single one of them costs less than a millionth of a cent.

Dennard scaling broke first, around 2004 to 2006, for a specific physical reason. Threshold voltage cannot be reduced indefinitely, because a transistor with a very low threshold leaks current when it is supposed to be off, and that leakage rises exponentially as the threshold falls. Since supply voltage must stay comfortably above threshold, supply voltage stopped scaling. With voltage fixed, power density began rising with every shrink, and the free lunch ended.

sections.heading: RISC, CISC and the Argument About Instruction Sets
sections.body:
Through the 1970s instruction sets grew steadily more elaborate. The reasoning was sound at the time: memory was expensive and slow, compilers were weak, and much code was written in assembly language by hand. If a single instruction could copy a string, evaluate a polynomial or manage a stack frame, programs would be shorter and would need fewer memory accesses. The Digital VAX, introduced in 1977, took this furthest, offering hundreds of instructions with a dozen addressing modes usable almost interchangeably, including a single instruction that evaluated a polynomial.

In the late 1970s and early 1980s several groups independently questioned it. John Cocke's team at IBM working on the 801 project, David Patterson's group at Berkeley, and John Hennessy's at Stanford all reached a similar conclusion from measurement rather than taste: compilers overwhelmingly emitted a small subset of simple instructions, the elaborate ones were rarely used, and the microcode needed to support them lengthened the critical path and slowed down the common cases. Patterson coined the term RISC, reduced instruction set computer, for the alternative, and the older style was retroactively named CISC.

The RISC discipline is a set of related constraints rather than merely a smaller instruction count. Instructions are fixed-length, typically 32 bits, so fetching and decoding need no sequential parsing. Only explicit load and store instructions touch memory; all arithmetic operates register to register, which is why the style is sometimes called load-store architecture. There are many registers, typically 32, so that intermediate values rarely spill to memory. Addressing modes are few and simple. Instructions are designed so that each can complete in one pipeline stage, which makes pipelining efficient. The cost is that programs contain more instructions, so RISC trades memory bandwidth, which was becoming cheap, for simplicity in the hardware, which was becoming the bottleneck.

The commercial history is more interesting than the technical argument. RISC designs — MIPS, SPARC, IBM's POWER, DEC's Alpha, and Acorn's ARM — dominated workstations and servers through the 1990s and were consistently faster per transistor. But x86 survived because software compatibility mattered more than efficiency in the volume market, and because Intel found a way to have it both ways. From the Pentium Pro of 1995 onward, x86 processors decode their complex instructions in hardware into simple internal micro-operations and execute those on a RISC-like core. The architecture visible to software stayed CISC; the machine underneath became RISC. Both camps could claim vindication.

Today the distinction has largely dissolved as a performance argument and survives as a licensing and power-efficiency one. ARM, originally designed by Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber at Acorn in 1985 for a desktop computer, turned out to be superbly suited to battery-powered devices precisely because its simplicity kept the decoder small and the power low. That accident of fit put ARM into virtually every mobile phone on Earth, and more recently into laptops and data centres.

sections.heading: Pipelining, Caches and Out-of-Order Execution
sections.body:
Raw transistor count does not produce speed by itself. Turning devices into performance required a sequence of architectural ideas, each of which extracts more work from the same clock.

Pipelining is the first and most important. Rather than completing one instruction before starting the next, the processor divides the work into stages — classically fetch, decode, execute, memory access and write-back — and keeps a different instruction in each stage simultaneously, like an assembly line. With five stages the machine can retire one instruction per clock cycle instead of one every five, a fivefold improvement without any faster transistors. Pipelining also permits higher clock rates, because each stage does less work and so the critical path is shorter. The Pentium 4 pushed this to twenty and later thirty-one stages specifically to chase clock frequency.

Pipelines stall on hazards. A data hazard occurs when an instruction needs a result that is still in flight; the fix is forwarding, routing the result directly from one stage to another before it is written back. A control hazard occurs at a branch, because the processor does not know which instruction to fetch next until the branch resolves several stages later. The fix is branch prediction: hardware that records the recent behaviour of each branch and guesses, speculatively executing down the predicted path and discarding the work if wrong. Modern predictors, using multi-level history tables and neural-inspired perceptron schemes, achieve accuracies above 95 percent, which is essential because a misprediction on a deep pipeline costs fifteen to twenty cycles.

Caches solve a different problem. Processor speed grew far faster than memory speed, opening a gap sometimes called the memory wall: a main-memory access that took a few cycles in 1980 takes 200 to 400 cycles today. A cache is a small, fast memory holding recently or nearby used data, exploiting the empirical fact that programs reference a small working set repeatedly. Modern designs use a hierarchy: a level-one cache of perhaps 32 to 64 kilobytes accessible in four cycles, a level-two of a megabyte at fifteen cycles, a shared level-three of tens of megabytes at forty. Cache design — associativity, line size, replacement policy, prefetching — determines a great deal of real-world performance, and writing software that respects cache behaviour often matters more than the algorithm's theoretical complexity.

Superscalar execution issues several instructions per cycle by duplicating functional units. Out-of-order execution goes further: the processor examines a window of dozens or hundreds of pending instructions, tracks their true data dependencies through register renaming, and executes any whose operands are ready regardless of program order, then retires the results in order so that the illusion of sequential execution is preserved. Simultaneous multithreading, marketed as hyper-threading, fills the remaining idle slots with instructions from a second thread. Together these mechanisms mean a modern core sustains perhaps two to six instructions per cycle on ordinary code, though the enormous machinery required to find that parallelism now consumes far more transistors and power than the arithmetic it feeds.

sections.heading: The Clock Wall and the Turn to Multiple Cores
sections.body:
For thirty years the simplest way to make software faster was to wait. Clock frequencies climbed from 740 kilohertz in 1971 to 100 megahertz in 1994 to 1 gigahertz in 2000, and existing programs sped up proportionally with no effort from anyone. Then it stopped. Frequencies reached roughly 3 to 4 gigahertz around 2004 and have essentially stayed there for two decades. Understanding why is important, because it explains the shape of every processor built since.

The cause is power density. Dynamic power in CMOS is approximately the switched capacitance multiplied by the square of supply voltage multiplied by frequency. Historically each shrink cut both capacitance and voltage, so frequency could rise while power per unit area held constant. When threshold voltage stopped falling — because a lower threshold means exponentially higher leakage current in the off state, and leakage was already approaching a third of total chip power by the mid-2000s — supply voltage stopped falling too. With voltage pinned near 1 volt, raising frequency raises power linearly, and worse, sustaining a higher frequency in a given process requires a higher voltage, so power rises closer to the cube of frequency. Intel's cancelled 4-gigahertz Pentium 4 and the abandoned Tejas project, which reportedly would have dissipated 150 watts, marked the practical wall. Cooling a chip that dissipates more than roughly 100 to 150 watts across a square centimetre with air is a genuinely hard problem, since that is a heat flux comparable to a cooktop element.

The industry's response was to spend the transistors Moore's law still provided on more cores rather than a faster one. Two cores at 3 gigahertz deliver twice the theoretical throughput of one at 3 gigahertz for the same clock and roughly twice the power, whereas one core at 6 gigahertz would need far more than twice the power and is not achievable anyway. Dual-core desktop chips arrived in 2005; mainstream desktop parts now carry eight to twenty-four cores, and server parts well over a hundred.

This shifted an enormous burden onto software. A single-threaded program gains nothing from additional cores. Extracting benefit requires decomposing work into concurrent tasks, which introduces data races, deadlocks and non-deterministic bugs that are among the hardest classes of defect to reproduce and fix. Amdahl's law sets the ceiling: if a fraction s of a program is inherently sequential, the maximum speedup from any number of processors is 1 divided by s. A program that is 95 percent parallelisable can never exceed twentyfold speedup no matter how many cores are available.

A further constraint, identified around 2011, is dark silicon. Because power scaling has failed while density scaling continued, a chip may contain more transistors than can be powered simultaneously within its thermal budget. Designers responded with aggressive power gating, dynamic frequency scaling that briefly boosts one core while others idle, and heterogeneous designs pairing a few large fast cores with several small efficient ones.

sections.heading: Embedded Processors, Microcontrollers and the Mobile Era
sections.body:
The visible history of microprocessors is about desktop computers, but the overwhelming majority of processors ever made have gone into things that are not computers. Understanding this branch is necessary to understand the revolution's real scale.

A microcontroller is a complete computer on one chip: processor core, program memory, data memory, and peripherals such as timers, analogue-to-digital converters and serial interfaces, all integrated so that a working system needs almost no external components. Texas Instruments' TMS 1000 of 1974 established the category. Today an 8-bit microcontroller with a few kilobytes of flash memory costs between ten and fifty cents in volume and draws microamps in sleep mode, and it is cheaper to use one than to design equivalent fixed logic. The consequence is that they are everywhere: in a modern car, in the fifty to a hundred and fifty control units managing engine timing, anti-lock braking, airbag deployment, climate, and each individual window and mirror; in appliances; in toys; in industrial sensors; in medical devices.

The design priorities in this world are inverted relative to desktop computing. Determinism often matters more than throughput, because a system that must respond to an event within a guaranteed 50 microseconds cannot tolerate the unpredictable timing that caches and out-of-order execution introduce. Power matters enormously, because a device may need to run for ten years on a coin cell, which permits an average current of a few microamps and forces designs that sleep almost all the time and wake for milliseconds. Cost matters to the cent, because volumes are in the hundreds of millions. Real-time operating systems, or often no operating system at all, replace the general-purpose kind.

The mobile phone represents the convergence of the two worlds and is where ARM's dominance was won. ARM Holdings does not manufacture chips; it licenses designs and instruction-set architectures to companies that integrate them into their own systems on a chip. That business model let Apple, Qualcomm, Samsung, MediaTek and others build processors tailored to their products, combining ARM cores with graphics processors, image signal processors, cellular modems and, latterly, neural network accelerators on a single die. A modern phone chip contains fifteen to twenty billion transistors and delivers performance that would have qualified as a supercomputer in the 1990s, within a power budget of a few watts, because it must not become uncomfortably hot in a hand.

Two further shifts deserve mention. Systems on a chip made the distinction between processor and computer largely meaningless, since the whole machine is now one component. And RISC-V, an open instruction-set architecture published by Berkeley in 2010 and free of licensing fees, has begun to erode the assumption that an architecture must be a proprietary product, with adoption growing rapidly in embedded and accelerator roles.

sections.heading: How a Chip Is Actually Manufactured
sections.body:
Semiconductor fabrication is arguably the most precise manufacturing process humans perform, and its physical reality explains why leading-edge factories cost twenty billion dollars and why only three firms still build the most advanced chips.

The starting material is a wafer of monocrystalline silicon, typically 300 millimetres across, sliced from an ingot grown by the Czochralski method in which a seed crystal is slowly withdrawn from molten silicon while rotating. The crystal is purer than almost any other manufactured material, with impurities below one part per billion.

Everything is then built up in layers by repeating one cycle: deposit a film, coat it with photoresist, project a pattern through a mask, develop, etch the exposed material, strip the resist. A leading-edge process repeats variants of this sixty to a hundred times, each aligning with the previous to within a few nanometres.

Photolithography sets the limit on feature size. Optical resolution is roughly the wavelength divided by twice the numerical aperture, so shorter wavelengths draw finer lines. The industry moved from mercury lamps to 248-nanometre and then 193-nanometre deep-ultraviolet excimer lasers, then bought another decade through immersion lithography, in which water between lens and wafer raises the effective numerical aperture.
