Extreme ultraviolet lithography at 13.5 nanometres needs vacuum because air absorbs the light, mirrors rather than lenses, and a source made by striking molten tin droplets with a laser fifty thousand times a second.

Contamination is the enemy throughout. A single particle a fraction of a micrometre across can destroy a die, so the work happens in cleanrooms holding fewer than one particle per cubic foot, and operators wear garments that protect the wafer from the human rather than the reverse.
steps: Grow a monocrystalline silicon ingot by the Czochralski method, then saw it into wafers and polish them to an atomically flat mirror finish.
Grow or deposit the working film: thermal silicon dioxide for insulation, polysilicon or metal for gates, or a metal layer for wiring.
Spin on photoresist to a uniform thickness of a fraction of a micrometre and bake it to drive off solvent.
Expose the resist through a patterned mask using a stepper, which projects a reduced pattern onto one die site at a time and then steps to the next.
Develop the resist, dissolving either the exposed or the unexposed regions depending on whether the resist is positive or negative.
Etch the underlying film where it is now uncovered, usually with a reactive plasma that removes material almost vertically so sidewalls stay steep.
Implant dopant atoms by accelerating ions into the exposed silicon, then anneal to repair lattice damage and activate the dopant.
Strip the remaining resist, clean the wafer, and repeat the cycle for the next layer, aligning to registration marks within a few nanometres.
Build the interconnect stack: ten or more layers of copper wiring separated by low-permittivity insulators, planarised by chemical-mechanical polishing.
Probe-test each die on the wafer, mark the failures, then saw the wafer apart and package the good dies.
Bin the packaged parts by tested speed and power, since variation means nominally identical dies perform differently.

sections.heading: Graphics Processors, Accelerators and the End of One Chip for Everything
sections.body:
When single-core performance stopped improving rapidly, the field's attention shifted from making one general-purpose processor faster to building specialised hardware that does one class of work far more efficiently. This has proved to be the defining trend of the past two decades.

The graphics processing unit is the clearest case. Rendering three-dimensional graphics involves performing the same arithmetic on millions of independent vertices and pixels, which is embarrassingly parallel work with regular memory access patterns. That workload suits a completely different design: instead of a few complex cores with deep out-of-order machinery predicting branches, a GPU uses thousands of simple arithmetic units executing in lockstep, with wide memory interfaces and enough concurrent threads that memory latency is hidden by switching to other work rather than by caching. A high-end GPU sacrifices single-thread performance entirely and in return delivers ten to fifty times the arithmetic throughput per watt on suitable problems.

The pivotal moment was the recognition that many non-graphics problems have the same shape. NVIDIA released CUDA in 2007, providing a general programming model for its hardware, and scientific computing, financial simulation, cryptography and, most consequentially, machine learning migrated onto GPUs. Training a large neural network is dominated by dense matrix multiplication, the single operation GPUs perform best, and the resulting demand reshaped the entire semiconductor industry within about fifteen years.

Specialisation went further into fixed-function accelerators. Google's tensor processing unit, first deployed internally around 2015, implements a systolic array of multiply-accumulate units designed for exactly one job. Every phone contains dedicated blocks for video encoding and decoding, image processing, and cryptography, because a hardwired unit performing a specific transform can be one or two orders of magnitude more energy-efficient than general-purpose code doing the same work. Bitcoin mining moved from processors to GPUs to field-programmable gate arrays to fully custom chips within about four years, each step delivering a large efficiency gain, which is a compressed demonstration of the whole pattern.

The trade-off is generality. A specialised unit that fits its workload is transformative; the same silicon is worthless when the workload changes. This is a serious commercial risk given that designing a leading-edge chip costs hundreds of millions of dollars and takes three years, during which the algorithm it was built for may be superseded. It also fragments the software ecosystem, since code must now be written or compiled for each target.

The architectural consequence is that the interesting unit of design is no longer the processor but the system on a chip: a collection of heterogeneous engines sharing memory, with the general-purpose cores increasingly acting as coordinators that dispatch work to accelerators rather than doing it themselves. Data movement, not arithmetic, has become the dominant cost in both time and energy, which is why memory bandwidth and on-package memory now drive design more than clock speed does.

sections.heading: Failure Modes: Defects, Bugs, Wear and Security
sections.body:
Processors fail in several distinct ways, and confusing them leads to bad diagnosis. It is worth separating manufacturing defects, design errors, wear-out mechanisms and architectural vulnerabilities.

Manufacturing defects are unavoidable at these scales. A wafer carries randomly distributed flaws — particles, crystal dislocations, lithographic imperfections — and any die containing one in a critical place does not work. The fraction of working dies is the yield, and because defects are roughly Poisson-distributed, yield falls exponentially with die area. This is why large chips are disproportionately expensive and why the industry increasingly builds big processors from several smaller chiplets bonded together, and why designs include redundant cache rows and spare cores that can be disabled to salvage a partly defective die. Parts are then binned by tested speed, which is why nominally identical chips are sold at different frequencies.

Design errors are ordinary. The most famous is the Pentium FDIV bug of 1994, in which five entries were missing from a lookup table used by the floating-point division algorithm, producing wrong results in the fourth significant digit for certain rare operand pairs. Intel initially argued that the error would affect a typical user once in 27,000 years, was forced by public pressure into an unconditional recall, and took a charge of $475 million. Published errata lists for modern processors run to hundreds of entries; many are worked around by microcode updates or by the operating system, which is why processors now accept signed microcode patches at boot.

Wear-out is real but slow. Electromigration gradually moves metal atoms along conductors carrying high current density, eventually opening a void in a wire. Time-dependent dielectric breakdown degrades the extremely thin gate insulator, which in advanced processes is only a few atomic layers thick. Negative-bias temperature instability shifts threshold voltages over years of operation. All of these accelerate sharply with temperature and voltage, which is the concrete reason that running a chip hot or overvolted shortens its life, and why designs target roughly ten years at rated conditions.

The newest failure class is architectural. Speculative execution, the technique that lets a processor guess past a branch and do work in advance, was assumed to be invisible to software because wrong guesses are discarded. Spectre and Meltdown, disclosed in January 2018, showed that discarded speculative work leaves traces in the cache that can be measured by timing, allowing a program to read memory it should not be able to reach. The vulnerabilities were not bugs in any single chip but consequences of a performance technique used industry-wide for twenty years, and mitigating them cost real performance. A steady stream of related side-channel attacks has followed. The general lesson is that a mechanism invisible in the architectural specification can still be observable through timing, power or electromagnetic emission, and that performance optimisations and isolation guarantees are in genuine tension.

sections.heading: Limits, Honest Uncertainty and What Comes Next
sections.body:
It is fair to say that the classical form of the microprocessor revolution has ended, and worth being precise about which parts have ended and which have not.

Dennard scaling ended around 2005, and with it the automatic frequency gains. Moore's law in its original economic sense — cost per transistor falling with each generation — has been faltering since roughly the 16-nanometre node, because the multiple-patterning and extreme-ultraviolet steps required to keep shrinking cost more than the density gain saves. Transistors still get smaller, but they no longer reliably get cheaper, which removes the mechanism that drove the whole trajectory. Process node names, meanwhile, have become marketing labels rather than measurements: a so-called 3-nanometre process contains no feature that is 3 nanometres across, and the numbers are not comparable between manufacturers.

Hard physical limits are approaching. A silicon lattice spacing is about 0.54 nanometres, so a channel a few nanometres long is only a handful of atoms, at which point quantum tunnelling lets carriers pass through a barrier that classical physics says should stop them. Leakage, variability between nominally identical devices, and heat removal all worsen. Gate-all-around transistor structures, which wrap the gate entirely around a stacked channel, and three-dimensional stacking of dies buy further generations, but nobody credibly claims another factor of a thousand in density from silicon alone.

Several directions are being pursued and it is genuinely uncertain which will matter. Chiplet-based designs and advanced packaging, in which many small dies are bonded on an interposer with very high bandwidth between them, are already in production and look durable. Domain-specific accelerators continue to deliver large gains where a workload is stable. Photonic interconnect addresses data movement rather than computation. Carbon nanotube and two-dimensional-material transistors have been demonstrated in laboratory processors but face severe manufacturing obstacles. Quantum computing is often mentioned in this context and should be understood clearly: it is not a faster general-purpose processor, it addresses a narrow class of problems, and useful fault-tolerant machines remain a research goal with a genuinely unknown timeline.

For a practitioner, the useful conclusions are pragmatic. Performance now comes from parallelism, from data locality, and from choosing the right hardware for the workload, rather than from waiting for a faster clock. Energy per operation, not operations per second, is the binding constraint in almost every context from a phone to a data centre. Software efficiency has regained real economic value after decades in which hardware improvement made it optional.

And the industry has acquired a strategic fragility worth noting plainly. Leading-edge fabrication is concentrated in a handful of facilities, extreme-ultraviolet lithography systems come from a single manufacturer, and a modern chip's supply chain crosses many national borders. That concentration is a consequence of the extraordinary fixed costs the process demands, and it is now a matter of open geopolitical concern rather than a technical footnote.

guides.title: History of the Personal Computer
guides.summary: The story of how computers shrank from room-sized institutional machines to devices owned by individuals: the microprocessor breakthrough, the hobbyist era, the Apple II and IBM PC, the graphical interface, the software industry, portability, the internet, and the smartphone that ended the PC's reign.

sections.heading: What 'Personal' Meant: An Orientation
sections.body: For the first three decades of electronic computing, a computer was an institution, not a possession. Machines like the ENIAC of 1945 filled rooms, consumed the electricity of a small neighbourhood, and were tended by teams in white coats; even in 1970, a respectable computer cost as much as a house and belonged to a corporation, a university, or a government agency. Ordinary people encountered computing, if at all, as punch cards in a utility bill. The personal computer inverted that relationship. Within a single decade, roughly 1975 to 1985, computing became something an individual could buy, own, program, break, and fix, sitting on a desk at home. That inversion is one of the defining economic and cultural events of the twentieth century, and understanding how it happened requires holding several threads at once. There was a hardware thread: the relentless miniaturization of electronics, formalized as Moore's law, which packed the switching elements of a room-sized machine onto a fingernail of silicon and kept doubling the count every couple of years. There was a commercial thread: established computer companies, most famously IBM and Digital Equipment Corporation, largely dismissed small machines until outsiders forced their hand, and the industry that emerged was built substantially by hobbyists, dropouts, and startups. There was a software thread: a computer is only as personal as what it can do, and the machines became indispensable the moment programs like the VisiCalc spreadsheet gave businesses a reason to buy them. And there was an ideological thread, often underestimated: in the counterculture of 1960s California, activists and engineers around ventures like the People's Computer Company and the Homebrew Computer Club argued explicitly that computing power should belong to individuals rather than institutions, a conviction that shaped who built these machines and how. The result of these converging threads was not merely a smaller computer but a new kind of object. A personal computer was general-purpose, meaning its owner could make it do arbitrary new things by loading software; it was interactive, responding immediately at a keyboard rather than through batch jobs submitted and returned hours later; and it was owned, which meant experimentation carried no permission slip. Those three properties, far more than any particular chip or company, are what the history is about. This guide traces the arc from the mainframe world through the microprocessor breakthrough of 1971, the hobbyist explosion of 1975, the consumer machines of 1977, the IBM PC of 1981 and the clone industry it accidentally spawned, the graphical revolution taken from Xerox's research labs by Apple and Microsoft, the rise of portable machines and the internet-connected PC of the 1990s, and finally the smartphone era, in which the personal computer's own descendants ended its dominance while completing its founding promise: a computer for every person.

sections.heading: Before the Micro: Mainframes, Minis, and Time-Sharing
sections.body: The personal computer did not spring from nothing; it was the third act of a story about shrinking cost and shrinking distance between human and machine. The first act was the mainframe era. Machines of the 1950s and 1960s, dominated by IBM and especially its System/360 family announced in 1964, were operated in batch mode: programmers wrote code on paper, punched it onto cards, handed the deck to operators, and received printed output hours or days later. Computing was a scarce industrial resource, scheduled like machine time in a factory, and an IBM mainframe leased for thousands of dollars per month. The second act was the minicomputer, made possible when transistors and then early integrated circuits replaced vacuum tubes. Digital Equipment Corporation's PDP-8, introduced in 1965 at about 18,000 dollars, was the size of a refrigerator rather than a room, and its successor the PDP-11 became the workhorse of laboratories and engineering departments everywhere. Minis put the machine in the same room as its users, and a generation of scientists learned to program with their hands on the actual switches. Alongside the hardware shrank the social distance, through time-sharing: systems such as MIT's CTSS in 1961 and the Dartmouth Time-Sharing System in 1964 let dozens of people use one computer simultaneously through typewriter-like terminals, each user enjoying the illusion of a private machine. Dartmouth's system mattered doubly because its creators, John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz, designed a deliberately friendly language for it, BASIC, whose simple line-numbered programs could be learned in an afternoon; BASIC would become the native tongue of the personal computer a decade later. Time-sharing bred a culture of interactive computing, of games, of shared program libraries, and of the first email and chat systems, mostly on university PDP-10s. By the early 1970s the trajectory was visible to anyone who cared to extrapolate: each hardware generation cost a tenth as much as the last, and each brought the user closer to the machine. A few visionaries said so out loud. Alan Kay at Xerox sketched the Dynabook in 1972, a notebook-sized personal computer for children, and coined the term personal computer in roughly its modern sense; Douglas Engelbart had already demonstrated in 1968, in what is now called the Mother of All Demos, a working system with a mouse, windows, hypertext links, and live collaboration, technologies that would take twenty years to reach the mass market. What blocked the personal computer in 1972 was not imagination but economics: a machine with a processor, memory, and terminal still cost tens of thousands of dollars because its logic was assembled from hundreds of discrete chips. Collapsing all that logic onto one chip was the step that remained, and it arrived from an unexpected direction, a contract to build calculator components.

sections.heading: The Microprocessor: A Computer on a Chip
sections.body: The enabling invention of the personal computer was the microprocessor, a complete central processing unit fabricated on a single piece of silicon, and it arrived almost by accident. In 1969 a Japanese calculator company, Busicom, contracted the young Intel Corporation to build a set of twelve custom chips for a printing calculator. Intel engineer Ted Hoff proposed a radical simplification: instead of twelve fixed-function chips, build one general-purpose processor that could be programmed to act like a calculator, plus memory chips to hold the program. Federico Faggin, using the new silicon-gate transistor technology he had pioneered, squeezed the design into working silicon, and in November 1971 Intel advertised the result, the 4004, as a computer on a chip. It was laughably weak by mainframe standards, handling data four bits at a time with about 2,300 transistors and a clock of 740 kilohertz, but it established the pattern: processing power as a mass-produced component, priced at tens of dollars rather than tens of thousands. Intel followed quickly with the eight-bit 8008 in 1972 and then the pivotal 8080 in 1974, which ran at 2 megahertz, addressed 64 kilobytes of memory, and was genuinely capable of running a small computer system. Competitors multiplied the possibilities. Motorola's 6800 appeared in 1974; a breakaway team from Motorola at MOS Technology shipped the 6502 in 1975 at the disruptive price of 25 dollars when the 8080 sold for hundreds, and the 6502 went on to power the Apple II, the Commodore PET and 64, the Atari machines, the BBC Micro, and the Nintendo Entertainment System. Zilog, founded by Faggin after he left Intel, produced the Z80 in 1976, an enhanced 8080-compatible that became the heart of the TRS-80, countless CP/M business machines, and the Sinclair Spectrum. Underneath this proliferation ran the engine that made each generation inevitable: Gordon Moore's 1965 observation, revised in 1975, that the number of transistors that could be fabricated economically on a chip doubled roughly every two years. Moore's law was never a law of nature but a self-fulfilling industrial roadmap; companies planned products, factories, and prices around the doubling, and by doing so made it come true for five decades. The doubling explains the whole shape of personal computer history: the 4004's 2,300 transistors became the 8086's 29,000 in 1978, the 386's 275,000 in 1985, the Pentium's 3.1 million in 1993, and passed a billion in the 2000s, while the cost per transistor fell about a hundred-million-fold. Equally important was what the microprocessor commoditized. Once the processor was a catalogue part, anyone with a soldering iron and a few hundred dollars could design a computer, and the barrier to entering the computer industry collapsed from building a semiconductor company down to reading a datasheet. The people who walked through that open door were not IBM's engineers; they were hobbyists.

sections.heading: 1975: The Altair 8800 and the Hobbyist Explosion
sections.body: The machine that detonated the personal computer era was, by any practical measure, nearly useless, and that fact is itself instructive. The Altair 8800, designed by Ed Roberts of MITS, a struggling calculator company in Albuquerque, New Mexico, appeared on the cover of the January 1975 issue of Popular Electronics as a kit costing 397 dollars, built around Intel's 8080 processor. It shipped with 256 bytes of memory, no keyboard, no screen, and no storage; the owner programmed it by flipping front-panel toggle switches to enter binary instructions and read the results from a row of red lights. Roberts hoped to sell a few hundred; thousands of orders arrived within weeks, revealing a pent-up demand nobody in the established industry had believed existed. The Altair's true product was possibility, and its most important consequences were the institutions and companies that condensed around it. Its open S-100 bus, the connector into which expansion boards plugged, became a de facto standard, and dozens of small firms sprang up selling memory boards, serial cards, and disk controllers, creating the first personal computer ecosystem. In Menlo Park, California, the Homebrew Computer Club began meeting in March 1975 so hobbyists could swap parts and ideas; its mimeographed newsletter and combative show-and-tell sessions incubated more than twenty companies, including Apple. And in Cambridge, Massachusetts, a Harvard undergraduate named Bill Gates and his friend Paul Allen saw the Popular Electronics cover and telephoned MITS claiming, falsely but only temporarily, that they had a BASIC language interpreter running for it. Working on a simulated 8080, they produced one in eight weeks; Allen hand-loaded it from paper tape on a real Altair he had never touched, and it worked. Micro-Soft, as it was first styled, was founded in April 1975 on that interpreter, and BASIC became the operating environment of the entire early industry. The era also staged its first great ideological fight. Hobbyists freely copied the paper tapes of Microsoft BASIC, and in February 1976 the twenty-year-old Gates published an Open Letter to Hobbyists accusing them of theft and arguing that software must be paid for if anyone was to write it professionally; the club's culture of free exchange, descending through figures like Lee Felsenstein from the community-access ideals of the People's Computer Company, never accepted the argument, and the tension between proprietary and shared software has structured the industry from that day to the present. Rivals and successors crowded in behind the Altair: the IMSAI 8080, famous later from the film WarGames; Processor Technology's Sol-20 with a keyboard and video output; and the Cromemco and North Star machines that turned S-100 hardware into serious small-business systems. By 1976 a complete industry existed in embryo, with hardware makers, a software company, magazines like Byte, retail stores, and trade shows, all waiting for the machine that would carry computing past the soldering hobbyist to the ordinary customer.

sections.heading: 1977: The Trinity — Apple II, PET, and TRS-80
sections.body: Nineteen seventy-seven was the year the personal computer became an appliance: three machines arrived fully assembled, with keyboard and video output, that a customer could carry home, plug in, and use. The press later called them the 1977 Trinity. The Commodore PET 2001, announced first, came from a calculator company whose founder Jack Tramiel had acquired MOS Technology, giving Commodore its own 6502 processor supply; the PET integrated keyboard, monitor, and cassette drive into one angular metal case for 795 dollars and sold especially well to schools. The Tandy TRS-80 Model I, built around the Z80 and sold for 599 dollars through Radio Shack's three thousand American stores, was the volume champion of the late 1970s precisely because of that retail reach; a customer in a small town could buy a computer where he bought batteries, and Tandy sold hundreds of thousands. The machine that defined the category, though, was the Apple II. Steve Wozniak's design, refined from his hand-built Apple I of 1976, was a virtuoso piece of engineering economy: a 6502 at 1 megahertz whose circuitry generated colour graphics and sound with a handful of chips, wrapped by Steve Jobs's insistence in a friendly moulded plastic case and sold for 1,298 dollars. Two decisions made it durable. Wozniak gave it eight internal expansion slots, over Jobs's objection, so the machine could grow; and in 1978 Apple shipped the Disk II floppy drive, again a Wozniak tour de force that used software to replace most of a disk controller's hardware, making the Apple II the cheapest machine with fast, reliable storage. The Apple II family stayed in production for sixteen years and carried the company to its 1980 public offering, one of the largest of its era. What turned these consumer machines into business necessities was software, above all one program. In 1979 Dan Bricklin, a Harvard business student who watched professors erase and recompute entire blackboard ledgers cell by cell, wrote with Bob Frankston the first electronic spreadsheet, VisiCalc, initially only for the Apple II. A financial model that took an afternoon to recompute by hand updated instantly when one number changed, and accountants who saw it bought whatever computer ran it; VisiCalc became the archetypal killer application, the program that by itself justifies the purchase of a machine, and contemporaries estimated a large fraction of Apple IIs were bought purely to run it. Alongside it grew a genuine software industry: the WordStar word processor on CP/M business machines, the dBASE II database, and Microsoft's languages. By 1980 the personal computer had proven itself in the home, the classroom, and the small business, and the sales curves were impossible for anyone to ignore, including the company whose name was synonymous with computing itself.

sections.heading: The IBM PC: The Establishment Arrives
sections.body: When IBM decided in 1980 to enter the personal computer market, it was the most powerful computer company on Earth, and its problem was itself: IBM's normal development process took years and built everything in-house. A skunkworks team of about a dozen people under Don Estridge in Boca Raton, Florida, code-named Project Chess, was given twelve months and permission to break every corporate rule. They bought the processor from Intel, choosing the 8088, a version of the 16-bit 8086 with an 8-bit external bus that kept supporting chips cheap. They bought the operating system from outside too, and that transaction became the most consequential business deal in the industry's history. IBM approached Digital Research, whose CP/M ruled business micros, but negotiations stalled; Microsoft, already contracted for languages, offered to supply an operating system it did not have, bought a CP/M workalike called 86-DOS from Seattle Computer Products for a total of about 75,000 dollars, polished it into PC DOS, and, crucially, retained the right to license the same software to other manufacturers as MS-DOS. The IBM PC, model 5150, launched in August 1981 at 1,565 dollars for a base configuration with 16 kilobytes of memory, a cassette port, and IBM's superbly engineered keyboard. It was technically conservative but competent, and it carried the three letters that made computers respectable to corporate purchasing departments; the saying of the era was that nobody ever got fired for buying IBM. Sales demolished forecasts, hundreds of thousands in the first year, and by 1983 the PC had displaced the Apple II as the business standard, VisiCalc's successor Lotus 1-2-3 became its killer application, and Time magazine had named the computer Machine of the Year for 1982. IBM's openness was deliberate and double-edged. The PC used off-the-shelf parts, a documented expansion bus, and a published technical reference containing the full source listing of its BIOS, the firmware layer that boots the machine and mediates hardware access, because IBM wanted an ecosystem of add-on boards and software. The one thing it owned was that BIOS code, protected by copyright. Compaq, founded in 1982 by three Texas Instruments managers, financed a clean-room reverse engineering effort: one team of engineers who had never seen IBM's code read the published listing and wrote a specification of what the firmware did, and a second, legally quarantined team implemented new code from the specification alone. The result was a fully compatible BIOS that copyright could not touch, shipped in the Compaq Portable in 1983, which sold 53,000 units in its first year, a startup record. When Phoenix Technologies began selling clean-room BIOS chips to all comers in 1984, the last barrier fell: anyone could now assemble a fully IBM-compatible computer from catalogue parts plus MS-DOS, and hundreds of firms did. IBM had created the industry standard and, in the same stroke, guaranteed it would not control it.

sections.heading: Clone Wars: How the Standard Escaped Its Maker
sections.body: The decade after 1984 is the story of the IBM-compatible standard outgrowing IBM, and of the centre of gravity shifting from the machine's assembler to the suppliers of its two irreplaceable components, the processor and the operating system. The clone industry competed the price of a business computer down relentlessly: Compaq set the quality benchmark, Dell, founded by a University of Texas freshman in his dormitory in 1984, pioneered built-to-order direct sales that cut out the dealer margin, and by the late 1980s no-name assemblers in Taiwan and the United States sold compatibles for a fraction of IBM's prices. The compatibles were often better as well as cheaper: in 1986 Compaq, not IBM, was first to ship a machine built on Intel's 32-bit 80386 processor, a public demonstration that the standard's technical leadership had left Boca Raton. IBM tried to recapture control in 1987 with the PS/2 line, whose Micro Channel expansion bus was faster than the open AT bus but proprietary and royalty-bearing; the clone makers simply declined to follow, standardized among themselves, and the market followed the clones. IBM remained a large seller, but the architecture was now called the PC compatible, not the IBM PC, and IBM's share slid from dominance toward the single digits until it sold its PC division to Lenovo in 2005. The economics of the standard concentrated profit in its two chokepoints. Intel supplied the processors, and after ending the practice of licensing second sources fought a long legal war with its licensee AMD, which in 1991 won the right to sell its own 386-compatible chips, beginning the two-supplier rivalry that still defines the x86 processor market. Microsoft's position was stronger still, because MS-DOS was licensed per machine to every clone maker, often under contracts that charged a royalty on every computer shipped whether or not DOS was installed, an arrangement the United States government eventually forced Microsoft to abandon in 1994. Every clone sold anywhere in the world paid the same two tolls, and by the early 1990s Intel and Microsoft, not any computer maker, captured most of the industry's profit, a structure summarized in the word Wintel. The standard's openness at every other layer produced ferocious commodity competition and world-changing price declines: the machine that cost 3,000 dollars in 1984 cost under 1,000 by 1995 while becoming fifty times faster. It also produced remarkable longevity through backward compatibility. Each processor generation, the 286, 386, 486, and Pentium, still booted the software of its predecessors, and businesses could carry two decades of accumulated programs forward across hardware generations, a continuity no rival platform matched and a large part of why challengers with technically superior designs, from the Amiga to the Macintosh, could never dislodge the compatible from the office desk.

sections.heading: Home Computers: The 8-Bit Boom and Bust
sections.body: While the business world standardized on the PC, a parallel and even larger world of cheap home computers flourished, crashed, and left a deep cultural legacy. The home machines were built to a price, sold in department stores, and plugged into the family television. In the United States the defining company was Commodore, whose founder Jack Tramiel, a Auschwitz survivor with the motto that business is war, used his ownership of chip maker MOS Technology to undercut everyone. The VIC-20 of 1981 was the first computer to sell for under 300 dollars and the first to pass a million units; its successor the Commodore 64, launched in 1982 at 595 dollars and soon far cheaper, remains by most accounts the best-selling single computer model of all time, with lifetime sales usually estimated between twelve and seventeen million. The 64's hardware explains its hold on memory: 64 kilobytes of RAM, the VIC-II graphics chip with hardware sprites and scrolling, and the SID sound chip, a genuine three-voice synthesizer whose character defined the sound of a generation of game music. In Britain, Clive Sinclair's ZX81 and ZX Spectrum brought prices lower still, the Spectrum of 1982 costing 125 pounds, and the government-backed BBC Micro from Acorn put a robust, expandable machine in nearly every British school; the Spectrum seeded the British games industry, and Acorn's engineers, seeking a faster processor for a successor machine, designed the ARM chip in 1985, which decades later would power essentially every smartphone. Japan standardized differently, with the MSX specification and strong domestic lines from NEC, Sharp, and Fujitsu. The boom's end in America was violent. Tramiel provoked a price war in 1983, halving the 64's price repeatedly; Texas Instruments, selling its 99/4A below cost to fight him, lost hundreds of millions and quit; Atari, mismanaged under Warner ownership, collapsed alongside the coincident video game crash of 1983, and the American home computer market consolidated even as machines kept selling by the million. A late golden generation of 16-bit home machines, Commodore's Amiga with its astonishing custom chips for graphics and digital video, and the Atari ST beloved of musicians for its built-in MIDI ports, kept creative computing vibrant into the early 1990s before both companies failed and the falling price of PC compatibles absorbed their markets. The cultural legacy of the 8-bit era outweighs any balance sheet. These machines booted directly into BASIC, presenting every child not with a desktop of icons but with a blinking prompt that asked to be programmed; type-in program listings from magazines taught a generation to code, and the bedroom programmers of the Spectrum and 64 founded studios that still lead the games industry. An enormous share of the software engineers born between 1965 and 1980 wrote their first line of code on a home computer wired to a television, and the machines' limitations, kilobytes of memory and processors near 1 megahertz, taught an economy of craft that its veterans still praise.

sections.heading: Xerox PARC: Inventing the Interface
sections.body: Nearly every element of the modern computer interface, overlapping windows, icons, menus, the mouse pointer, what-you-see-is-what-you-get editing, laser printing, and the office network connecting them, existed in working form by 1975 inside a single building: the Xerox Palo Alto Research Center. Xerox, rich from photocopier patents and fearful of a paperless future, founded PARC in 1970 and hired brilliantly, taking Bob Taylor, who had funded the ARPANET, to run the computer lab, and recruiting veterans of Douglas Engelbart's Augmentation Research Center nearby. Engelbart's own 1968 demonstration in San Francisco had already shown a live audience the mouse, which he had invented with Bill English in 1964, along with windows, hypertext, and screen sharing, but his oN-Line System ran on a mainframe and was aimed at trained knowledge workers. PARC's synthesis was to put such power into a personal machine. The Alto, first running in 1973, gave each user a computer with a full-page bitmapped display, in which every screen pixel is backed by memory and can be drawn individually, making arbitrary fonts and graphics possible; a three-button mouse; and a connection to Ethernet, the local networking scheme Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs invented at PARC in 1973 precisely so Altos could share files and the world's first laser printer, Gary Starkweather's invention, also built there. On this hardware PARC's software teams created the modern working environment: Butler Lampson and Charles Simonyi's Bravo editor showed text on screen exactly as it would print; Smalltalk, the language and environment built by Alan Kay's Learning Research Group with Dan Ingalls and Adele Goldberg, pioneered overlapping windows, pop-up menus, and object- oriented programming as a unified vision of personal computing that Kay framed with his Dynabook ideal of a computer for children of all ages. About two thousand Altos were eventually built for internal use and research partners, so PARC employees lived a decade ahead of the world, emailing, laser printing, and window-managing in 1975. Xerox's management, oriented to copier sales, never successfully commercialized the work; its one direct attempt, the 1981 Star office system, was technically visionary, introducing the desktop metaphor with document icons and folders, but cost 16,595 dollars per workstation before the required network and printer and sold only tens of thousands. The ideas escaped anyway, through publications, through departing researchers who founded or staffed Adobe, 3Com, and Microsoft's applications group, and through one famous door: in December 1979 Steve Jobs traded Apple pre-IPO stock for two demonstrations of Smalltalk, and the Apple engineers he brought, several of whom Apple then hired away from PARC along with Larry Tesler, left convinced they had seen the future. Jobs later said PARC had shown him three revolutions, the graphical interface, object programming, and networking, and that he had been so blinded by the first that he initially missed the other two.

sections.heading: Lisa and Macintosh: The GUI Goes Mainstream
sections.body: Translating PARC's research into a product ordinary people could afford took Apple two attempts, a palace intrigue, and one of the most famous advertisements ever broadcast. The first attempt, the Lisa, shipped in January 1983 as the first mass-market computer with a graphical user interface. Its software was in several respects ahead even of PARC, contributing inventions now universal: the pull-down menu bar, the double-click, the clipboard with cut, copy, and paste, named by Larry Tesler, who had come from PARC and campaigned against modes, states in which the same keystroke means different things. But the Lisa cost 9,995 dollars, ran slowly on its 5-megahertz Motorola 68000, and sold about 10,000 units in year one; corporate buyers stayed with the IBM PC. The second attempt began as a skunk project under Jef Raskin, who wanted a 500-dollar appliance computer and named it for his favourite apple variety, the McIntosh. Steve Jobs, exiled from the Lisa team, took the project over in 1981, grafted the Lisa's mouse-and-windows interface onto Raskin's appliance concept, and drove a small team wearing pirate flags to build what he called an insanely great machine. The Macintosh, launched on 24 January 1984 at 2,495 dollars, packed a 68000 processor, 128 kilobytes of memory, a 400-kilobyte 3.5-inch floppy drive, and a sharp black-on-white 9-inch bitmapped display into a friendly upright case that smiled at the user when it booted. Its introduction was theatre: the Ridley Scott television commercial 1984, aired during the Super Bowl, showed an athlete shattering a Big Brother telescreen, promising that Apple would save computing from IBM's conformity, and Jobs pulled the machine from a bag on stage and let it introduce itself in synthesized speech. The Mac's constraint was memory; 128 kilobytes was too little for its ambitious graphics, and serious use awaited the 512K model and the 1986 Mac Plus. Its salvation was a niche that valued what only it could do. With Apple's LaserWriter printer in 1985, Adobe's PostScript page description language, and Aldus PageMaker, the Mac created desktop publishing: a designer could compose a page of mixed type and images on screen and print it at professional quality, work that had required typesetting bureaus, and publishing, advertising, and education became Apple strongholds that sustained the platform for a decade. Jobs himself lost a boardroom struggle with the chief executive he had recruited, John Sculley, and left Apple in September 1985 to found NeXT, whose elegant Unix-based workstations sold poorly but whose software would return to rescue Apple twelve years later. The Macintosh settled into a profitable minority share, hovering near a tenth of the market, proof that the graphical interface was what users wanted, and a standing challenge that the dominant DOS world had not yet answered.

sections.heading: Microsoft's Long Game: From DOS to Windows 95
sections.body: Microsoft's conquest of the personal computer's software layer was not a single victory but a fifteen-year campaign of persistence, leverage, and timing. Through the 1980s its foundation was MS-DOS royalties from every clone maker, but Bill Gates understood early that the graphical interface would eventually replace the command line; Microsoft was among the Macintosh's first application developers, and announced its own DOS-based windowing layer, Windows, in 1983, more than two years before it could ship the barely usable Windows 1.0 in November 1985 with awkward tiled, non-overlapping windows. Windows 2.0 in 1987 brought overlapping windows and provoked Apple's great copyright lawsuit claiming the look and feel of the Macintosh; Apple lost in 1992, courts holding that most disputed elements were either licensed under a 1985 agreement or were unprotectable ideas rather than copyrightable expression, a ruling that effectively legalized the graphical desktop as common property. Through the same years Microsoft publicly partnered with IBM on OS/2, a serious next-generation operating system, while quietly hedging. The breakthrough came in May 1990 with Windows 3.0, the first version that was fast, attractive, and stable enough for ordinary offices, thanks substantially to the 386 processor's memory management; it sold ten million copies in two years, Microsoft chose Windows over OS/2 and effectively ended the IBM partnership, and the vast DOS software world began migrating. Microsoft's applications strategy compounded the platform victory: Word and Excel, honed first on the Macintosh, were bundled in 1990 into Microsoft Office, which within a few years crushed the incumbent category kings WordPerfect and Lotus 1-2-3, aided by their late and clumsy Windows versions. The climax was Windows 95, launched on 24 August 1995 with a 300-million-dollar campaign licensing the Rolling Stones' Start Me Up for its new Start button. Windows 95 merged DOS and Windows into one product with 32-bit preemptive multitasking, long file names, the taskbar, and plug-and-play hardware detection; customers queued at midnight, seven million copies sold in five weeks, and the PC's identity completed its shift from a machine that ran DOS to a machine that ran Windows, soon on well over ninety percent of desktops. Parallel to the consumer line, Dave Cutler, hired from Digital Equipment in 1988, built Windows NT, a fully modern kernel with protected memory and portability across processors, released in 1993 for servers and professionals; the consumer and NT lines converged in Windows XP in 2001, retiring the DOS lineage. Dominance drew the state: the United States sued Microsoft in 1998 over the bundling of Internet Explorer and restrictive contracts with PC makers, a court found the company an abusive monopolist, and though the ordered break-up was reversed on appeal in 2001, the settlement's conduct rules and the trial's chastening effect shaped the company's behaviour into the following decade.

sections.heading: The Hardware Engine: Chips, Memory, Disks, and Buses
sections.body: Beneath the visible drama of companies and interfaces ran the quieter machinery that actually made personal computers better every year, and its components deserve to be understood separately. The processor story after the 8-bit era is largely the x86 lineage: Intel's 16-bit 8086 and 8088, the 80286 of 1982 with protected memory modes, the 32-bit 80386 of 1985 that made multitasking practical, the 486 of 1989 integrating the floating-point unit and cache, and the Pentium of 1993, after which marketing names replaced numbers because trademark law does not protect digits. Clock speeds climbed from the original PC's 4.77 megahertz through 66 megahertz Pentiums to a gigahertz by 2000, and when heat ended the megahertz race around 2005, the industry pivoted to multiple cores on one die. Rival architectures pressed from the workstation world; the RISC philosophy of simple, fast instructions produced SPARC, MIPS, and the IBM-Motorola-Apple PowerPC that Macintoshes used from 1994 until Apple's 2006 switch to Intel, but the x86 world's manufacturing scale and software inertia outlasted them all on the desktop. Memory obeyed its own doubling: the dynamic RAM chip, invented at Intel as the 1103 in 1970, grew from the 16-kilobit generation of the late 1970s to gigabit-class chips, while the price of a megabyte fell from hundreds of dollars in the early 1980s to fractions of a cent, and typical machine capacities ran from the Altair's 256 bytes to 640 kilobytes in DOS days, megabytes under Windows 95, and gigabytes in the 2000s. Storage advanced on two tracks. Removable media went from cassette tape through 8-inch, 5.25-inch, and 3.5-inch floppy disks holding 1.44 megabytes, to CD-ROM in the early 1990s with 650 megabytes that enabled multimedia encyclopedias and enormous games, to DVD and finally USB flash drives. Fixed disks, descended from IBM's Winchester technology, reached the PC as 5- and 10-megabyte drives costing thousands of dollars in the early 1980s; areal density then improved even faster than Moore's law, delivering gigabyte drives by the mid-1990s and terabytes by the 2010s, until solid-state drives built from flash memory, with no moving parts and hundredfold better random access, displaced spinning disks from mainstream machines during the 2010s. The connective tissue standardized in waves: the PC's open ISA expansion bus gave way to PCI in 1993 and PCI Express in the 2000s; graphics evolved from IBM's text-mode adapters through VGA's 640 by 480 pixels in 1987 to dedicated 3D accelerators, with the 1996 3dfx Voodoo igniting consumer 3D and NVIDIA's 1999 GeForce coining the term graphics processing unit; and the tangle of serial, parallel, and keyboard ports collapsed into USB after 1996. Displays traced their own arc from television sets and green phosphor terminals through colour CRT monitors to the liquid-crystal flat panels that, around 2003, finally freed desks from thirty-kilogram glass tubes.

sections.heading: Computers That Travel: The Portable Story
sections.body: The desire to carry a computer is as old as the machines themselves, and the portable lineage recapitulated the whole industry's progress in miniature. The first commercially successful portable, the Osborne 1 of 1981, was a 10.7-kilogram sewing-machine-sized case with a tiny 5-inch screen and a bundle of business software whose price, 1,795 dollars including programs worth more than that separately, invented software bundling as a sales strategy; the company's famous collapse in 1983, popularly blamed on announcing its successor too early, gave the industry the cautionary phrase Osborne effect. Compaq's 1983 portable carried IBM compatibility in the same luggable format, and Kaypro's rugged metal boxes sold well to writers, but true portability required a different shape. The clamshell form factor, screen folding flat over keyboard, arrived with the GRiD Compass in 1982, a 8,000-dollar magnesium-cased machine with an orange electroluminescent display that flew on the Space Shuttle; Radio Shack's TRS-80 Model 100 of 1983, a flat slab with an eight-line screen, built-in modem, and twenty-hour battery life on AA cells, became the beloved field tool of journalists, who could write and file a story from anywhere with a phone line. Through the late 1980s the pieces of the modern laptop assembled: Toshiba's T1100 of 1985 established the battery-powered clamshell PC compatible; backlit liquid crystal displays became readable indoors; 2.5-inch hard disks replaced floppies; and Intel began designing processors specifically for low power. Apple's PowerBook line of 1991 fixed the ergonomics for everyone by pushing the keyboard back and placing a trackball, later a trackpad, front and centre, creating palm rests, and IBM's ThinkPad of 1992, black, square, with its red pointing stick and superb keyboards, became the corporate standard and, later, the basis of Lenovo's rise after it bought IBM's PC business in 2005. Batteries improved from nickel-cadmium through nickel-metal-hydride to lithium-ion after 1991, roughly tripling energy density; Intel's Centrino platform of 2003 married efficient Pentium M processors to built-in Wi-Fi just as wireless networks spread through homes, offices, and coffee shops, and the laptop stopped being a compromise. In 2008 Apple's MacBook Air, pulled from a manila envelope on stage, and the brief boom of cheap netbooks both pointed the same direction, toward thin, light, all-day machines with solid-state storage, a template Intel later formalized as the ultrabook. Portable sales passed desktop sales worldwide around 2008, completing a quiet inversion: the personal computer's default form became the one you close and carry. A parallel handheld lineage, from the Psion organisers and Apple's ill-fated Newton of 1993 through the Palm Pilot of 1996 and the BlackBerry, explored how small a useful computer could be, and taught hard lessons about handwriting recognition, battery budgets, and one-handed interfaces. The portable story thus seeded the next era twice over, since the engineering disciplines it forced, power management, integration, wireless networking, and miniaturized storage, together with the handhelds' interface experiments, were exactly the capabilities the smartphone would require and combine.

sections.heading: Wiring the Home: Modems, Online Services, and the Web PC
sections.body: The personal computer's second great transformation was its connection to the world, and the plumbing of that connection shaped a whole culture. The instrument was the modem, which converts digital bits into audible tones that ordinary telephone lines can carry; Dennis Hayes's Smartmodem of 1981 standardized the command language and made dialling programmable, and speeds climbed from 300 bits per second, at which text arrives slower than fast reading, through 2400, 14,400, and 28,800 bits per second to the practical ceiling of 56 kilobits in 1997. In the 1980s, calling long-distance was expensive, so online life was local: hobbyists ran bulletin board systems, BBSes, single computers with a modem or several that neighbours dialled to leave messages, swap shareware, and play turn-based games, and store-and-forward networks like FidoNet relayed mail between boards overnight. Commercial services layered on top: CompuServe offered forums, stock quotes, and email by the hour; Prodigy and GEnie followed; and America Online, with its friendly interface, carpet- bombed the continent with free trial diskettes and CDs until, for millions of households, its welcome chime and the phrase You've Got Mail simply were the internet. They were not the internet, though; they were walled gardens, and the actual internet, the academic TCP/IP network descended from the ARPANET, was opened to commercial traffic in the early 1990s just as Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web, invented at CERN in 1989-91, gave it a face. The releases of the Mosaic browser in 1993 and its commercial successor Netscape Navigator in 1994 turned the PC into a window onto a global hypertext library, and every walled garden had to open its gates or die. Getting online remained a ritual of the dial-up years: the modem's shriek of negotiation tones, the tied-up family phone line, the metered hours, and the disconnection when someone picked up the receiver. Broadband dissolved the ritual during the 2000s as cable modems and DSL brought always-on connections at megabits per second, and Wi-Fi, standardized as 802.11b in 1999, untethered the connection from the wall jack. A connected PC was a different object from a standalone one. Email became the reason many households bought their first computer; the web made the machine a shopping mall, library, bank, and travel agent; Napster in 1999 demonstrated, traumatically for the music industry, that a network of PCs was a distribution system of unprecedented power; and the browser itself became a battleground, with Microsoft bundling Internet Explorer into Windows to defeat Netscape, winning the browser war and drawing the antitrust suit that defined its decade. By 2000 the personal computer's centre of gravity had moved decisively from the processor to the network socket, and every subsequent development, web applications, cloud storage, streaming media, social networks, assumed the connection as a given.

sections.heading: Free Software, Linux, and Apple's Second Act
sections.body: Two counter-movements that began at the margins reshaped the personal computer's final decades, one ideological and one corporate. The ideological movement was free software. Richard Stallman, a programmer at MIT's Artificial Intelligence Laboratory who had watched its open hacker culture dissolve into proprietary licensing, announced the GNU project in 1983 to rebuild a complete Unix-like operating system whose users would have the legal right to run, study, modify, and share it; his GNU General Public License of 1989 enforced that freedom with copyright law's own tools, requiring derivative works to carry the same license. By 1991 GNU had produced compilers, editors, and utilities but lacked a working kernel, the core program that manages hardware, and a Finnish undergraduate named Linus Torvalds filled the gap almost casually, posting to a newsgroup that he was writing a hobby operating system, just for fun, that would never be big and professional. Linux, licensed under the GPL and developed by e-mail among thousands of volunteers, matured with startling speed; combined with GNU userland and, from 1993, packaged in distributions like Debian and Red Hat, it gave anyone a free, robust Unix on commodity PC hardware. Linux never conquered the consumer desktop, plateauing at a few percent there, but it conquered nearly everything else the PC industry fed into: the web servers of the internet boom, the render farms of Hollywood, the supercomputer lists, eventually the cloud datacentres of Amazon and Google, and, through the Android operating system built on its kernel, the majority of the world's smartphones. The open model also produced the Apache web server, the Firefox browser, and the tool chains on which almost all modern software development rests, vindicating at scale the Homebrew-era conviction that shared code compounds. The corporate second act was Apple's. By 1996 the company was dying, its Macintosh share shrivelling, its operating system decrepit, and its board bought NeXT for 429 million dollars to obtain a modern foundation, returning Steve Jobs in the bargain. Jobs took control in 1997, accepted a stabilizing 150-million-dollar investment from Microsoft alongside a five-year Office commitment, cut the product line to a two-by-two grid, and shipped the Bondi-blue iMac in 1998, a gumdrop all-in-one that sold two million units and made the computer a fashion object. Mac OS X, released in 2001, wrapped NeXT's Unix core in the Aqua interface, giving the Mac industrial-grade plumbing; the 2001 iPod and the iTunes Store of 2003 taught Apple consumer electronics and digital retail; and the 2006 transition to Intel processors let Macs run Windows software, removing the last excuse not to buy one. Apple entered 2007 healthier than at any point in its history, with a skill set, hardware-software integration, miniaturization, retail, and media distribution, that was about to be aimed at the telephone, with consequences that would end the PC era itself.

sections.heading: The Post-PC Era: Smartphones, Clouds, and the PC's Legacy
sections.body: The personal computer was not defeated by a rival computer; it was absorbed by its own descendants. The iPhone, introduced by Steve Jobs on 9 January 2007 as three products in one, a widescreen iPod, a phone, and an internet communicator, was in hardware terms a small ARM-based Unix computer with a capacitive touchscreen, and its 2008 App Store recreated the PC's decisive advantage, an open field for third-party software, at a scale no desktop platform ever approached. Google's Android, launched commercially in 2008 and given away to handset makers, replayed the Microsoft licensing strategy against Apple's integrated model, and the two of them settled the market between them within five years. Annual smartphone shipments passed PC shipments in late 2010 and soon exceeded them fivefold, passing a billion units a year by 2013 while PCs plateaued near three hundred million and declined; for most of humanity, including billions who never owned a desktop, the first and only personal computer is a phone. Steve Jobs framed the shift in 2010 as cars and trucks: PCs, like trucks, would remain essential for heavy work, programming, engineering, media production, but most people only ever needed a car. The tablet, which Apple's iPad defined in 2010, filled the space between. What remained of the desktop world consolidated and stratified: laptops became the default PC, desktops a specialty for gamers, traders, and creators; Google's Chromebooks turned the browser itself into the operating system for schools; and Apple in 2020 began replacing Intel processors in Macs with its own ARM-based M1 chips, descendants of its phone silicon, closing a circle that began when Acorn engineers sketched the ARM for a home computer in 1985. Meanwhile the cloud inverted the PC's founding premise. The autonomy that defined personal computing, your programs and files on your machine, gave way to software running in datacentres and rented by subscription, with the local device reduced to a beautifully engineered terminal, a return, at planetary scale, to the time-sharing model the PC had overthrown. The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020 briefly reversed the PC's decline, as remote work and schooling made a real keyboard and screen essential again, a reminder that the truck still hauls the economy. The legacy of the personal computer era is best measured not in the fate of its artifacts but in its settlements: it established that computing belongs to individuals; that open platforms attract the software that decides which hardware wins; that the interface is the product; that commodity scale beats elegance; and that each generation's liberating platform becomes the incumbent the next generation overthrows. Mainframe to mini to micro to phone to cloud, the wheel has turned four times, and there is no reason to believe it has stopped.

sections.heading: Myths, Failure Modes, and How to Read This History
sections.body: Popular histories of the personal computer are unusually rich in legend, and part of being educated on the subject is knowing which stories are simplified, which are contested, and what the record actually supports. The most persistent legend holds that Xerox fumbled everything and Apple simply stole the graphical interface during one visit. The reality is a licensed demonstration paid for with investment access, years of independent engineering afterward, genuine Apple inventions such as the menu bar and the clipboard model, and a Xerox that did try to sell the technology, in the Star, and failed on price and channel rather than on vision; the courts, in Xerox's own belated 1989 suit against Apple and in Apple's against Microsoft, declined to grant anyone ownership of the desktop idea. The Osborne effect, the tale that pre-announcing a successor killed Osborne Computer, is repeated as a business law, yet participants and later historians document that the company's deeper wounds were inventory mismanagement, price war, and cash exhaustion; treat single-cause corporate death stories with suspicion generally. The famous quotations deserve scepticism too: there is no reliable source for Thomas Watson saying the world needed only five computers, and Bill Gates has convincingly denied ever saying 640 kilobytes ought to be enough for anybody. A subtler distortion is survivor bias. The clean narrative from Altair to Apple to IBM to Microsoft ignores the hundreds of failed platforms that were, at various moments, plausible futures: CP/M machines, the Texas Instruments 99/4A, the Coleco Adam, IBM's own PCjr, the Amiga, the Atari ST, OS/2, and NeXT hardware among them, and the counterfactuals they represent, for instance had Digital Research licensed CP/M-86 on IBM's terms in 1980, are genuinely open. The history is also less purely American than its mythology: Britain's Sinclair and Acorn, Japan's NEC PC-98 and MSX worlds, and France's Minitel network each shaped national computing cultures for a decade, and the ARM processor at the heart of the post-PC world is a British design. Women are systematically under-credited in the standard telling, from the ENIAC programmers through Grace Hopper's compilers to Adele Goldberg's Smalltalk and Susan Kare's Macintosh icons and typefaces, a gap recent scholarship has begun to close. Finally, the era's failure modes repay study because they recur: platform owners who close what should stay open, Micro Channel, then lose their ecosystem; incumbents who see the next wave clearly, as Xerox and IBM and Microsoft each did, yet cannot act against their existing profit engine, the pattern Clayton Christensen named the innovator's dilemma; and companies that mistake early dominance for permanence. Read this way, the personal computer's history is not a museum piece but a casebook, and its central lesson, that control of computing keeps devolving outward to whoever empowers the individual user, is still being applied, for and against, in every platform fight of the present day.

guides.title: The Home Computer Era
guides.summary: The rise, golden age, and end of the home computer, from the Altair and the 1977 Trinity through the Commodore 64, Sinclair Spectrum, and Amiga, and how a decade of cheap machines created modern computing culture.

sections.heading: When Computers Moved Into the Living Room
sections.body:
For the first thirty years of the electronic computer's existence, ordinary people never touched one. Computers were institutional machines - room-sized, air-conditioned, tended by specialists, costing as much as an office building. Then, in a window of roughly fifteen years from about 1977 to the early 1990s, computing crossed the threshold of the home. Machines costing a few hundred dollars or pounds, plugged into the family television and loading programs from audio cassettes, appeared in millions of living rooms and bedrooms across North America, Europe, Japan and beyond. This is the home computer era, and it deserves study not as nostalgia but as the moment personal computing's culture was formed: who programs, who plays, what software costs, how a machine invites or repels its owner's curiosity.

A home computer, in the period sense, was a specific kind of object, distinct both from the business microcomputer (the IBM PC and its kin, sold through offices at office prices) and from the video game console (a closed appliance that played only cartridges). The home computer was cheap enough for a family purchase - the most successful models sold between about 100 and 600 dollars - and open by design: it booted directly into a programming language, almost always some dialect of BASIC, presenting a blinking cursor that would do nothing until its owner typed something. It used the household television as its display, a cassette recorder or cheap floppy drive as its storage, and it was sold in department stores and toy shops beside the appliances. Parents bought them because advertising promised homework help and a head start on the future; children used them to play games; and a remarkable fraction of those children, finding that games could be listed, modified and written from scratch, became the programming generation that staffed the software industry for the following three decades.

The numbers involved were unprecedented. The Commodore 64, the era's best-selling machine, sold somewhere between 12.5 and 17 million units - claims vary, and the truth is genuinely uncertain - making it by most reckonings the best-selling single computer model in history. Britain in 1983 had the highest per-capita home computer ownership in the world. Yet by about 1994 the category was dead: the IBM-compatible PC absorbed the serious uses, dedicated consoles absorbed the games, and the all-purpose cheap machine that booted into BASIC vanished. Understanding why it rose, what it was actually like to use, and why it disappeared is the purpose of this guide, and along the way it explains the machines themselves - the chips, the graphics tricks, the tape loaders - because in this era, unusually, the hardware's personality shaped the culture around it.

sections.heading: Before the Trinity: Kits, Clubs, and the Altair
sections.body:
The home computer's immediate ancestor was a hobbyist kit that did almost nothing. In January 1975, Popular Electronics magazine carried on its cover the Altair 8800, built by a small Albuquerque calculator company called MITS, run by Ed Roberts. For 397 dollars in kit form the buyer received an Intel 8080 microprocessor, 256 bytes of memory - bytes, not kilobytes - a steel case, and a front panel of toggle switches and red lights that constituted the entire user interface. There was no keyboard, no screen, no storage. Programs were entered by flipping switches, one machine-code instruction at a time, and output was read as binary from the lights. It was, by any practical measure, useless; and it sold thousands of units within months, because for the first time a private individual could own a genuine computer. The pent-up demand it revealed changed several lives at once. In Boston, Paul Allen showed the magazine to Bill Gates; within weeks the pair had written a BASIC language interpreter for a machine they had never seen, simulating the 8080 on a Harvard mainframe, and licensed it to MITS as the first product of their new partnership, Micro-Soft. The interpreter fit in about four kilobytes and established the company's founding business: selling languages for other people's hardware.

In Silicon Valley, the Altair catalysed the Homebrew Computer Club, first convened in a Menlo Park garage in March 1975 - a fortnightly gathering of engineers, students and enthusiasts who swapped schematics, chips and code in an atmosphere closer to a gardening club than an industry. Among the regulars was Steve Wozniak, a Hewlett-Packard engineer who designed, purely to show his friends, a complete computer on a single circuit board with a keyboard interface and video output to an ordinary television - radical economies at the time. His friend Steve Jobs persuaded him to sell it. The Apple I, offered in 1976 as a bare assembled board for 666.66 dollars, sold perhaps two hundred units, enough to fund something far more ambitious.

Around the same cluster of years came the competing kit and small-batch machines - the IMSAI 8080 (famous later from the film WarGames), Southwest Technical Products' 6800 machine, the Sol-20 with its walnut sides - and the essential enabling economics: Intel's 8080 processor cost hundreds of dollars, but in 1975 MOS Technology introduced the 6502 at 25 dollars, a price so low attendees at its launch assumed a misprint. Cheap processors, television output, cassette storage and a resident BASIC were now all available piecemeal. What remained was for someone to integrate them into an appliance an ordinary family could unbox, plug in and use. In 1977, three companies did so within months of each other, and the hobby became an industry.

sections.heading: 1977: The Trinity Arrives
sections.body:
Nineteen seventy-seven is the home computer's year zero. Within a single summer, three fully assembled, consumer-ready machines reached the market, a trio later nicknamed the 1977 Trinity. In June came the Apple II, Steve Wozniak's masterpiece: a 6502 processor at 1 megahertz, 4 kilobytes of memory in the base model, BASIC in read-only memory, sound, game paddles, and - its sensation - colour graphics, achieved through an ingenious exploitation of the American NTSC television standard's colour encoding that let Wozniak conjure colour from digital timing tricks with almost no extra hardware. At 1,298 dollars it was the expensive, aspirational member of the Trinity, and its eight internal expansion slots - insisted upon by Wozniak against Jobs's preference for simplicity - made it a platform strangers could extend in unforeseen directions, a decision with large consequences. Also in June, Commodore shipped the PET 2001, an all-in-one unit with a nine-inch monochrome monitor, cassette drive and infamously unusable chiclet keyboard built into a single wedge of sheet metal, at 795 dollars. Commodore's founder Jack Tramiel, an Auschwitz survivor with a famously combative business style, owned MOS Technology itself - Commodore had bought its own chip supplier - and could therefore build computers from chips at cost, an advantage he would later weaponise. In August, Radio Shack's parent Tandy launched the TRS-80 Model I at 599 dollars complete with monitor and cassette deck, built around the rival Zilog Z80 processor. Distribution decided its early lead: Radio Shack had over 3,000 stores across America, and the TRS-80 outsold both rivals through the late 1970s, its owners tolerating the nickname Trash-80 with defensive affection.

The Trinity established the template every later home computer followed: processor, BASIC in ROM so the machine was usable seconds after power-on, television or bundled monitor for display, cassette tape for storage, expansion via cartridge slots or edge connectors. It also established the market's fault lines. Apple drifted upmarket toward schools and small business, especially after the spreadsheet VisiCalc appeared exclusively on the Apple II in 1979 and gave the machine a serious commercial justification - the first killer application, software so valuable that customers bought the hardware to run it. Tandy served its store-loyal base. And Commodore, vertically integrated and cost-obsessed, aimed downward at price points no one else could survive, a strategy that would shortly redraw the entire market. None of the three yet sold in numbers that look large today - tens and hundreds of thousands, not millions - but the category now existed, with shelf space, magazines, and a rapidly forming software trade to feed it. Byte magazine, which coined the Trinity label in retrospect, was already thick with advertisements; user groups met in libraries; and the question hanging over the young industry was no longer whether ordinary people would buy computers, but how cheap the machines could be pushed - a question Commodore was about to answer with a violence nobody anticipated.

sections.heading: The Chips That Made It Possible
sections.body:
Every home computer was, economically speaking, a thin plastic wrapper around a microprocessor and a few support chips, and the era's shape follows directly from semiconductor pricing. Two processors powered almost the entire category. The MOS Technology 6502, designed in 1975 by a small team under Chuck Peddle - engineers who had left Motorola after that company showed no interest in a cheap version of its 6800 - was an exercise in ruthless minimalism: about 3,500 transistors, a simple but fast instruction set, and above all a launch price of 25 dollars when Intel's 8080 listed at around 179 and Motorola's 6800 similar. Peddle's team achieved the price partly through design economy and partly through a manufacturing insight: they fixed mask defects iteratively until yields - the fraction of chips on a silicon wafer that actually worked - reached unheard-of levels. The 6502 powered the Apple II, the Commodore PET, VIC-20 (in 6502 form) and, as the slightly modified 6510, the Commodore 64, plus the Atari 8-bit line, the BBC Micro and, later, the Nintendo Entertainment System's core. The Zilog Z80, designed by Federico Faggin and Masatoshi Shima - both veterans of Intel's original 4004 and 8080 projects - was the other pole: an enhanced, cheaper, binary-compatible superset of the 8080 that powered the TRS-80, the Sinclair machines, the Amstrad CPC, the MSX standard and the business world's CP/M machines. Between them, the 6502 and Z80 ran essentially the whole 8-bit era, both typically clocked between 1 and 4 megahertz and addressing at most 64 kilobytes of memory - the defining constraint of the period, since 16 address lines can distinguish no more than 65,536 locations.

Around the processor sat the support silicon that gave each machine its character: video chips, sound chips, and input-output controllers. Here vertical integration decided winners. Commodore, owning MOS, could commission custom graphics and sound chips and pay only fabrication cost - the reason the Commodore 64 could include hardware that outclassed machines twice its price. Atari likewise designed custom chips of exceptional sophistication. Companies without a fab bought commodity parts - the Texas Instruments TMS9918 video chip and General Instrument AY-3-8910 sound chip recur across dozens of machines - or, in Sinclair's case, compressed all the glue logic into a single semi-custom part called a ULA (uncommitted logic array) to hit absurdly low prices.

Behind everything ran the curve Gordon Moore had described in 1965: transistor counts per chip doubling roughly every two years, with costs falling to match. Memory illustrates it best. The 4 kilobytes of RAM that helped price the 1977 Apple II at 1,298 dollars cost a few dollars by 1983, which is how a 64-kilobyte machine came to sell for 199. The home computer era is what the middle of Moore's curve looked like at retail: each Christmas, more machine for less money, until the category undercut itself out of existence.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Home Computer
sections.body:
Switch on a home computer of the classic period and the essential architecture announces itself in under two seconds: a coloured border, a copyright line, a memory report - 38911 BASIC BYTES FREE, in the Commodore 64's famous formulation - and a blinking cursor awaiting typed commands. There was no operating system in the modern sense, no desktop, no files visible anywhere. The machine's soul lived in read-only memory (ROM): a BASIC interpreter plus a thin layer of routines (Commodore called its layer the KERNAL) for reading the keyboard, drawing characters and talking to tape and disk. The ROM was the user interface, the programming environment and the recovery mechanism at once - no crash could damage it, so the reset button always returned the familiar cursor.

Physically, nearly every machine adopted the same layout: a single circuit board inside a keyboard housing, because the keyboard was the computer. On the board sat the processor, ROM, RAM, the video and sound chips, and a modulator that disguised the video signal as a weak television broadcast so the family set could display it - typically 40 or 32 columns of chunky text, because a domestic television's blurry picture could resolve no more. Around the edges ran the ports that defined the machine's social life: a cartridge slot delivering instant-loading software (really just ROM mapped into the address space), joystick ports (the Atari nine-pin standard becoming universal), a cassette interface, a serial or parallel port for printers and disk drives, and often an expansion bus exposing the processor's raw signals to whatever a soldering-iron owner dared connect.

The memory map was the machine's true geography, and period programmers knew it like a home town. Within the 64-kilobyte address space, fixed regions held ROM, RAM, and - crucially - memory-mapped hardware: the video chip's registers, the sound chip, the input ports all appeared as ordinary memory addresses. Writing the number 0 to address 53280 on a Commodore 64 turned the screen border black; every child who owned one learned POKE 53280,0 as a first incantation. This transparency was accidental pedagogy. Nothing was hidden, nothing was protected; the same POKE command that changed a border colour could, with different numbers, corrupt the interpreter and freeze the machine, teaching cause, effect and the reset button in one lesson. Screen output itself was usually character-based: the display hardware read a grid of byte codes and painted each as an 8-by-8 pixel pattern fetched from a character set, which programs could redefine - the standard trick behind most games' graphics. A few machines offered true bitmap modes at the cost of memory and speed. Understanding this anatomy explains the era's texture: why software loaded into strange addresses, why magazines printed pages of numbers to be typed into DATA statements, and why owners spoke of their machines with mechanics' intimacy. The box invited its own disassembly, intellectual if not physical, and an entire generation accepted.

sections.heading: BASIC: The Language Everyone Learned
sections.body:
