Subscriptions and services layered a recurring-revenue business on top, online multiplayer access fees from Xbox Live's 2002 debut onward, then Netflix-style libraries led by Game Pass, and live-service games monetize continuously through cosmetic items and battle passes, a model imported from Asian free-to-play markets. The through-line from 1983 to today is unbroken: whoever controls the gate between software and customer captures the industry's profit, and every commercial war in this history, cartridge lockout chips, disc formats, exclusivity contracts, store commissions, has been a war over that gate.

sections.heading: Inside the Box: How Console Hardware Evolved
sections.body: Reading the machines themselves, generation by generation, reveals a coherent engineering story with three recurring themes: chasing the display, taming cost, and moving the bottleneck. The earliest consoles, as the first generation showed, could not afford to store a picture, so their circuits generated video in real time, and the second generation's programmable machines inherited the constraint: the Atari 2600's Television Interface Adaptor held only a single scanline's worth of state, so the processor rebuilt the display line by line, 60 times a second, leaving a scant few thousand cycles per frame for the actual game. The third and fourth generations solved graphics with dedicated video chips built around two abstractions that dominated for fifteen years: tiles, small reusable 8-by-8-pixel patterns composing scrolling backgrounds cheaply, and sprites, independent movable objects composited by hardware, with the NES handling 64 sprites and the Super Nintendo adding layered backgrounds, transparency effects, and Mode 7's plane rotation. Sound followed a parallel path from programmable square-wave and noise generators, whose constraints created the chiptune aesthetic now cultivated deliberately, through frequency-modulation synthesis on the Genesis to the SNES's sample-playback chip and then compact-disc audio. The fifth generation's pivot to polygonal 3D changed the mathematics of the job: instead of compositing pre-drawn art, hardware now transformed three-dimensional vertices through matrix arithmetic, rasterized triangles, and mapped textures onto them, and the PlayStation's dedicated geometry engine, the Nintendo 64's combined Reality Coprocessor, and their successors were early instances of what the PC world would later call the graphics processing unit, or GPU. Storage co-evolved: cartridges, instant but tiny and expensive, gave way to the compact disc's 650 megabytes, the DVD's 4.7 gigabytes, and Blu-ray's 25 to 50, each jump enabling new genres, recorded speech, full-motion video, open worlds, while adding the loading delays that only the ninth generation's solid-state drives finally abolished. Processor history traces the wider industry's arc away from exotic architecture: 8-bit 6502 variants, the 68000, licensed MIPS and PowerPC designs, the deliberately strange Cell of the PlayStation 3, whose difficulty convinced everyone to stop being clever, and finally, from 2013, commodity x86 systems-on-a-chip from AMD integrating CPU and GPU on one die, with the Switch choosing an ARM-based Nvidia Tegra from the smartphone lineage instead. Memory grew from the 2600's 128 bytes to the PlayStation 5's 16 gigabytes, a factor of roughly 130 million, while unified memory pools replaced the fragmented banks that once made porting miserable. Controllers evolved their own grammar, joystick, cross-shaped pad, shoulder buttons, dual analog sticks with the 1997 DualShock, motion sensing, and haptics, and each addition became a permanent floor because software assumes it. Thermals and reliability became first-class constraints as consoles reached 200-plus watts, the Xbox 360's red-ring failures being the cautionary tale. The through-line: every console is a bet, frozen years before launch, on which single bottleneck, memory, geometry, bandwidth, storage latency, most limits the experiences designers will want five years later, and the machines remembered fondly are the ones that guessed right.

sections.heading: Failures, Flops, and What Goes Wrong
sections.body: A history that recorded only winners would miss half the mechanism, because the industry's rules were mostly written by its disasters, and the failure modes repeat with diagnostic regularity. The commonest is the price-value inversion: consoles priced above the perceived worth of their libraries die almost regardless of quality, as the 699-dollar 3DO, the 649-dollar Neo Geo, priced as a luxury import, the launch PlayStation 3, and the 599-dollar stereoscopic Nintendo Virtual Boy of 1995, discontinued within a year after inducing headaches and selling under a million units, all demonstrated. Second is the confused proposition: hardware whose purpose consumers cannot state in a sentence, the Wii U's tablet-that-is-not-a-tablet, Kinect's you-are-the-controller after the novelty faded, most mid-1990s multimedia boxes like the Philips CD-i, fails at the shelf no matter the engineering. Third is the add-on trap: peripherals that split the installed base, the Sega CD and 32X, the 64DD disk drive, motion wands, virtual-reality headsets to date, starve because developers rationally target the whole base rather than a subset, a lesson also visible in the failure of the mid-generation upgrade consoles to attract exclusive software. Fourth is losing the third parties: the Nintendo 64's cartridges, the Saturn's architecture, and the Wii U's weak sales each drove publishers to rivals, and no first-party catalogue has ever fully compensated, though Nintendo's has come closest. Fifth is platform-holder hubris at the moment of maximum strength, Atari in 1982, Nintendo's licensing arrogance inviting the Sony alliance that became its nemesis, Sony's 2006 pricing, Microsoft's 2013 policies, a pattern so reliable it functions as a leading indicator: dominance breeds the mistake that ends it. Sixth, and least forgiving, is running out of money mid-war: console generations are five-to-seven-year capital sieges, and Sega, profitable nowhere near long enough to absorb the Saturn and Dreamcast losses, remains the exemplar that engineering brilliance and beloved software cannot substitute for a balance sheet. Beyond the corporate failures lies a quieter, structural one: preservation. Games are the first art form whose originals require functioning machines to experience, and the machines die, capacitors leak, optical drives wear out, cartridge batteries that hold save files expire, while digital storefronts close, the Wii Shop in 2019, the original Wii U and 3DS stores in 2023, taking purchasable access to hundreds of titles with them, and always-online games simply cease to exist when servers shut. Emulation, software that mimics old hardware on new, is the de facto preservation tool, legally contested though the underlying technique was validated in American case law around 2000, and institutions such as the Video Game History Foundation and the Internet Archive now work the problem seriously, but large fractions of early source code are already lost, and one careful 2023 study found 87 percent of games released in the United States before 2010 commercially unavailable in any form. For the reader, the practical takeaways are simple: judge platforms by libraries and prices rather than specifications, expect the leader to stumble, treat digital purchases as revocable licenses rather than property, and, if any of this history matters to you, back up what you own while the hardware still boots.

guides.title: History of the Internet and ARPANET
guides.summary: The full story of how the internet came to be: from Cold War research and packet switching theory through ARPANET, TCP/IP, the protocol wars, the World Wide Web and commercialization, to the governance, security battles and design lessons that shape the network today.

sections.heading: Why the Internet's History Matters
sections.body: The internet is the largest engineered artifact in human history, a voluntary federation of tens of thousands of independent networks connecting more than five billion people, and yet it began as a four-computer experiment run by a small office of the United States Department of Defense in 1969. Understanding how it grew from one to the other is not antiquarian curiosity; the network's history is frozen into its architecture, and nearly every property that delights or torments us today traces to a decision made decades ago by identifiable people under identifiable constraints. The internet has no central switchboard because its designers distrusted central points of failure. Anyone can attach a new application without permission because the network was built by researchers who wanted to experiment without asking. Spam, fraud and denial-of-service attacks flourish because the original community was a few hundred trusted colleagues who saw no need to build identity or accountability into the plumbing. Addresses ran scarce because a research project reasonably chose a 32-bit number it never expected to exhaust. History also corrects myths that distort public debate. The internet was not invented by any single person, not built to survive nuclear war in the form popular legend suggests, and not an inevitability; at several junctures, notably the international standards battles of the 1980s, a very different network, centrally administered by national telephone monopolies, was the smart-money favorite. The story is best understood as three overlapping revolutions. The first, from roughly 1961 to 1972, established packet switching, the counterintuitive idea that messages should be chopped into small blocks and forwarded hop by hop by computers, and proved it at scale with ARPANET. The second, from 1973 to about 1985, solved internetworking, the harder problem of joining many dissimilar networks into one seamless whole, producing TCP/IP, the protocol suite that still carries every byte you send. The third, from 1985 through the 1990s, transformed a government research facility into a commercial, global, civilian medium, a transition catalyzed by the National Science Foundation's backbone, by the abolition of restrictions on commercial traffic, and above all by the World Wide Web, which turned the network from a tool for specialists into a place the public wanted to be. Around and after these revolutions run continuing struggles over governance, security and control that remain unresolved. Throughout, a consistent character emerges: an engineering culture that valued working code over committee consensus, openness over proprietary advantage, and rough pragmatism over elegance, expressed in David Clark's famous credo that the community rejects kings, presidents and voting in favor of rough consensus and running code. That culture, as much as any technology, is what this history explains, and knowing it is the best available guide to judging the network's present controversies, from platform power to protocol ossification, with clear eyes.

sections.heading: Cold War Roots: ARPA, SAGE and the Time-Sharing Revolution
sections.body: The chain of events begins with a shock. On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, and the United States, stung by the appearance of technological inferiority, created the Advanced Research Projects Agency, ARPA, in February 1958 to fund high-risk, high-payoff research across the armed services. ARPA was tiny by Pentagon standards but unusually free, empowered to place bets that individual services would not, and in 1962 it acquired an Information Processing Techniques Office, IPTO, to fund computing research. Its first director was Joseph Carl Robnett Licklider, universally called Lick, a psychoacoustician from MIT who had been converted to computing by working on SAGE, the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment air defense system. SAGE itself deserves a place in the ancestry: built in the 1950s to track Soviet bombers, it pioneered real-time interactive computing, graphical displays, light guns and, crucially, the transmission of digital data over telephone lines by modem, proving that computers could converse across a continent. Licklider's 1960 paper Man-Computer Symbiosis argued that computers should be interactive partners in human thought rather than batch calculators, and in a playful 1963 memo he addressed colleagues as members of the Intergalactic Computer Network, sketching a future in which everyone works through connected machines. He funded the research groups, at MIT, Stanford, Berkeley, UCLA and elsewhere, that would later build the network, seeding both the technology and the community. The enabling technical shift was time-sharing. Early computers ran one job at a time from punched cards; systems like MIT's Compatible Time-Sharing System, demonstrated in 1961, sliced a machine's attention among many simultaneous users at terminals, giving each the illusion of a personal computer and making interactive computing normal within the research world. Time-sharing created both the means and the motive for networking: the means, because computers now had operating systems capable of juggling concurrent conversations, and the motive, because expensive machines with distinct specialties, an artificial intelligence system here, a graphics system there, sat isolated in separate cities. The proximate irritation is preserved in a story told by Robert Taylor, who ran IPTO from 1966: his Pentagon office contained three separate terminals connected to three separate computers in Massachusetts and California, each requiring its own login and commands, and the absurdity of needing a new terminal for every new computer crystallized the project. Taylor secured a million dollars, reportedly in a twenty-minute meeting with ARPA's director Charles Herzfeld, and recruited Lawrence Roberts of MIT's Lincoln Laboratory to manage it. Roberts had already run the decisive preliminary experiment: in 1965 he and Thomas Marill linked the TX-2 computer in Massachusetts to the Q-32 in Santa Monica over a dedicated telephone circuit. The machines communicated, but the ordinary circuit-switched connection proved slow and unreliable at computer timescales, evidence that a fundamentally different transmission discipline was required.

sections.heading: Packet Switching: Baran, Davies and Kleinrock
sections.body: The telephone network of the 1960s worked by circuit switching: dialing a call caused switches to reserve a continuous electrical path end to end, held for the call's whole duration whether or not anyone was speaking. For voice this was tolerable; for computer traffic, which arrives in bursts, a keystroke here, a file there, separated by silence, it was ruinously wasteful, like renting an entire railway line to send occasional postcards. Three researchers, working largely in ignorance of one another, converged on the alternative. Paul Baran at the RAND Corporation, worried that America's command-and-control communications could not survive a nuclear first strike, published between 1960 and 1964 the series On Distributed Communications, proposing a network of many interconnected nodes with no center, in which messages are divided into standard message blocks, each carrying its destination address and forwarded independently from node to node by a scheme he called hot-potato routing. His analysis showed that a distributed network with modest redundancy could absorb heavy damage and still function, and that digital transmission allowed each hop to regenerate a clean signal. AT&T, whose network would have had to host the idea, dismissed it, and Baran's proposal sat unbuilt. Independently, Donald Davies at Britain's National Physical Laboratory arrived at nearly the identical design from a peacetime motive, efficient interactive computing, and gave the concept its lasting name in 1965 and 1966: packet, from the small parcel of data. Davies's team built a working single-node network, the NPL Mark I, serving its laboratory by 1970, but Britain never funded the national network he urged. The third stream was theoretical. Leonard Kleinrock's 1962 MIT doctoral thesis applied queueing theory, the mathematics of waiting lines, to store-and-forward communication networks, showing analytically how shared links could be statistically multiplexed among bursty sources and what delays would result, work that gave the eventual builders confidence the approach would perform. The streams merged at a 1967 computing symposium in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, where Lawrence Roberts presented ARPA's tentative networking plan and Roger Scantlebury of Davies's group introduced him to packet switching and to Baran's buried RAND reports. Roberts adopted the approach wholesale: the ARPA network would move packets, not circuits, over leased 50-kilobit-per-second telephone lines. The intellectual point deserves emphasis because it recurs throughout computing history. Packet switching trades guaranteed, reserved capacity for statistical sharing: each packet finds its own way, links are used whenever any sender has data, and the network promises only best effort, with correctness restored at the edges by retransmission. Every objection raised against it, that packets would arrive out of order, that congestion would be unmanageable, that no serious carrier would run this way, was in some measure true, and the succeeding decades were spent engineering around those truths, because the economic advantage of sharing was overwhelming. The postcard beat the railway.

sections.heading: Building ARPANET: IMPs, UCLA and the First Message
sections.body: In the summer of 1968 ARPA issued a request for quotation to build the network's heart: a small computer at each site, the Interface Message Processor or IMP, that would accept messages from the local host computer, break them into packets of at most about a thousand bits, route them over leased lines, and reassemble them at the destination. Placing a dedicated minicomputer at each site was a crucial simplification, because it spared the wildly dissimilar host machines from implementing the network's internals and spared the network from depending on any host's cooperation. Of the dozen bidders, the contract went in January 1969 not to a computing giant, IBM and AT&T had declined to bid or scoffed, but to Bolt Beranek and Newman, BBN, a Cambridge acoustics-turned-computing consultancy stocked with MIT talent, whose proposal team under Frank Heart included Robert Kahn, Severo Ornstein, William Crowther and David Walden. BBN had roughly nine months and about a million dollars to deliver working hardware, and did, building each IMP on a ruggedized Honeywell DDP-516 minicomputer with twelve thousand words of memory, writing the routing, error-control and flow-control software from scratch, and adding the watchdog and remote-debugging facilities that let a small Cambridge team operate machines across a continent. The first IMP arrived at the University of California, Los Angeles, over Labor Day weekend 1969, chosen because Leonard Kleinrock's group there held the contract for the Network Measurement Center, and it was talking to UCLA's Sigma-7 host within hours of delivery. The second went in October to Douglas Engelbart's Augmentation Research Center at Stanford Research Institute, home of the oN-Line System and the newly invented mouse, with the University of California, Santa Barbara and the University of Utah completing the first four nodes by December. The network's first message was sent on the evening of October 29, 1969, when UCLA student programmer Charley Kline attempted to log in to the SRI machine, typing L, then O, at which point the SRI system crashed; the internet's first transmitted word was LO, completed to LOGIN an hour later after a fix. The anticlimax is fitting: no ceremony, no famous sentence, just two computers and a bug. From there growth was steady, about one new node per month through 1970 and 1971, reaching both coasts and some fifteen sites including MIT, Harvard, RAND and BBN itself. The persuasive moment came in October 1972 at the International Conference on Computer Communication in Washington, where Robert Kahn organized a live public demonstration: dozens of terminals in a hotel ballroom, running real applications on machines across the country, before a thousand skeptical telecommunications professionals. The demonstration ran convincingly, packet switching stopped being a curiosity, and delegates from several countries went home to start networks of their own, a moment many participants later marked as the technology's coming of age.

sections.heading: Protocols From the Ground Up: RFCs, NCP and Email
sections.body: Hardware alone does not make a network; the machines needed shared conventions for conversation, and the way those conventions were created became as influential as the conventions themselves. The host sites assigned the problem mostly to graduate students, who organized themselves as the Network Working Group. In April 1969 Steve Crocker of UCLA wrote up the group's early thinking and, anxious not to presume authority over senior colleagues, titled the memo Request for Comments. RFC 1, Host Software, dated April 7, 1969, began a numbered series that continues past nine thousand documents today and established a remarkable institutional culture: specifications published openly, free to anyone, inviting critique, deriving authority from adoption rather than decree. The group's first major product was the Network Control Program, NCP, completed around 1970, which gave hosts a common transport layer on which applications could be built. The early applications defined the network's useful life. Telnet let a user at one site log in to a distant machine as if locally connected, directly serving the resource-sharing rationale that had justified the project's budget. The File Transfer Protocol, standardized in 1972, moved data and programs between dissimilar machines. But the application that mattered most was unplanned. In 1971 Ray Tomlinson, an engineer at BBN, adapted a local electronic mail program to send messages between machines, choosing the @ sign to separate user from host because it was an otherwise unused character that read naturally as at. Network mail spread explosively; a 1973 ARPA study found electronic mail composing roughly three quarters of all network traffic, to the mild embarrassment of an agency that had promised computational resource sharing and delivered, primarily, human conversation. Mailing lists followed almost immediately, the first large one devoted to science fiction, and with them the recognizable dynamics of online community, debate, etiquette disputes and all. The lesson, that connectivity's killer application is people, would be relearned with USENET, with instant messaging, and with the social web. The NCP era also surfaced the network's first operational pathologies, congestion among them, and hardened the engineering culture's distinctive method: build, deploy, observe, revise. That method had a legal underpinning easy to overlook. Because ARPANET was government-funded research, its protocols were public goods; no company owned the specifications, no license fee guarded implementation, and a student anywhere could read the RFCs and write compatible software. When proprietary networking architectures arrived later in the decade, IBM's Systems Network Architecture and Digital's DECnet among them, they were often more polished, but they bound customers to vendors. The open, unowned protocol stack, maintained by a meritocratic volunteer community and documented in plain public memos, proved the more evolvable organism, and that organizational invention, as much as packet switching itself, is ARPANET's enduring bequest.

sections.heading: The Internetworking Problem: Cerf, Kahn and TCP/IP
sections.body: By 1973 the deeper problem had announced itself: ARPANET was one network, but it would not be alone. ARPA was funding a packet radio network in the San Francisco Bay Area, PRNET, for mobile military use, and a satellite network, SATNET, linking the United States and Europe; Norman Abramson's ALOHAnet in Hawaii had pioneered wireless packet broadcasting in 1971; and other countries and companies were building networks with their own formats, speeds and reliability guarantees. Robert Kahn, now at ARPA, framed the question as open-architecture networking: how do you join arbitrary, dissimilar, independently administered networks so that any host can talk to any other, without requiring any network to change its internals? He recruited Vinton Cerf, newly a Stanford professor and a veteran of the NCP work, and in September 1973 they presented, then in May 1974 published in IEEE Transactions on Communications, A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication, the paper that defined the internet's architecture. Its central ideas remain the network's constitution. Between networks sit gateways, machines later renamed routers, which forward packets between dissimilar systems; a universal envelope format lets any network carry any packet as cargo; and hosts, not the network, take responsibility for reliability, numbering their data, acknowledging receipt, and retransmitting losses. The network itself promises only best effort, which means it may delay, drop, duplicate or reorder packets, and correctness is restored at the endpoints. This end-to-end placement of intelligence, articulated formally in a classic 1984 paper by Jerome Saltzer, David Reed and David Clark, is why the internet could absorb technologies its designers never imagined, from Ethernet to Wi-Fi to fiber, and applications from voice to video to cryptocurrency, without central redesign: the middle is a dumb, general courier, and innovation happens at the edges without asking permission. The original design bundled everything into one Transmission Control Program; experience, and pressure from researchers like Danny Cohen who wanted to carry real-time voice for which retransmitted stale packets are worthless, split it in 1978 into two layers, IP, the Internet Protocol, providing bare addressed delivery, and TCP providing ordered reliable streams for those who want them, with the minimal UDP alongside for those who do not. Addresses were fixed at thirty-two bits, about 4.3 billion possibilities, a choice Cerf later described as seeming ample for an experiment that then escaped the laboratory. Development proceeded through funded implementations at Stanford, BBN and University College London, and a milestone demonstration in 1977 sent packets from a van driving on a California freeway through PRNET, across ARPANET, over SATNET to Europe and back to California, three networks, two continents, one seamless conversation, proof that the architecture worked. The term internet itself is simply the shortening of internetwork, and 1974's RFC 675 already used it.

sections.heading: Flag Day 1983, the DNS and Growing Pains
sections.body: A protocol is only real when everyone runs it, and the internet's founding moment as an operational fact was January 1, 1983, the famous flag day on which ARPANET switched off NCP and required TCP/IP of every attached host. The transition had been announced years ahead, enforced by occasionally turning NCP off for a day to concentrate administrators' minds, and it succeeded; buttons circulated reading I survived the TCP/IP transition. The same year the network formally split, with military operational traffic moving to a separate MILNET behind controlled gateways, leaving ARPANET as the research internet's backbone. Growth immediately stressed the naming system. Since the early 1970s every host had been listed in a single file, hosts.txt, maintained at the Stanford Research Institute's Network Information Center and copied periodically by every machine; with hosts multiplying past the thousands, the file was perpetually stale, name collisions loomed, and the single distribution point was both bottleneck and failure risk. Paul Mockapetris designed the replacement in 1983: the Domain Name System, a distributed, hierarchical, cached database in which authority is delegated along the dots, the root delegates com to one set of servers, com delegates example.com to its owner, and any resolver can find any name by walking the hierarchy. The familiar top-level domains, com, edu, gov, mil, org, net and the country codes, arrived in 1984 and 1985, and the first commercial registration, symbolics.com, was recorded on March 15, 1985. The DNS embodied the same architectural instinct as the rest of the stack, no central operator in the data path, authority distributed to those with the knowledge, caching for scale, and it remains among the largest distributed systems ever built. Numbers, meanwhile, needed a registrar, a role filled with legendary care by Jon Postel of the University of Southern California's Information Sciences Institute, who for nearly thirty years personally stewarded the address and protocol number registries as the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority and edited the RFC series. Operational adolescence brought the network's first systemic crisis. In October 1986 the internet suffered congestion collapse: as links saturated, hosts retransmitted aggressively, retransmissions worsened the congestion, and useful throughput between Berkeley and Stanford, sites 400 metres apart, fell by a factor of nearly a thousand. Van Jacobson's 1988 response wove congestion control into TCP itself: slow start, probing available capacity gradually; additive increase, multiplicative decrease, expanding gently and backing off sharply on loss; and using packet loss as the congestion signal. Every host voluntarily throttling itself by the same algorithm became, and remains, the invisible discipline that lets millions of independent parties share links no one owns, arguably the most consequential piece of cooperative software ever deployed. By decade's end the machinery of the modern internet, protocols, names, numbers, congestion control and the culture maintaining them, was operating at national scale.

sections.heading: Rival Visions: USENET, BITNET, Minitel and the Protocol Wars
sections.body: The internet's triumph was not foreordained, and through the 1980s it grew amid rivals embodying different philosophies of what networking should be. Grass-roots systems spread connectivity beyond ARPA's contract walls. USENET, begun in 1979 by Duke and University of North Carolina graduate students using the UUCP dial-up copying tools bundled with Unix, propagated threaded newsgroup discussions machine to machine each night, calling itself the poor man's ARPANET and reaching tens of thousands of sites; it gave the online world durable vocabulary, FAQ, flame, spam among it. BITNET, from 1981, linked university mainframes and gave academics LISTSERV mailing lists; FidoNet, from 1984, wove hobbyist bulletin board systems into a store-and-forward mail network over night-time phone calls; CSNET, funded by the National Science Foundation in 1981, brought computer science departments without defense contracts into email contact with ARPANET, an explicit on-ramp. The serious institutional rival was the world's telephone establishment. The international standards bodies of the carriers promoted X.25, a packet network service in which the carrier's network, not the customer's host, guaranteed reliability, a design faithful to telephone-company instincts about control and billing, and national public data networks such as France's Transpac ran it at scale. Its consumer showcase was France's Minitel, launched nationally in 1982: millions of free terminals, a directory, banking, travel booking and notorious chat services, a genuinely mass online medium a decade before the Web, but a centrally administered one in which offering a service meant contracting with the operator. Through the 1980s the officially anointed future was OSI, Open Systems Interconnection, a meticulous seven-layer protocol suite from the international standards world that governments, including the United States with its GOSIP procurement mandate, formally required, and which industry roadmaps assumed would replace TCP/IP. The internet community's counter-position was empirical: TCP/IP was running, free, and improving monthly. The decisive act had come in 1983 when ARPA funded the University of California, Berkeley, to build TCP/IP into its widely used BSD Unix distribution; 4.2BSD shipped with a solid, free networking stack and a clean programming interface, the sockets API, so every university department buying a Unix workstation, from Sun and its competitors, received the internet protocols as a default. Vendors implemented OSI in brochures and TCP/IP in products. By the early 1990s the contest was over, memorialized in David Clark's 1992 credo, rough consensus and running code, and in the community's joke that OSI was a beautiful description of a network that did not exist. The episode carries the history's clearest lesson: between an architecture optimized for administrative control and one optimized for permissionless growth, growth won, and the working implementation freely in students' hands beat the standard mandated by governments.

sections.heading: Ethernet, Workstations and the Local Area Explosion
sections.body: While the wide-area story unfolded, a parallel revolution in the office building created the demand that would make internetworking universal. In 1973 Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs at Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center designed Ethernet, a way to connect the computers of a single building over a shared coaxial cable at 2.94 megabits per second, adapting ALOHAnet's idea of transmitting whenever ready and recovering from collisions, refined with carrier sensing, collision detection and randomized exponential backoff. Ethernet's genius was its minimalism, no central switch, no allocated time slots, just a cable and a discipline, and it scaled with technology, standardized at 10 megabits in 1980 by a Digital, Intel and Xerox consortium and as IEEE 802.3 in 1983, later carried over telephone-style twisted pair, which made wiring offices cheap. Through the 1980s local area networks multiplied for reasons initially unrelated to the internet, sharing expensive laser printers and file servers among the new personal computers and engineering workstations. The IBM PC of 1981 put a computer on every professional desk; Sun Microsystems and its rivals sold Unix workstations that, thanks to Berkeley's BSD, spoke TCP/IP natively, and Sun's slogan, the network is the computer, captured the emerging assumption. Suddenly organizations owned dozens of internal networks, Ethernets, token rings, proprietary systems, and needed them joined: to each other across the campus, and to the wider world. Joining networks was precisely what IP had been designed for, and a market appeared for the gateway boxes the architecture called routers. Cisco Systems, founded in 1984 by Stanford staff members Leonard Bosack and Sandy Lerner to commercialize multiprotocol router software developed on campus, grew with the phenomenon into one of the defining companies of the era; competitors like Proteon and Wellfleet fought over the same boom. The campus pattern also settled the internet's addressing habits, subnetting arrived to let one organization's address block be divided among many internal networks, and the sockets programming interface from BSD became the lingua franca in which a generation wrote networked software. The local revolution mattered strategically for a further reason: it moved networking's center of gravity from a few dozen time-shared mainframes to millions of independently purchased machines, each of which made TCP/IP adoption a little more inevitable, since the protocols were the only ones implemented everywhere, on the PC, the workstation, the minicomputer and the router alike. When the National Science Foundation built its national backbone in the mid-1980s, it found a landscape of campus networks ready to plug in, and when the Web arrived a few years later, the wiring it spread across was already in the walls. The internet did not descend from the wide area to the desktop; it was pulled outward from a hundred million desktops.

sections.heading: NSFNET and the Road to Commercialization
sections.body: The internet's passage from military research project to public utility ran through the National Science Foundation. In 1985 the NSF funded five national supercomputer centers and, in 1986, linked them and regional university networks with NSFNET, a national backbone that opened internet access to the whole of American academia rather than only defense contractors. Demand instantly swamped its 56-kilobit lines; upgrades to 1.5-megabit T1 service in 1988 and 45-megabit T3 in 1991, operated by the Merit consortium with IBM and MCI, kept pace with traffic that doubled roughly every seven months. Around the backbone grew a three-tier ecology, campus networks feeding regional networks feeding the national core, and it was this NSF-fostered structure, not ARPANET itself, that carried the internet's first mass growth; the original ARPANET, obsolete and expensive, was quietly decommissioned in 1990, its sites absorbed into the newer fabric. One rule shaped everything: the backbone's Acceptable Use Policy, which, reflecting its research funding, forbade commercial traffic. The prohibition incubated a commercial industry anyway, since firms wanting TCP/IP service built their own networks, UUNET and PSINet among the first around 1989 and 1990, and in 1991 several of them formed the Commercial Internet Exchange, agreeing to interconnect and exchange traffic directly, settlement-free, entirely outside the government backbone, a template for the peering economics that still knit the internet together. Congress nudged the door open, with 1992 legislation allowing NSFNET to carry mixed-use traffic, and the NSF then planned its own exit with unusual grace: rather than privatize the backbone to one owner, it dissolved the monopoly entirely, specifying network access points where competing commercial backbones would interconnect, funding a routing arbiter, and, on April 30, 1995, switching NSFNET off. The internet's core became a competitive market, and traffic flowed on without interruption, the rare infrastructure privatization remembered mainly for how little drama it caused. The same years brought the public online through a different door. Consumer services, CompuServe, Prodigy and America Online, had grown as proprietary walled gardens with their own content and mail; competitive pressure forced them first to exchange email with the internet around 1992, then to offer full access, and AOL's carpet-bombing of free trial disks became the era's icon, delivering millions of households to the network between 1994 and 1996. Dial-up internet service providers multiplied from hundreds to thousands, selling modem access over ordinary phone lines at 14.4, then 28.8, then 56 kilobits per second. The regulatory context deserves note: American telephone regulators exempted these data calls from the per-minute access charges levied on voice carriers, a quiet subsidy that made flat-rate unlimited internet pricing viable and habituated a nation to being online for hours. By 1995 the pieces of a mass medium, competitive carriage, consumer on-ramps and open protocols, were assembled; what the medium would show was arriving simultaneously from Geneva.

sections.heading: The World Wide Web: CERN, Mosaic and Netscape
sections.body: The internet moved bytes; the Web made them legible, and its arrival converted a network of specialists into a mass medium in barely five years. Tim Berners-Lee, a British physicist turned software engineer at CERN, the European particle physics laboratory near Geneva, proposed in March 1989 an information management system for the laboratory's sprawling, ever-changing documentation, built on hypertext, the decades-old idea, prefigured by Vannevar Bush's 1945 essay As We May Think and named by Ted Nelson in the 1960s, of documents linked directly to other documents. His manager's written verdict, vague but exciting, authorized the side project. Working on a NeXT workstation through 1990, Berners-Lee with Robert Cailliau built the complete system: HTML, a simple markup language for pages; HTTP, a lightweight protocol for fetching them; the URL, a universal address naming any resource on any server; and the first server and browser-editor, the whole running over ordinary TCP/IP. Three design choices proved decisive. The Web asked no permission of a site owner to be linked; links could dangle, a broken link cost an error page rather than global consistency machinery, which let the system scale without coordination; and in April 1993 CERN placed the technology in the public domain, renouncing royalties, days after the University of Minnesota's rival Gopher system had spooked implementers by reserving the right to charge, a contrast that settled which system the world would build on. The remaining barrier was presentation, and it fell in February 1993 when Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina of the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois released Mosaic, a polished, easily installed browser that displayed images inline with text and soon ran on Windows and Macintosh, not just Unix. Web traffic on the backbone grew by thousands of percent within the year; servers multiplied from some two hundred in early 1993 to tens of thousands two years later. Andreessen decamped to Silicon Valley, co-founded Netscape with Jim Clark in 1994, and shipped Navigator, whose August 9, 1995 stock offering, a money-losing company reaching billions in valuation on its first trading day, rang the opening bell of the dot-com boom. Microsoft, initially dismissive, licensed Mosaic's code, shipped Internet Explorer, bundled it with Windows, and the ensuing browser war drove furious innovation, JavaScript, secure connections for commerce, style sheets, while the bundling became the centerpiece of the antitrust case United States versus Microsoft. Navigation itself became an industry: Yahoo began in 1994 as a hand-curated directory, AltaVista in 1995 demonstrated full-text search of the entire Web, and in 1998 two Stanford students, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, commercialized PageRank, ranking pages by the link structure of the Web itself, founding Google on the insight that the Web's own topology encoded human judgment about relevance.

sections.heading: Governance: IETF, ICANN and Who Runs the Internet
sections.body: A perennial question, who runs the internet, has a precise and surprising answer: nobody, and several bodies with narrow, mostly voluntary authority. Technical standards belong to the Internet Engineering Task Force, formalized in 1986 as the successor to the research task forces of the ARPA era. The IETF has no members, no fees and no votes; anyone may join a working group's mailing list, attend its meetings, and argue, decisions are taken by rough consensus, sometimes gauged by humming, and a standard becomes real only when independent implementations interoperate. Documents still issue as RFCs, edited in a series continuous with Steve Crocker's 1969 memo, and the culture's self-description remains David Clark's line about rejecting kings, presidents and voting. Oversight bodies, the Internet Architecture Board and the Internet Engineering Steering Group, exist to coordinate rather than command, and the World Wide Web Consortium, founded by Berners-Lee at MIT in 1994, plays the analogous role for Web formats. Names and numbers required something more institutional, because uniqueness demands a single root of allocation. For decades that root was, astonishingly, one man, Jon Postel, whose Internet Assigned Numbers Authority function at the University of Southern California allocated addresses and managed the DNS root under a chain of research contracts; the arrangement's fragility became undeniable as domain names acquired commercial value, trademark litigation erupted, and governments noticed that the root file of a global medium rested on a Californian contractor. After a heated international process, the Clinton administration's 1998 white paper produced ICANN, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers, a California nonprofit administering names and numbers through a multistakeholder structure of registries, registrars, governments in an advisory role, and users; Postel died weeks after its creation. Regional Internet Registries allocate address blocks on each continent; root DNS service is provided by thirteen named server constellations, operated by universities, companies, nonprofits and United States agencies, replicated worldwide by anycast into well over a thousand physical instances. The United States retained a residual contractual supervision of the IANA functions until 2016, when, over congressional objections, it transferred stewardship to the global multistakeholder community, ending formal governmental control of the root. The arrangement is perpetually contested. Authoritarian states and some developing countries have pressed, at the International Telecommunication Union and the United Nations, for intergovernmental control of internet resources, arguing sovereignty and equity; the multistakeholder camp replies that the network's value flows precisely from being governed by its operators and users rather than its regulators. Meanwhile, the governance that most shapes daily online life has migrated elsewhere entirely, into the terms of service of a handful of platform corporations, a form of private rule the founding institutions never anticipated and do not reach.

sections.heading: Broadband, Mobile and the Physical Internet
sections.body: The 1990s internet arrived through a screeching modem at up to 56 kilobits per second, an experience that rationed images and made video unthinkable, and the two decades that followed were dominated by revolutions in access. Broadband came first over existing wires: digital subscriber line technology squeezed megabits from ordinary telephone copper by using frequencies above the voice band, while cable television operators, using the DOCSIS standards from 1997 onward, turned their coaxial plant into shared data networks. Always-on connections changed behavior more than speed did, making the network ambient rather than a place one visited, and household penetration of broadband passed dial-up in the United States around 2004. Fiber to the home, pioneered at scale in Japan, South Korea and later by carriers and municipalities elsewhere, multiplied speeds toward gigabits. The second revolution was untethering. Wi-Fi, standardized as IEEE 802.11 in 1997 and popularized after 1999, dissolved the cable between laptop and wall; cellular data grew from the trickle of 2G GSM and GPRS through 3G, launched commercially in Japan in 2001, to the point where the January 2007 introduction of Apple's iPhone, followed by Android in 2008, fused the internet with the telephone. 4G LTE networks from 2009 made mobile bandwidth broadly comparable to home broadband, and sometime in the mid-2010s the majority of global internet use shifted to handheld devices; for billions of people in developing countries, the smartphone was and remains the first and only computer, making mobile networks the internet's true mass medium. Underneath these consumer layers, the physical and commercial geography of the network reorganized. Intercontinental traffic travels almost entirely through submarine fiber-optic cables, hundreds of them, hair-thin glass strands in armored hose on the seabed, whose landing points and occasional anchor-dragging breaks constitute real geopolitical chokepoints; satellites, including the low-orbit constellations of the 2020s, carry a growing but still small share, prized mainly where cables cannot reach. Content moved closer to users: content delivery networks, pioneered by Akamai from 1998, replicate popular data in thousands of locations so that a video streams from a server in your city rather than across an ocean, and the largest platforms built private global backbones and placed caches inside consumer providers' buildings. Internet exchange points, the shared switching fabrics where networks interconnect, multiplied into the hundreds worldwide, flattening the old three-tier hierarchy into a dense mesh in which most traffic takes short paths from nearby caches. The consequence is an internet physically unlike its diagrams: a map of today's traffic shows not a cloud of equal nodes but a small number of enormous content sources delivering, via oceanic fiber and city-block data centers, most of what humanity watches, a concentration with performance benefits and systemic risks that the founding architecture neither forbids nor addresses.

sections.heading: Security: The Morris Worm, Spam and the Crypto Wars
sections.body: The internet was designed by and for a community of colleagues, and its protocols assumed good faith: mail servers relayed anyone's messages, routers believed one another's announcements, and nothing in the architecture verified that a packet's stated source was true. The costs of that inheritance arrived in stages. On November 2, 1988, Robert Tappan Morris, a Cornell graduate student, released a self-replicating program that exploited flaws in common Unix services; intended, he said, to measure the network's size, a coding error made it reinfect machines aggressively, and within a day it had crippled several thousand of the internet's roughly sixty thousand hosts. The Morris worm ended the age of innocence, produced the first conviction under the new Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, and prompted the creation of the Computer Emergency Response Team at Carnegie Mellon, the first institution dedicated to coordinating vulnerability response. Nuisance scaled with commerce: unsolicited bulk email, named spam after a Monty Python sketch, had a 1978 precedent on ARPANET, but its modern era began in April 1994 when two immigration lawyers advertised across every USENET newsgroup, and by the 2000s spam constituted the large majority of all email, beaten back only by industrial-scale filtering. Attacks matured from vandalism to business, distributed denial-of-service floods from networks of hijacked machines, phishing for credentials, ransomware, and state espionage and sabotage, exemplified by the Stuxnet operation revealed in 2010. The infrastructure itself proved fragile against error and malice alike: in 2008 Pakistan Telecom, intending to censor YouTube domestically, announced YouTube's addresses to the world's routers and blackholed the service globally for hours, a demonstration of how much the routing system still runs on trust, and Dan Kaminsky's 2008 DNS cache-poisoning disclosure forced coordinated patching of the world's name servers. The defensive struggle was also legal and political. Strong encryption was regulated as a munition in the United States; Phil Zimmermann spent three years under criminal investigation for releasing the PGP mail-encryption program in 1991, and the government's 1993 Clipper chip proposal, encryption with a built-in government key escrow, was defeated by a coalition of technologists and civil libertarians in what became known as the crypto wars. Netscape's SSL protocol, introduced in 1995 to secure Web commerce and standardized as TLS, spread slowly beyond payment pages until Edward Snowden's 2013 disclosures of pervasive state surveillance triggered a mass migration: within a decade the overwhelming majority of Web traffic was encrypted in transit, aided by the free automated certificate authority Let's Encrypt from 2015. Later hardening efforts, DNSSEC for name integrity and route-origin validation for routing announcements, crept forward for years precisely because they require coordinated adoption across independent operators who capture little individual benefit. The pattern throughout is retrofit, identity, integrity and confidentiality bolted onto a fabric that assumed trust among a few hundred colleagues, imperfectly, expensively, and forever incompletely, which is why security remains the internet's largest unpaid debt.

sections.heading: Running Out of Numbers: IPv6, NAT and Ossification
sections.body: The internet's growth collided with a limit set in 1978: the 32-bit IP address, about 4.3 billion possible values, minus large early allocations handed out with research-era generosity, entire 16-million-address blocks to single American corporations and universities. Alarm formed in the early 1990s, and the engineering community responded on two tracks. The permanent fix was a new Internet Protocol, IPv6, standardized in 1998, with 128-bit addresses, some 340 undecillion of them, enough to number every grain of sand with room to spare, plus assorted modernizations. The temporary fixes were classless routing, which sliced address space more frugally, and above all network address translation, NAT, in which a household or company hides behind one public address while a router rewrites traffic for the private machines inside, using reserved private ranges such as the familiar 192.168 block. The temporary fixes worked too well. NAT became universal in home routers and later in carrier equipment, and because it postponed address exhaustion while requiring nothing of anyone else, the collective-action problem of migrating to IPv6, where the benefit accrues only when others also move, festered for decades. The central pool of IPv4 addresses at IANA ran dry in February 2011, the regional registries exhausted their free pools in the years following, and a market emerged in which IPv4 addresses trade for tens of dollars apiece, an absurdity for integers, yet IPv6, despite carrying an ever-growing share of traffic at large mobile and residential providers, still had not displaced its predecessor forty years after the problem was identified. Both protocols run side by side indefinitely, a permanent dual-stack compromise. The episode illustrates a broader affliction the community calls ossification. The original architecture assumed the network's middle was transparent, but decades of middleboxes, NATs, firewalls, load balancers, traffic inspectors, each making assumptions about what traffic looks like, mean that packets deviating from common patterns are silently dropped, so new transport protocols became effectively undeployable; proposals languished because they could not cross the installed base. The escape routes are instructive. Google's QUIC transport, standardized in 2021 as the basis of HTTP/3, reclaims innovation room by disguise: it runs atop UDP, which middleboxes pass, and encrypts its own control information so intermediaries cannot see, and therefore cannot ossify around, its internals. Encryption, adopted for privacy, thus doubles as an anti-ossification coating, restoring by stealth the end-to-end freedom the original architecture granted openly. The deeper lesson generalizes far beyond addressing: in infrastructure, the temporary patch that works becomes permanent, migrations lacking local incentives stall regardless of engineering merit, and flexibility, once lost to accumulated assumptions, must be re-purchased with cleverness. The internet's famous adaptability, these decades show, is not a law of nature but an asset that requires active, sometimes devious, defense.

sections.heading: Myths, Lessons and the Unfinished Network
sections.body: Every important technology accretes legend, and the internet's history closes properly by separating myth from mechanism. The nuclear-war myth contains a kernel and a confusion: Paul Baran's packet-switching studies at RAND were explicitly about surviving attack, but ARPANET itself was built to share expensive computers among researchers, and its architects spent careers correcting the embellishment; the design's robustness was a structural virtue inherited from Baran's mathematics, not the project's mission. The single-inventor myth dissolves on contact with the record, which shows distinct, indispensable contributions from Licklider's vision, Baran's and Davies's switching, Kleinrock's analysis, Roberts's program management, BBN's engineering, Cerf's and Kahn's internetworking, Postel's stewardship, Berners-Lee's Web, and thousands of RFC authors; Al Gore, mocked for a claim he never quite made, in fact sponsored the 1991 High Performance Computing Act that funded, among much else, the laboratory where Mosaic was written, earning him public thanks from Cerf and Kahn themselves. The inevitability myth is subtler: at multiple junctures, AT&T's refusals, the OSI mandates, Gopher's licensing stumble, CERN's royalty-free release, history could have branched toward a permissioned, carrier-controlled network of national Minitels, and the open outcome was contingent on specific choices worth understanding precisely so they can be defended. The genuine design lessons are few and deep. Layering with a narrow waist, everything over IP, IP over anything, let technologies above and below evolve independently for half a century. Pushing intelligence to the edges made innovation permissionless, which is why a dorm room could launch a global service. Rough consensus and running code beat committee anticipation. Trust assumptions embedded in infrastructure outlive the community that justified them, and retrofitting security costs orders of magnitude more than designing it. Temporary fixes are permanent. And openness is not self-sustaining: the network that decentralized publishing also enabled unprecedented concentrations of private power in platforms, clouds and content networks, while more than sixty states now filter, throttle or switch off their national internets at will, a fragmentation, sometimes called the splinternet, that the founders' protocols cannot by themselves prevent. What should a reader do with this history? Treat the internet as an artifact with owners of its choke points and institutions worth knowing, IETF, ICANN, the registries, not as weather; distrust claims that any current arrangement is technically necessary, since the record brims with necessities that weren't; and when evaluating proposals to remake the network, for security, for sovereignty, for child protection, for profit, ask the question this whole history sharpens: does the change preserve the property, edge innovation without permission, from which everything the internet gave us actually came. The experiment that began with the letters LO remains unfinished, and its next chapters will be written by people who either know this story or repeat it.

guides.title: History of Programming Languages
guides.summary: The story of programming languages from Ada Lovelace and machine code through FORTRAN, LISP, ALGOL, C, and the object-oriented and functional revolutions to the modern era of memory-safe, web-native languages, and the recurring forces that decide which languages live and die.

sections.heading: Why the History of Languages Matters
sections.body: A programming language is a notation for telling a machine what to do, but it is also something stranger: a crystallized theory of how humans should think about computation. Every language embodies opinions about what programs are made of, whether procedures, mathematical functions, objects exchanging messages, or logical assertions, and about how much the machine should be trusted to manage and how much the programmer must control. The history of programming languages is therefore not a parade of product releases but a running argument, seventy-plus years long, about the right way to bridge the gap between human intention and electrical switching. Knowing that history pays practical dividends. Thousands of programming languages have been created, with some catalogs listing near nine thousand, yet perhaps two dozen carry almost all the world's working code, and the reasons those particular languages won are rarely the reasons a newcomer would guess. Technical elegance predicts survival poorly; attachment to a platform people must use, an ecosystem of libraries, and the accident of timing predict it well. The ideas themselves, meanwhile, circulate on a much slower clock than the languages that carry them. Garbage collection, the automatic reclamation of unused memory, was invented for LISP in 1959 and reached the mainstream with Java in 1995, a thirty-six-year lag. Closures, pattern matching, type inference, and generics each spent decades in academic languages before appearing, to acclaim, in the popular ones, so a reader who knows where today's features came from can often see tomorrow's coming. History also explains the frustrations. Why do dates in some banking systems still pass through COBOL written before the Moon landing? Why does JavaScript, the language of the entire web, have equality rules programmers memorize like tax law? Why do buffer overflows discovered in 2026 trace to design choices Dennis Ritchie made in 1972? None of these are mysteries once the sequence of events is laid out; they are the fossil record of decisions that were locally sensible and globally permanent. Software is unusual among engineering artifacts in that its raw material, the language, is itself an artifact that someone designed under deadline, with incomplete knowledge, for hardware that no longer exists. Finally, the history is a story about people and institutions as much as syntax: a Victorian countess writing the first published algorithm for a machine that was never built, a Navy officer insisting computers could understand English-like words, committees in postwar Europe inventing the notation still used to define languages today, corporate laboratories tossing off world-changing tools as side projects, and lone designers whose personal taste, for indentation, for parentheses, for safety, became the daily habit of millions. This guide follows that story chronologically from the era before software through the great foundational languages of the 1950s, the structural revolutions of the 1960s and 1970s, the object-oriented and scripting waves, and the modern turn toward safety and concurrency, ending with the recurring patterns that decide why languages live and die.

sections.heading: Before Software: Looms, Engines, and the First Algorithm
sections.body: The idea of programming predates the electronic computer by more than a century, and it begins, oddly, in textiles. In 1804 Joseph Marie Jacquard demonstrated a loom controlled by chains of punched cards, each card's holes directing which warp threads lifted for one pass of the shuttle. The loom separated a machine's fixed mechanism from a changeable instruction sequence, and the punched card, a physical token of stored instructions, would carry data processing into the 1970s. Charles Babbage saw the implication. His Analytical Engine, designed from 1837 onward though never completed, was a general-purpose mechanical computer with a mill for arithmetic, a store for a thousand 40-digit numbers, card input for both operations and variables, and, crucially, the ability to branch conditionally and loop, the ingredients of universal computation. Ada Lovelace, daughter of the poet Byron and a mathematician tutored by Augustus De Morgan, translated an 1842 paper on the engine and tripled its length with her own notes. Note G contained a complete, stepwise procedure for computing Bernoulli numbers on the engine, tracing variables through each operation, and it is conventionally honored as the first published computer program. More prescient still was her observation that the engine might act upon things other than number, that it might compose music if the relations of pitched sounds could be expressed, together with her caution that the machine originates nothing and does only what we order it to perform, a claim debated to this day. Herman Hollerith made the card practical: his electric tabulators processed the 1890 United States census in a fraction of the expected time, and the company descended from his venture became IBM in 1924, ensuring the punched card was the incumbent medium when electronic computing arrived. The machines that arrived in the 1940s were programmed by hand at the most literal level. Colossus, operational at Bletchley Park in 1944 for breaking the German Lorenz cipher, was configured with switches and plugs. ENIAC, unveiled in 1946 with about 17,500 vacuum tubes, was programmed by physically routing cables and setting thousands of switches, a task taking days per problem, performed by a team of six women, Kathleen McNulty, Frances Bilas, Betty Jean Jennings, Ruth Lichterman, Elizabeth Snyder, and Marlyn Wescoff, whose pioneering work went largely uncredited for decades. The escape from plugboards was the stored-program concept, articulated in the 1945 First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC circulated under John von Neumann's name, drawing on work by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly and, more distantly, Alan Turing's 1936 theoretical universal machine: put the instructions in the same memory as the data, and the machine can load a new program in seconds, and programs can even manipulate programs. On 21 June 1948 the Manchester Baby ran the world's first stored program, 17 instructions hunting for a highest factor, for 52 minutes. From that morning forward, the machine was general; what remained primitive was the language, and the next decade would be spent climbing out of raw binary.

sections.heading: Assembly, Autocodes, and the Dream of Automatic Programming
sections.body: Programming a stored-program machine in the late 1940s meant composing instructions as raw numbers: opcodes and addresses in binary, octal, or on some machines a base-32 alphabet, entered on switches or paper tape. Programmers kept notebooks of numeric codes, and a misplaced digit could cost a night of machine time, which was often more valuable than the programmer's own. The first mercy was symbolic assembly: let the human write mnemonic operation names and symbolic labels, and let the machine translate them to numbers, one instruction each. The EDSAC team at Cambridge under Maurice Wilkes ran such a scheme from 1949, with initial orders that converted letter-coded instructions on the fly, and David Wheeler's technique for calling and returning from subroutines, the Wheeler jump, plus the first subroutine library, established reuse as a working practice; the 1951 textbook by Wilkes, Wheeler, and Stanley Gill was effectively the first book on programming. Assembly removed transcription pain but not conceptual pain: the programmer still thought in the machine's terms, one instruction at a time, and every new machine meant relearning everything. The bolder idea, called automatic programming, was to let people write in a notation closer to mathematics and have the machine translate wholesale. Konrad Zuse had sketched exactly this in wartime Germany: his Plankalkul, designed between 1942 and 1945 for his relay computers, included assignments, loops, conditionals, and structured data, arguably the first high-level language design, but it went unpublished until 1972 and unimplemented until 1998, a reminder that ideas without machines and institutions leave no lineage. In the United States, Grace Hopper, a Navy reservist and mathematician who had programmed the Harvard Mark I in 1944, joined the UNIVAC effort and built the A-0 system in 1952, which stitched subroutines together from a coded specification, followed by A-2 and the business-oriented FLOW-MATIC around 1955 to 1957, the first language to use English-like words for operations. Hopper popularized the word compiler and spent years arguing, against genuine skepticism, that programs could be written in something resembling language rather than arithmetic. Interpreted helper systems proliferated in the same years: John Backus's Speedcoding for the IBM 701 in 1953 simulated floating-point operations the hardware lacked, trading roughly a tenfold slowdown for enormously easier arithmetic, and Alick Glennie's Autocode for the Manchester Mark 1 in 1952 is often counted the first working compiled language, with Tony Brooker's more usable Mark 1 Autocode following in 1954. The obstacle to going further was not imagination but arithmetic economics: machine time was so expensive that professional programmers widely believed no automatic translator could generate code efficient enough to justify itself, and early systems mostly confirmed the prejudice. The stage was set for a demonstration project that would take efficiency as its explicit obsession, and it came from Backus's small team at IBM, whose product would show that the compiler skeptics were wrong and would still be running physics codes in the twenty-first century.

sections.heading: FORTRAN: Proof That Compilers Could Compete
sections.body: In late 1953 John Backus proposed to IBM a system that would let scientists write formulas and have the machine translate them into efficient code for the forthcoming IBM 704. The proposal's radical claim was economic: programming and debugging consumed up to half the cost of running a computer center, and a practical automatic system could cut that drastically, but only if the generated code ran nearly as fast as hand-written assembly, because otherwise the expensive machine would be wasted. The FORTRAN project, for FORmula TRANslation, thus became history's first serious optimizing compiler effort. The team of about ten, including Backus, Sheldon Best, Harlan Herrick, Irving Ziller, Robert Nelson, Roy Nutt, David Sayre, Richard Goldberg, Lois Haibt, and Peter Sheridan, spent over two years on translation techniques that remain textbook material: parsing arithmetic expressions with operator precedence, allocating the 704's three index registers by analyzing the frequency of execution of program regions, moving invariant computation out of loops, and Monte Carlo simulation of program flow to guide register decisions. When the system shipped to customers in April 1957, the results settled the argument. Programs that had taken weeks in assembly took hours or days in FORTRAN, program length dropped by an order of magnitude, and the object code commonly reached a large fraction of hand-coded speed, close enough that resistance collapsed; within a year a survey of 704 installations found over half of all instructions being produced by the compiler. The language itself, seen from today, was austere and machine-shaped. It offered arithmetic expressions, assignment, DO loops, subscripted arrays, subroutines and functions, arithmetic IF with three-way branching, GO TO, and formatted input and output; variables beginning with I through N were implicitly integers, a convention memorialized in the joke that God is real unless declared integer. Blanks were insignificant, an infamous trap: a period typed for a comma silently turns a loop header into an assignment, an error class connected in legend, somewhat inaccurately, to the loss of the Mariner 1 probe in 1962. What FORTRAN lacked, recursion, pointers, rich data structures, it compensated for with speed and with something new under the sun: machine independence. When FORTRAN was implemented on other machines, programs moved with tolerable effort, and the idea that a program could outlive its computer was born. Standardization followed through FORTRAN II with separately compiled subroutines in 1958, FORTRAN IV, then the American standards of 1966 and 1977, and later modernizations in 1990, 2003, 2008, and 2018 that added recursion, modules, array operations, and parallel features. The language never stopped working for a living: it remains a first-class citizen of high-performance computing, weather models, and the numerical libraries beneath much of scientific Python. Backus himself, characteristically restless, went on to co-invent the notation for defining languages and, in his 1977 Turing Award lecture, to attack the very style of word-at-a-time imperative programming FORTRAN epitomized, advocating functional programming instead, one designer thus bookending two eras of the field.

sections.heading: LISP: Computing with Symbols
sections.body: While FORTRAN aimed at formulas, John McCarthy at MIT wanted a language for reasoning, for the newborn field he had named artificial intelligence at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop. The result, LISP, for LISt Processing, designed in 1958 and running by 1959 with Steve Russell's crucial implementation work, was built on a single audacious simplification: represent everything, both data and programs, as nested lists of symbols. A list is written in parentheses, so the sum of two and the product of three and four is written as the list, plus, two, times, three, four, in fully parenthesized prefix form. Because a program is itself a list, programs can construct, inspect, and transform other programs as ordinary data, a property later named homoiconicity, and McCarthy's paper defined a universal function, eval, that interprets any LISP expression, an interpreter for the language written in about a page of the language itself. Alan Kay later called this the Maxwell's equations of software. Around that kernel LISP accumulated a startling number of firsts. It had recursion as the natural mode of computation and conditional expressions that returned values, both of which McCarthy pushed into other languages via the ALGOL committee. It had first-class functions, built on Alonzo Church's lambda calculus from the 1930s, so functions could be passed and returned like numbers. It had dynamic typing, values carrying their types at run time. And to manage list cells that programs created freely, McCarthy's team introduced garbage collection in 1959: the system itself finds memory no longer reachable and reclaims it, freeing the programmer from manual deallocation, at the cost of periodic pauses that critics would cite for decades. The interactive read-eval-print loop, the REPL, made LISP a conversation with a running system rather than a batch submission, pioneering the exploratory style that notebooks and consoles universalized much later. LISP became the working language of artificial intelligence for thirty years, powering symbolic mathematics in Macsyma, early natural-language and planning systems, and the MIT hacker culture; dedicated LISP machines from Symbolics and LMI in the 1980s put the language in hardware, then died with the AI winter at that decade's end. The language radiated dialects: MacLisp and Interlisp in the 1970s, Scheme in 1975, in which Gerald Sussman and Guy Steele distilled LISP to a tiny core with lexical scoping and proved elegant enough to anchor the influential textbook Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, Common Lisp standardized in 1984 to unify the industrial dialects, and, in 2007, Clojure, which set LISP on the Java virtual machine with immutable data structures for concurrency. The parentheses that outsiders mock are the price of the macro system insiders prize: because code is data, a Lisp programmer can extend the language itself, defining new control constructs indistinguishable from built-ins. LISP's deepest legacy, though, is as the field's idea bank; garbage collection, closures, dynamic typing, conditionals as expressions, metaprogramming, and the REPL were all withdrawn from it, usually decades later, by languages that put them in front of millions.

sections.heading: COBOL and the Business of Data
sections.body: Scientific computing got FORTRAN in 1957, but the larger market, payroll, inventory, billing, insurance, had no comparable tool, and each manufacturer was sprouting incompatible business languages. In April 1959 a meeting at the University of Pennsylvania, followed by a request to the Department of Defense, convened the Conference on Data Systems Languages, CODASYL, with a mandate to define one common business language. The short-range committee drew on existing designs, above all Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC, the only English-like business language actually in customer use, and IBM's proposed COMTRAN, and delivered COBOL, the COmmon Business Oriented Language, in December 1959; compilers from RCA and Remington Rand ran the same program in December 1960, a deliberate demonstration of the portability that was the whole point. Hopper, whose advocacy of English-like programming shaped the enterprise and who served as a technical adviser, became known, with some simplification, as its grandmother. COBOL's design choices look eccentric today but were reasoned. Programs are organized into four divisions, identification, environment, data, and procedure, separating machine-dependent details from logic. Syntax approaches stylized English, add overtime to gross-pay giving total, in the hope, only partly realized, that managers and auditors could read programs. Its greatest technical strength lay in the data division: hierarchical record descriptions with picture clauses specifying the exact layout of every field, and native fixed-point decimal arithmetic, which represents money exactly where binary floating point cannot, a matter of legal significance when accounts must balance to the cent. The language was verbose by design, sixty-odd reserved words in the original, and it omitted the recursion and dynamism academics prized, for which Edsger Dijkstra delivered the famous verdict that its use cripples the mind. The market disagreed. Backed by the Defense Department's refusal to lease computers without it, COBOL became the most widely used language in the world by the 1970s and held the title for years. Estimates in the 2000s credited it with a couple of hundred billion lines of live code processing a large share of the world's business transactions, and surveys during the COVID-19 unemployment surge of 2020, when American state governments publicly appealed for COBOL programmers to shore up benefit systems, suggested the figure had grown, not shrunk. The Y2K episode was its most public moment: two-digit year fields, a rational economy in the era of costly storage, threatened miscalculation at the century rollover, and a worldwide remediation effort costing hundreds of billions of dollars combed through COBOL portfolios line by line; the near-absence of disasters is cited both as proof the panic was overblown and as proof the remediation worked. Successive standards in 1968, 1974, 1985, 2002, which added object orientation, and 2014 modernized it, but COBOL's real lesson for language history is sociological: software embedded in institutions outlives fashion, critics, and often its own authors, and replacement is so risky and expensive that working systems simply persist, which is why banks still run, and quietly hire for, a language older than the microchip.

sections.heading: ALGOL: The Language That Shaped Languages
sections.body: No language did more to define what programming languages are than one that barely achieved commercial use. In the late 1950s, European and American computing societies, each fearing a Babel of national and corporate languages, convened a joint committee to design a universal algorithmic language.
