The 1958 Zurich meeting produced a preliminary design, and the January 1960 Paris meeting, whose thirteen participants included John Backus, John McCarthy, Alan Perlis, Peter Naur, and Friedrich Bauer, produced ALGOL 60, described in a report of about seventeen pages that is among the most influential documents in computer science. Its first innovation was in how it was defined. Backus had proposed, and Naur refined, a formal metalanguage for specifying syntax, now called Backus-Naur Form or BNF, in which each grammatical category is defined by production rules over symbols. For the first time, a language's syntax was a mathematical object: parsers could be derived from it systematically, compiler construction became a discipline rather than a craft, and the entire theory of formal languages and parsing that followed, through Chomsky hierarchies to parser generators like yacc, had a practical anchor. Every language reference manual that defines syntax in a grammar is imitating the ALGOL 60 report. The language's second contribution was structure. ALGOL introduced block structure: statements grouped by begin and end, with variables declared inside a block visible only there, enabling nested scopes and making lexical locality a fundamental principle of program organization. It made recursion available in a mainstream imperative language, with procedures that could call themselves, over resistance from committee members worried about implementation cost, and the resulting technique of stack-based activation records became the universal runtime model. It offered two parameter-passing modes, call by value and the subtle, ultimately abandoned call by name, whose surprising behaviors, exhibited in Jensen's device and in the difficulty of writing a simple swap procedure, taught the field how deep parameter semantics run. Typed declarations, compound statements, if-then-else as both statement and expression, and for loops rounded out a notation so clean that for two decades algorithms in journals were published in ALGOL as a matter of course; it was the language of thought even where FORTRAN was the language of work. Commercially it lost, in America almost totally, for mundane reasons: IBM had FORTRAN, the report deliberately omitted input and output, leaving each implementation incompatible at the edges, and there was no sponsoring vendor with a machine to sell. Its successor ALGOL 68, a technically ambitious but famously complex design, split the committee, provoking a minority report and the departure of Niklaus Wirth and C. A. R. Hoare, who took the simplicity faction's convictions into Pascal and into decades of writing on software reliability. Hoare's later remark that ALGOL 60 was an improvement on almost all of its successors is only half a joke: through Pascal, C, Simula, Ada, and their descendants, virtually every mainstream language today is, in skeleton, an ALGOL, with block structure, lexical scope, recursion, and BNF-defined syntax as its inheritance.

sections.heading: The 1960s Ferment: BASIC, PL/I, APL, and Simula's Objects
sections.body: The 1960s multiplied languages in every direction, and four of that decade's creations mark the field's diverging ambitions. BASIC, the Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code, went live at Dartmouth College at 4 a.m. on 1 May 1964, created by John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz with undergraduate labor to serve a radical institutional vision: every student, not just scientists, should use the college's time-sharing system. BASIC's numbered lines, plain keywords like PRINT and GOTO and INPUT, and instant feedback made it the first language designed foremost for learners, and when microcomputers arrived in the late 1970s, a BASIC interpreter in read-only memory was the standard face of the machine; an entire generation, including the founders of Microsoft, whose first product was Altair BASIC in 1975, met computing through it. IBM's PL/I, also of 1964, embodied the opposite philosophy: one language to serve both scientific and business computing for the new System/360 family, absorbing features of FORTRAN, COBOL, and ALGOL into a huge whole, with exception handling and concurrency besides. It found real use, but its scale defeated the unification dream, teaching a durable lesson about kitchen-sink design. Kenneth Iverson's APL, published as a notation in his 1962 book A Programming Language and implemented in 1966, compressed computation on whole arrays into single expressive symbols on a special keyboard, so a line of APL could replace pages of loops; famously terse, adored by finance and actuarial users, it planted array programming, which lives on in J, k, MATLAB, R, and the NumPy conventions beneath modern data science. The decade's most consequential invention, though, came from Oslo. Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard, building discrete-event simulations of ferries, harbors, and queues at the Norwegian Computing Center, found ALGOL's procedures inadequate for modeling many concurrent entities, each with its own state and behavior. Their Simula 67 introduced the class, a template combining data with the procedures that operate on it; the object, an instance created from a class; subclassing, letting a specialized class extend a general one; and the virtual procedure, letting a subclass override behavior so that the right version is chosen at run time. These four ideas, class, object, inheritance, and dynamic dispatch, are the complete kernel of object-oriented programming, invented not as software ideology but as simulation necessity: a ship in a harbor model simply is an object with its own state. Simula remained a niche language, but its readers changed the world: Alan Kay absorbed it into Smalltalk, Bjarne Stroustrup missed its expressiveness so acutely that he grafted it onto C, and through those channels Simula's model became, by the 1990s, the industry's default way of organizing software. Meanwhile the systems-programming lineage quietly seeded: Martin Richards's BCPL of 1967, a typeless simplification of the Cambridge CPL project, traveled to Bell Labs, where Ken Thompson pared it into B, the immediate parent of C, connecting this decade's ferment to the next one's revolution.

sections.heading: Structured Programming, Pascal, and C
sections.body: By the late 1960s software had a crisis officially: the 1968 NATO conference at Garmisch adopted the term software engineering to name the gap between what was promised and what shipped, as projects like IBM's OS/360 devoured budgets. Edsger Dijkstra's March 1968 letter to the Communications of the ACM, published under the editor's title Go To Statement Considered Harmful, crystallized one diagnosis: unrestricted jumps produce programs whose runtime behavior no human can track, spaghetti whose correctness cannot be reasoned about. The structured programming movement he led argued that all control flow should be built from sequence, choice, and repetition, which the 1966 Bohm-Jacopini result showed is always possible, and more deeply that programs should be developed with their correctness argument, by stepwise refinement. The movement needed a teaching vehicle, and Niklaus Wirth supplied it. Fresh from the ALGOL 68 split, where he had championed simplicity, Wirth designed Pascal in 1970: a small, rigorously typed ALGOL descendant with records, sets, enumerations, and pointers, meant to teach disciplined program construction. Its strict compile-time type checking caught whole classes of errors before execution, and its portable implementation, a compiler emitting P-code for a simple abstract machine that anyone could implement, spread it to microcomputers; through the 1970s and 1980s Pascal was the introductory language of universities and, in Borland's Turbo Pascal of 1983, priced at 49.95 dollars with an integrated editor and compiler of astonishing speed, a mass-market phenomenon, later evolving into Delphi. Wirth continued through Modula-2 and Oberon, preaching lifelong that reliability comes from simplicity. The same years produced structured programming's worldly twin. At Bell Labs, after the withdrawal from the Multics project, Ken Thompson wrote the first Unix on a scavenged PDP-7 and a language, B, derived from BCPL; when the PDP-11 arrived with byte addressing, Dennis Ritchie extended B with types, characters, structures, and pointer arithmetic, producing C in 1972. In 1973 Thompson and Ritchie rewrote the Unix kernel itself in C, an act of consequence rivaling any language design: it demonstrated that an operating system, the most machine-bound of programs, could be written almost entirely in a portable high-level language, and thereafter Unix and C spread together through universities, each advertising the other. C's philosophy was trust and economy: it is close to the machine, with arrays as thin sugar over pointers, no bounds checking, no garbage collection, and undefined behavior wherever checking would cost cycles, and it assumes the programmer knows what they are doing. The 1978 book by Brian Kernighan and Ritchie, a model of terse exposition, and the ANSI standard of 1989 fixed the language, and it conquered systems programming permanently; kernels, databases, interpreters, and embedded firmware are C country today. The bill for the trust arrived later: buffer overflows and memory corruption, the direct fruit of unchecked pointers, became the dominant security vulnerability class of the internet era, the Morris worm of 1988 exploiting exactly such a flaw, a trade-off the industry is still unwinding half a century on.

sections.heading: Smalltalk, C++, and the Object-Oriented Wave
sections.body: Object orientation was invented in Oslo, but it grew up in Palo Alto. Alan Kay, arriving at Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center in 1970 with a vision of a personal Dynabook for children, conceived programming as biology rather than mechanism: a system should be built from cells, objects, each hiding its interior and communicating only by messages, so that complexity stays local. Smalltalk, developed by Kay, Dan Ingalls, Adele Goldberg, and colleagues through versions 72, 76, and the released Smalltalk-80, made everything an object, integers, classes, even the control structures, which are messages carrying code blocks, and it ran inside a live graphical environment of overlapping windows, menus, and a bitmapped display that the team invented alongside the language, with a browser for exploring and changing any class in the running system. The famous 1979 Xerox PARC demonstrations to Apple, which influenced the Lisa and Macintosh, carried the interface to the world; the language itself carried the pure message-passing model into Objective-C, which Brad Cox created in the early 1980s and which NeXT and then Apple made the language of the Macintosh and iPhone, and into Ruby and the design wisdom of a generation. Kay later insisted the big idea was messaging, not classes, a distinction the industry largely ignored. The version of object orientation that actually conquered industry came from Bell Labs by a different route. Bjarne Stroustrup, who had used Simula for his Cambridge doctoral simulations and found it expressive but ruinously slow, resolved to add Simula's classes to C without sacrificing a cycle of C's performance. C with Classes appeared in 1979, renamed C++ in 1983, with virtual functions, operator overloading, references, and later multiple inheritance, exceptions, and templates; Stroustrup's governing rules were the zero-overhead principle, that you pay only for what you use, and compatibility, that existing C code and programmers must carry over. Placed as a superset of the industry's dominant language, C++ spread through the late 1980s and 1990s into operating systems, databases, telephony, finance, and games, everywhere performance mattered and abstraction was craved. Templates, added for type-safe containers, turned out to be a Turing-complete compile-time language, spawning generic programming and the Standard Template Library of Alexander Stepanov in 1994, a triumph with a price in error messages of legendary opacity and a language whose full rulebook few humans hold. The object wave crested culturally in the 1990s: methodologies, modeling notations culminating in UML, the 1994 Design Patterns book by Gamma, Helm, Johnson, and Vlissides cataloging reusable arrangements of classes, and the marketing of everything as object-oriented. The hangover followed: deep inheritance hierarchies proved brittle, shared mutable state proved hostile to concurrency, and the 2000s counsel became composition over inheritance, with later languages like Go and Rust pointedly declining implementation inheritance altogether. The lasting residue is undramatic and universal: encapsulated state behind interfaces, and dynamic dispatch where behavior varies, are simply how software is organized now, in whatever paradigm's clothing.

sections.heading: Functional and Logic Programming: ML, Prolog, and Haskell
sections.body: While objects conquered industry, two other paradigms matured in the academy, and their ideas would arrive in everyone's languages a generation later. Functional programming treats computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions: no assignment statements mutating variables, no side effects hiding in procedures, just values flowing through expressions, an inheritance from Alonzo Church's lambda calculus and from LISP. Its modern form crystallized around Robin Milner at Edinburgh in the early 1970s. Building LCF, a system for machine-checked mathematical proof, Milner needed a metalanguage in which only valid proofs could be constructed, and the safety had to come from types; the result, ML, introduced the type discipline that defines the family. ML's types are inferred, not declared: the Hindley-Milner algorithm deduces the most general type of an expression automatically, so programs carry full static safety with almost no annotation. Its algebraic data types let a programmer declare that a value is one of several shaped alternatives, a tree is a leaf or a node with two subtrees, and pattern matching takes such values apart by shape, with the compiler warning when a case is forgotten, a mundane-sounding feature of enormous practical worth. ML grew into Standard ML and the French dialect OCaml, in 1996, which found industrial niches in finance and in compiler construction; Milner received the Turing Award in 1991. Logic programming went further still from the machine: state facts and inference rules, and let the system search for solutions. Prolog, created in Marseille by Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel in 1972 with theoretical foundations from Robert Kowalski, computes by unification, matching terms containing variables against each other, and backtracking through alternatives; a Prolog program for family relationships or scheduling reads as a set of logical clauses, and the same relation can run forward or backward. Prolog became the banner language of Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Systems project, launched in 1982, a national bet that logic machines would leapfrog conventional computing; the project's disappointing end by 1992 chilled the paradigm's prospects, though Prolog's descendants thrive quietly in constraint solving, scheduling, and database theory, and Datalog enjoys a modern revival. The functional line's purest expression came by committee: in 1987, researchers tired of a dozen incompatible lazy functional languages convened to define a common one, and Haskell, named for the logician Haskell Curry and first defined in 1990, became the field's laboratory. Haskell is lazy, evaluating expressions only when their values are demanded, which permits infinite data structures and new composition styles, and it is pure, isolating all side effects, input, output, mutation, inside a type-level construct called the monad, worked out by Philip Wadler and others, so that effects are visible in a function's type. For years its unofficial motto was avoid success at all costs, yet its exports are everywhere: type classes begat Rust's traits and Swift's protocols, its option and result types became mainstream error handling, and lambdas, map, filter, and immutability-by-default are now ordinary practice in Java, C#, JavaScript, and Python, the quiet triumph of a paradigm that never needed to win by market share.

sections.heading: Scripting and the Web: Perl, Python, Java, and JavaScript
sections.body: The late 1980s and 1990s shifted the center of gravity from computation to connection, and the languages of that shift were built for gluing systems together and for the newborn web. Larry Wall, a linguist by training working as a Unix administrator, released Perl in 1987 to unify the shell's ad hoc text tools; with first-class regular expressions, associative arrays, and a cheerfully permissive philosophy summarized as there is more than one way to do it, Perl became the duct tape of the early internet, powering the CGI scripts behind the first generation of dynamic websites. Guido van Rossum began Python as a Christmas hobby project in 1989, releasing it in 1991: a language whose signature design choice, using indentation itself to delimit blocks, enforced readable layout, and whose batteries-included standard library and gentle learning curve made it the lingua franca first of scripting, then of scientific computing through NumPy and SciPy, and ultimately of machine learning; the painful decade-long migration from Python 2 to the incompatible Python 3, completed around 2020, became the standard cautionary tale about breaking a language community's code. Yukihiro Matsumoto's Ruby, from 1995, optimized for programmer happiness in a pure object model, and exploded globally when David Heinemeier Hansson's Rails framework in 2004 showed a database-backed website could be built in an afternoon; Rasmus Lerdorf's PHP, also 1995, grew from personal homepage tools into the language running most of the web's server pages, WordPress and early Facebook included, proof that deployment ease can outweigh design polish. The year 1995 was the hinge. Sun Microsystems launched Java that May: a C-syntax, garbage-collected, class-based language compiling to bytecode for the Java Virtual Machine, promising write once, run anywhere. Conceived by James Gosling's team for set-top boxes and repositioned for the web via browser applets, Java found its real home on servers and in enterprises, where the JVM's portability, threads, and steadily world-class garbage collectors and just-in-time compilers made it the backbone of business systems, later of Android, and the host of a family of successor languages. Meanwhile at Netscape, Brendan Eich wrote a scripting language for web pages in roughly ten days in May 1995; management required it to look like Java, so the LISP-and-Self-inspired design wore C-family syntax and, in a pure marketing maneuver, the name JavaScript, despite no meaningful relation to Java. Standardized as ECMAScript in 1997, it carried unusual ideas into the mainstream, prototype-based objects, closures everywhere, functions as values, alongside hasty-birth quirks in coercion and equality that developers memorize defensively. Being the only language in every browser proved decisive: after Google's 2008 V8 engine made it fast, Node.js in 2009 took it to servers, and JavaScript became by many measures the most widely used language on Earth, the fulfillment, in an ironic key, of the universal-language dream, achieved not by design excellence but by exclusive possession of history's largest platform.

sections.heading: The Managed Era and the Concurrency Reckoning
sections.body: The 2000s belonged to managed runtimes, virtual machines with garbage collection and just-in-time compilation, and to a hardware shock that rearranged language priorities. Microsoft, after a legal battle with Sun over its Java implementation, built its own platform: the .NET Common Language Runtime and C#, designed by Anders Hejlsberg, the creator of Turbo Pascal and Delphi, and released in 2000-2002. Beginning as a close Java relative, C# evolved fast, adding generics that survive at runtime in 2005, language-integrated query in 2007, and, in 2012, the async and await keywords for writing asynchronous code in straight-line style, a construct so successful that JavaScript, Python, Kotlin, Swift, and Rust all adopted it. The JVM meanwhile became a hosting platform in its own right: Martin Odersky's Scala, from 2004, fused object-oriented and functional programming with an ambitious type system and later became the language of the Spark data-processing engine; Rich Hickey's Clojure brought LISP with immutable persistent data structures in 2007; and JRuby, Groovy, and eventually Kotlin confirmed that a great runtime can outlive any single syntax. The shock arrived mid-decade. For thirty years, programs sped up automatically as clock frequencies rose; around 2004-2005, heat ended that, and manufacturers turned to multiplying cores instead. Herb Sutter's 2005 essay The Free Lunch Is Over named the consequence: software would now gain speed only through concurrency, and the dominant languages were dangerously bad at it, their model being threads sharing mutable memory guarded by locks, a regime of data races and deadlocks that resists both testing and reasoning. The search for safer models revived old ideas. Erlang, built by Joe Armstrong, Robert Virding, and Mike Williams at Ericsson in 1986 for telephone switches, had long embodied one: thousands of tiny isolated processes sharing nothing, communicating by messages, supervised so that failures are restarted rather than prevented, let it crash; its AXD301 switch reported availability with nine nines, and the model resurfaced in Scala's Akka library and Elixir, Jose Valim's 2012 Ruby-flavored language on the Erlang virtual machine, which powers messaging at WhatsApp scale. Google answered with Go in 2009, designed by Rob Pike, Ken Thompson, and Robert Griesemer with a deliberate poverty of features: fast compilation, one obvious way to do things, garbage collection, and concurrency via goroutines, lightweight threads multiplexed by the runtime, and channels for communication, under the slogan do not communicate by sharing memory, share memory by communicating, drawing on Tony Hoare's 1978 Communicating Sequential Processes. Go became the language of cloud infrastructure, Docker and Kubernetes both written in it. The era also exposed a self-inflicted constraint: CPython's global interpreter lock, which allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, pushed Python's scientific stack toward process pools and native extensions, and efforts to remove the lock stretched into the mid-2020s, a reminder that a language's implementation decisions, made casually in one decade, can bind a community in the next.

sections.heading: The Safety Turn: Rust, Swift, Kotlin, and TypeScript
sections.body: The defining movement of the 2010s was the industrialization of safety: taking guarantees long confined to research languages and packaging them for working programmers on the platforms where they already lived. The motivating data was security. Studies published by Microsoft and by Google's Chrome team around 2019 independently reported that roughly seventy percent of their serious security vulnerabilities were memory-safety bugs, the buffer overflows, use-after-free errors, and data races endemic to C and C++; the languages of systems programming were, statistically, the internet's largest attack surface. Rust was the direct response. Begun by Graydon Hoare as a personal project in 2006, sponsored by Mozilla from 2009, and reaching a stability-committed 1.0 in May 2015, Rust achieves memory safety without garbage collection through ownership: every value has exactly one owner, responsible for freeing it; values may be borrowed either by many readers or one writer, never both at once; and the compiler's borrow checker enforces these rules at compile time, rejecting programs that could dangle a pointer or race on shared data. The learning curve is real, fighting the borrow checker is a rite of passage, but the payoff is C-class performance with mathematical exclusion of the dominant bug class, and the endorsements accumulated: Rust entered the Linux kernel as an approved language in 2022, Microsoft and Google announced migrations of sensitive components, and the United States government's 2024 technical reports formally urged new products toward memory-safe languages. The same logic played out on the platforms. Apple introduced Swift in 2014, Chris Lattner's replacement for Objective-C: optionals force nil-handling into the type system, value types curb shared mutation, and automatic reference counting manages memory predictably, modern safety without leaving the Apple toolchain. JetBrains released Kotlin 1.0 in 2016, a concise JVM language whose types distinguish nullable from non-nullable references, retiring at a stroke the null-pointer exception that Tony Hoare, who introduced the null reference in ALGOL W in 1965, had called his billion-dollar mistake; Google blessed Kotlin for Android in 2017 and made it the preferred language in 2019, and its coroutines brought structured concurrency to the mainstream. The web's version of the safety turn was gradual typing. TypeScript, designed at Microsoft by Anders Hejlsberg once again and released in 2012, layers a static type system over JavaScript that compiles away entirely: any JavaScript is already TypeScript, teams adopt types file by file, and the type checker plus editor tooling catch errors across million-line codebases that dynamic typing left to runtime. Within a decade TypeScript became the default for large web development, and its success, alongside Python's type hints from 2014 and typed Ruby efforts, settled an old argument with a compromise: dynamic languages for reach and speed of writing, optional static types for scale. The common thread of the decade is unmistakable: languages stopped competing mainly on expressiveness and began competing on what classes of error they make impossible, a criterion by which the industry, after fifty years of shipping memory corruption, had finally decided to shop.

sections.heading: Why Languages Live and Die: Patterns and Lessons
sections.body: Seventy years of language history repeats its plots often enough to extract the mechanics. The strongest force is platform attachment: a language wins when it is the natural or only way to program something people must program. C rode Unix, JavaScript owned the browser, Objective-C and Swift owned the iPhone, Kotlin rode Android, Ruby rode Rails, and FORTRAN and COBOL rode the installed bases of scientific and business computing; conversely, elegant languages with no captive platform, ALGOL foremost, become influential ancestors rather than survivors. The second force is ecosystem gravity. Programmers choose languages for the libraries, and every package written deepens the moat; Python's dominance in machine learning owes less to syntax than to the compounding weight of NumPy, pandas, and the frameworks built on them, and modern package managers, from Perl's CPAN in 1995 through npm, PyPI, and crates.io, institutionalized this compounding. Third is the sponsor: languages need sustained funding and stewardship through their unprofitable adolescence, and the graveyard is full of well-designed orphans. Fourth is familiarity economics: C++, Java, C#, JavaScript, and TypeScript all wore C's syntax to lower switching costs, and gradual adoption paths, TypeScript over JavaScript, Kotlin beside Java, consistently beat rip-and-replace. The failure modes mirror the successes. Complexity kills: PL/I and ALGOL 68 collapsed under their own ambition, and Ada, the Defense Department's rigorously specified 1983 language, mandated for defense work until 1997, was resented as heavyweight and thrived only in its safety-critical niche, though its SPARK subset quietly verifies avionics to this day. Breaking the community's code kills slowly, as Python 2-to-3 and Perl's decade-lost Perl 6 project demonstrated. Losing the platform kills fastest of all: Flash's ActionScript vanished with the plugin, and Visual Basic 6, among the most-used languages on Earth in 2000, was orphaned by its own vendor's transition to .NET. Yet the deepest lesson is the longevity asymmetry: languages almost never die once embedded in institutions, they merely stop being fashionable, and FORTRAN, COBOL, and C, all older than most working programmers, still run the substrate of civilization, which means language choices are effectively permanent and deserve the seriousness of infrastructure decisions. For a practitioner choosing today, history counsels: choose the ecosystem and the platform, not the syntax; prefer boring, well-stewarded languages for long-lived systems; expect any code that works to outlive its assumptions; and learn languages from different paradigm families, since ideas migrate and the functional or logic concept that looks academic now is the mainstream feature of 2035. Looking forward, honest humility is required. The safe bets are continuations of visible trends, memory safety spreading, types becoming gradual and inferred, concurrency models maturing, WebAssembly loosening the browser's single-language monopoly. The open question of the 2020s is what large language models that generate code do to the discipline: whether they entrench today's incumbents, whose training data dominates, or finally make translation between languages cheap enough to unfreeze the installed base. History suggests only that the change will be slower than promised, faster than comfortable, and settled by platforms and economics rather than elegance.
